title: Nazianzen's cry for peace and the apostolic charge to cherish Protestant church peace
english: Preface — Peaceful and Apologetic. In the name of the Lord.
Preface to the Kind Reader.

With what sighs Gregory Nazianzen — most eloquent of the Greek Fathers after Chrysostom — once panted for Peace, pouring out these words in the tenth of his Orations (which is the third On Peace): O dear Peace, you who are a good praised by all, yet kept by few! Why, I ask, have you deserted us for so long already? When will you return to us?

By the same vows and complaints — or ones like them — the Ecclesiastical Peace of the Evangelicals, long and deeply desired by all who profess the Truth in Charity, comes to be pursued by me as well in this present season, and with even greater right. For a huge throng that boasts rashly enough of the Gospel of Peace we daily find not only despising and utterly neglecting that peace (a charge that, to our heavy grief, fits even some among the Reformed), but moreover harassing certain Lutherans — who with proud and dictatorial brow claim plain Universal Orthodoxy for themselves alone and their like — with futile and sometimes infamous scenes and with the scrapings of scurrilous satires and infamous pamphlets, and ignominiously spitting even on the bare name of this Peace, as if the sound itself struck fear, with quips and sarcasms.

So much so that if ever, now especially — though many nonetheless are wiser — all who love God in Christ, the supreme Prince of Christian Peace, must set themselves with steadfast mind to the promotion and defense of that Peace, and must repeat again and again, and commend again and again to each and every Evangelical of both parties, that apostolic charge: If therefore there is any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any affection and compassion, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind. Do nothing from rivalry or from empty glory, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others ([[Philippians 2:1-4 >> Bible:Philippians 2:1-4]]).

translator_notes.text: Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 10 (third On Peace); Strimesius cites the Latin form of the peace apostrophe.
Prefatio §I retained; densify adds Prefatio §II, Crimina heads, and Part I Protheoria opening. Whole 1708 folio (~1221 pp) not claimed.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit 'illud Apostolicum' quotation of Phil 2:1-4 in the Latin.

title: Called at Frankfurt an der Oder in 1679 to weigh controversies only by Scripture toward Protestant peace
english: As for me: as soon as, by divine providence and by the grace of the Great Frederick William of most blessed and immortal memory — the Brandenburg hero and, if anyone ever was, while he lived the most sincere esteemer and unwearied assertor and promoter of the Evangelicals' ecclesiastical peace — I obtained my lot among the cultivators of the heavenly vineyard in this most celebrated University in the year 1679, and had surveyed more than enough the weight of the Protestant controversies, I held nothing more important than this:

not to serve the base itch of certain theologians of one party or the other for quarreling and somehow defending their own cause, but to hang and weigh everything on the balance and scale of the Holy Codex alone — which reveals and first establishes not only theological truths, but also the widely varied degrees of their value and necessity, and which diligently and continually praises Christian love, gentleness, mildness, moderation, and tolerance.

According to the measure of theological knowledge and prudence, and according to the public office granted me by God — dedicated not only to the Frankfurt church through preaching labors, but also to the Christian church at large through professorial labors — I would strive conscientiously everywhere to consult for that one Protestant Peace which is of all things most necessary and most useful.

translator_notes.text: Frederick William the Great Elector of Brandenburg (d. 1688), named as patron of Protestant ecclesiastical peace.
Francofurtana = Frankfurt an der Oder (Viadrina), not Frankfurt am Main.

title: Prefatio §II: From the 1687 Tract on Ecclesiastical Peace to Critica Concionatoria and the Scultetus irenic exchange
english: § II. — Thus it came about that, after nearly two lustra — that is, in the year of the last century eighty-seven — almost by lot, a little Tract on Ecclesiastical Peace appeared, set forth by me in the form of a Preface to the Themes of the blessed Cornelius Bergius, once my predecessor in this chair, re-edited for the sake of our theology students; soon to be transferred into the vernacular by order of my superiors; adorned also in Batavia with a most friendly preface by a certain most learned man, and reprinted there in the year 1689; and having met with the varied fortune that men's — and especially theologians' — diverse pursuits produce,

I judged that for a time I ought to refrain from offering further that pearl of Ecclesiastical Peace — not indeed cast by me before swine, or prostituted to dogs — and turned my mind to other sacred labors: exegetical and didactic, and elenctic upon many controversies after the pattern of Spanheim's Elenchus, and practical as well, both privately upon the Holy Decalogue of God and outwardly (so-called by abuse) upon the Methodology of adorning the preacher.

From that last occasion there went forth into public light, a few years ago, my Critica Concionatoria, interspersed here and there with certain strictures and pacific persuasions, and received kindly enough even by many Lutheran brethren (as the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig for the year 1700 testify) — especially by the late Daniel Severinus Scultetus, theologian of Hamburg, not undistinguished among the learned of our time for excellent and pacific booklets.

To him, therefore — since he had supplied me so convenient and the more welcome an occasion the more unexpected it was — I could not in good conscience fail to publish a most gentle Irenic Epistle, devoted solely to fostering his so pious zeal for Peace. The excellent man replied with a special Tract titled On the Universal Diffusion of the Reformed, courteously inscribed to my name; and at that time I thought I ought to rest content with it, lest I irritate in any way a well-disposed mind by being forced to answer something of that more prolix kind of writing (not immune to rather frequent repetitions), which would more easily have dragged us both away from the Counsels of Peace into litigation — especially when he was lending his labor more to the theological truths themselves (about which for two centuries already men had disputed in vain with the greatest contention of mind) than to the weight and moment of those truths.

translator_notes.text: Prefatio §II densify: 1687 Tractulus de Pace Ecclesiastica (preface to Bergius themes), 1689 Batavia reprint, then Critica Concionatoria and the Scultetus irenic exchange. Spanhemianus = Spanheim elenctic pattern.
Honest partial: Prefatio §II career narrative only in this section; Prefatio Crimina defenses and remainder of the 1708 folio remain.

title: Prefatio §II: The 1703 threefold Pacific Writing, Lutheran approvals, and the Hexads' hostile reception
english: And the more willingly did I prescribe this quiet acquiescence to myself, because, stirred by this same man, I was meditating other Pacific Writings, from which it would be easy for him and for other theologians of the Lutheran party to judge that the Protestant controversies had hitherto been at least unduly multiplied and exaggerated (not to say anything heavier) by certain doctors of a quarrelsome temper especially, since on the Foundation of the Faith both parties entirely agree — of which I was already then most fully convinced in conscience, and afterward more and more fully confirmed; and my whole reply to be rendered to the most distinguished Scultetus would have aimed solely at proving that very point.

Exactly according to the counsel just set out, there came forth in the year 1703 a twofold Pacific Writing: one of them, exposing Dogmatically the Consensus of Lutherans and Reformed in the Foundations of the Faith; the other, Paradigmatically, through the example of the Consensus of Sandomierz, recommending Protestant Union; and a little later a Third supervened, On the Nature and Character of the Union to Be Kept, with an annexed most gentle Response — as was fitting — to the judgment of a certain most upright Lutheran doctor concerning the first of those three little tracts of mine, a doctor who at last in this very year has publicly professed his most celebrated name.

And although all these Three Writings of mine were also approved by the ballot of other most excellent Lutheran doctors besides the most learned Leipzig reviewers of March 1705 (as the most distinguished Cap. Calvor, known even among foreigners, most recently reports in the latest and most praised Consultation he has written On Entering into Ecclesiastical Peace among Protestants, p. 439, himself also voting for the same, both in what immediately precedes and elsewhere, especially pp. 30 and 31 of his Appendix — I pass over in silence for now Johann Fabricius, distinguished alike in theological knowledge and prudence, both in his most clear-sighted Consideration of his Controversies and in his most modest Defense of that Consideration);

yet there have not been wanting others also — especially after those three writings, all pertaining to the Fundamental Consensus of Protestants, had been followed by certain most gentle Hexads of mine, published in Academic fashion and submitted to public inquiry, merely setting out the Protestant Dissensus Beyond-the-Fundamentals — who, though never injured by me with so much as a word, either directly or indirectly through others' sides, were nonetheless so stirred with passion and stung by the gadfly of anger and envy that they rushed upon me and upon all my writings indiscriminately, not once or twice but in almost countless turns and ways, without measure or end, so that they must seem to have abstained from no manner of injury whatever.

translator_notes.text: 1703 duplex Scriptum Pacificum + third on Union; Leipzig / Calvor / Fabricius approvals; Hexades on Dissensus Praeter-Fundamentalem drew hostile fire.
Sendomiriensis = Consensus of Sandomierz (1570). Praeter-Fundamentalem = beyond / other-than the fundamentals.

title: Prefatio: Three Crimina charged — Supper consensus, oral manducation as cannibalism, and Sandomierz cruelty
english: But now I must return from the digression into the road; and those thicker clouds of the gravest accusations which my bitterest Adversaries pour out — not yet to be named by me, and without even designating the places and writings that fill and infect them, lest even so I should be said to have done them injury and, by uncovering their nakedness, to have exacted revenge (their words meanwhile being recited, and by them easily recognized) — now come to be calmly discussed, the rest vanishing into air by their own lightness. They are three in number:

FIRST, they charge me in a strange way with this: that I dared to assert that a Fundamental Consensus in the Doctrine of the Holy Supper really obtains between Lutherans and Reformed; and that, using Beza's words, I said the Body of Christ is as far from the Sacred Supper as Heaven is from Earth.
SECOND, with a great imprecation they accuse me of having imputed to their Forum the dogma of the Oral Manducation of Christ's Body and the Drinking of His Blood as Anthropophagy and Theophagy.
THIRD, they paint me as crueler than Nero himself, chiefly on this ground: that I have praised the Sandomierz Consensus of the Evangelicals, whose patrons they boast behaved cruelly toward Lutherans.

translator_notes.text: Three Crimina heads only — Strimesius's full replies occupy later Prefatio §§; densify stops at the charge-list before the long defenses.
Beza cited by adversaries: Corpus Christi a Coena ... tam procul ... quam a Terra Coelum.

title: Part I Protheoria: Controversies with Augsburg Confession theologians — six shared Evangelical fundamentals
english: The Principal Controversies with the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession, as they are called.
A Historical and Catallactic Protheory.

Although most unwillingly we also reckon these theologians among those with whom there is serious religious dissent, we do so for no other end than that beginners may not be ignorant what those Heads are by which the unhappy divorce of minds, of studies, and of churches is fostered.

While for both sides: 1. There is the same Rule, the same Principle — namely Holy Scripture — human and Papal traditions and the Tridentine Decrees being rejected by equal suffrage; 2. For both, the same Fundamental Doctrine, so often acknowledged and set out in the Harmony of Confessions — namely as to the Causes of our salvation, whether Efficient or Meritorious; as to the Person of Christ the Lord, the Truth and Union of the Natures, His Office and Benefits; and finally as to the gratuitous mode of Justification, far from merits or the causality of Works; 3. For both, the same Worship of the one true and Triune God, and of Christ the God-man, far from all Idolatry and Superstition or adoration of the Creature; and the same duties of the Christian man toward God and neighbor required for Sanctification; 4. For both, the same Protestation against Papal Errors even in the Head of the Holy Eucharist, against all Papal Idolatry, foul Superstitions, the Roman Hierarchy, savage Tyranny, impure Celibacy, and idle Monasticism; 5. For both, the same duties of forbearing love handed down ([[Ephesians 4:2 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:2]]) in those things which are built upon the foundation — taught indeed in diverse ways by them, yet with this foundation itself unmoved and unshaken; 6. Finally for both, the same interest, the same cause, the same motives for restoring Evangelical peace, and if not entire Concord, at least mutual and fraternal Tolerance, to be ratified forever.

From which there would certainly flow a happier propagation of the Gospel; the triumph of Evangelical Truth; a stronger assault upon Antichrist, and at last his fall; the repression of Tyranny daily waxing strong; the frustration of Jesuit schemes; the assertion of Protestant Liberty, today tottering; the removal of the heaviest Scandal from their midst; a new daily increase of Church and Commonwealth; the exultation at last of all the pious; the conversion of Schismatics; and even an easier drawing of the Greek Churches to the Unity of Faith and Spirit, which the Bohemian Churches had long ago attempted.

translator_notes.text: Part I tip: Praecipuae Controversiae cum Augustanae Confessionis Theologis — Protheoria Historica et Catallactica (reconciling).
Harmonia Confessionum = Harmony of Confessions. Inline Ephesians 4:2 for forbearing love / anexikakia.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit Ephes. iv. 2 in the Latin for forbearing love.

title: Part I Protheoria: Peace attempts from Marburg to Cassel, and Cassel's consensus on essentials
english: This business of Evangelical Consociation or Tolerance was usefully attempted at times, and is certainly to be attempted as a duty: first in the Marburg Colloquy, A.D. 1529, between Luther and Zwingli and those of another opinion — the Most Serene Landgrave of Hesse promoting pious Concord as far as in him lay, Melanchthon, Oecolampadius, Bucer, Jonas, A. Osiander, and others also being present — with little happy success, Luther with his own pressing too hard that Christ is corporally present in the Eucharist. Afterward the business was resumed in the Wittenberg Convention, A.D. 1536, Bucer and Capito then promoting it; a peace not destined to last while Luther lived, resting on Bucer's rather ambiguous Confession, Melanchthon writing the Formula. The same matter was acted, and more happily, in the Convention of Sandomierz, A.D. 1570, confirming a covenant among the associates of the Augsburg, Bohemian, and Helvetic Confessions.

Worthy of due praises in my judgment is the Cassel Convention, under the auspices of Wilhelm VI, Landgrave of Hesse, between the Marburg and Rinteln theologians, in the year 1661. There both sides agreed, in best faith, afterward repeated and confirmed, both in general concerning Consensus in the Essentials and the manner of preserving it, and in particular concerning the several Articles still in controversy.

And in general those venerable men pronounced on both sides: 1. That the Evangelicals agree on the Foundation of Faith and Salvation; that the controversial questions do not at all touch that Foundation, much less remove or overturn it; and that neither party thereafter, because of some difference, should cut the other off from fellowship or condemn them, and so on. 2. That for promoting that Consensus the remaining controversies ought either not to be treated in the churches from the pulpit, or certainly with the utmost modesty if necessity plainly required it — with no mention of dissenters, no harshness of words, no forced consequences, but only the declaration of truth from Scripture.

In particular, as to the Article of the Holy Supper, both Parties agreed that the Spiritual manducation of Christ's Body is altogether necessary to salvation and to the saving use of the Sacrament; and that otherwise the dissent between them as to the necessity of fraction and as to the oral manducation of Christ's Body, even by the mouth of an Unbeliever, is not such as would overturn the foundation of Salvation or shake the substance of the Sacrament. As to the Articles of Predestination, Grace, and Free Choice, they agreed: that after man's fall there are no residual powers left in him for spiritual good; that the whole business of human salvation depends on the Divine will, good pleasure, and grace; and that damnation is decreed to be inflicted on no one except because of sins. Controversies remained, but to be placed outside the census of fundamentals.

translator_notes.text: Historical chain: Marburg 1529, Wittenberg 1536, Sandomierz 1570, Cassel 1661 (Wilhelm VI of Hesse; Marburg vs Rinteln).
Cassel consensus on essentials, Supper, Predestination/Grace/Free Choice. Honest partial — Protheoria opening only; rest of Controversies and Part II remain.

title: Prefatio: Why the three Crimina are cited — not to litigate, but to show the necessity of one defense
english: IV.

Thus far I have brought forward the three most atrocious Accusations forged against me by the council of my Adversaries, collected from three Lutheran Doctors (those Orthodox ones, of course, who cannot err), framed in their own words. Not, to be sure, with a mind either to litigate with them about these things and proceed to empty or impious quarrels, or even to try to excuse myself before those most rigid Judges of mine after the sentence already passed against me by them (for that would be nothing else than imprudently and incautiously to provoke a heavier sentence against myself); but partly so that it may become known to a benevolent Reader, free from prejudices and passions, how hostilely they have invaded me, and with what atrocity — never having been injured by me — two of them, not even known to me by name before, have tried to tear the fame of a most innocent neighbor and to divert onto me the just indignation of the whole Lutheran Church (which, as holding directly and entirely the Foundation of the whole Christian Faith, I have always held ought to be pursued with fraternal charity), if what they said were true; partly so that I might show that I did not snatch at an occasion, but that the hardest necessity of snatching it was imposed on me — once only, and never hereafter — of alleging my Deeds and Words and of laying them before everyone's eyes, from which my adversaries have blushed at no one in sucking so much venom against me.

title: Prefatio Crimina I prior part: Fundamental Supper consensus defended from Reformed confessions and doctors
english: So then, as to the PRIOR PART of the FIRST CRIMINATION: Ah! how grave and hard a matter is here brought forward — namely, that I labored to this end: that it should be established that a Fundamental Consensus in the Doctrine of the Holy Supper really obtains between Lutherans and Reformed. I confess freely that I most earnestly gave myself to that work; but what crime is there in this, when, fully convinced in Conscience in this cause, I so acted, and may be understood to have so acted?

For when from the Confessions of the Reformed in part — the Anglican, Gallican, Brandenburg (Marchica), and Torun — and in part from the most evident expositions of many doctors of the Reformed Church, both older (Calvin, Bucer, and Zwingli himself) and more recent (Forbes, Trelcatius, Cosin, and others), brought forward everywhere in my writings and in those of the Lutherans themselves, it can be doubtful to no one (except to him who, against Christian Charity that hopes all things, calls into doubt all their faith and sincerity) that the Reformed sincerely believe and confess a real and substantial Presence of Christ's Body itself — not of the bare Virtue and Efficacy of that Body — and that Presence as preceded even by the Faith of the Communicants themselves, and accordingly a like Manducation, yet both Spiritual and Supernatural, not Corporal and Dimensional and Oral: what more can be wanting or desired, so that they may be understood to conspire Fundamentally with the Lutherans in the Doctrine of the Lord's Supper?

Does it belong to the Foundation of the Christian Faith to believe that Christ's Body is present in the Holy Supper also Corporaliter — that is, in a corporal and dimensional mode — and likewise manducated Oraliter, in a Corporal and Oral mode? But such a Presence and Manducation of Christ's Body many among the Lutherans themselves, at least the Scriptural ones, deny to be real — much less that they believe them, or require them to be believed, concerning the faith and the foundation of the Christian faith. Indeed all those Lutherans who, with Luther, teach that Christ's Body is present in the Holy Supper neither by Inclusion in the bread, nor by Descent from heaven and Ascent into the same, nor by Ubiquity (which slipped from Luther only once, and from which he afterward judged he should abstain — as the Helmstadt theologians note everywhere, adding that the Ubiquity dogma damns the novelty itself and all the remaining inhabitants of East and West for error) — inculcating only the Coexistence of Christ's Body with the Eucharistic bread, and indeed not so much with the bread as with the Communicants — a Coexistence admitted also by all those Reformed who contend that the Sacramental Signs are not nude-significant, but exhibiting of the things they signify, even Substantial ones. And this, as far as I know, all the Reformed to a man do; and by this very thing they interpret Christ's definitive Eucharistic proposition, "This is my body" (however you take its Subject as the Complex of bread and body), as remaining improper and synecdochic, through this of theirs: "This bread signifies — that is, exhibitively — my Body"; or: "This bread is the exhibiting Sign of my Body" — most evidently declaring the Eucharistic Complex from a heavenly and an earthly thing (what Thomas Pierce, the Reformed theologian, in his Pacificatorio Orthodoxo, called the AGGREGATE, and what is to be held as the prow and stern of the truly Lutheran sentence in this place).

translator_notes.text: Marchica = Brandenburg Confessio Marchica. Toruniensi = Consensus associated with Torun Thorn.
Thomas Pierce, Pacificatorio Orthodoxo — Strimesius cites Pierce AGGREGATUM for the heavenly–earthly Eucharistic complex.

title: Prefatio Crimina I posterior J.VI: The Beza–Calvin heaven-from-earth charge answered from the Scultetus letter
english: J. VI.

The POSTERIOR PART of the FIRST CRIMINATION — by which the accuser said I had written that Christ's Body is farther distant from the Holy Supper and from the blessed bread of the Holy Supper than the heaven of heavens is from the terraqueous globe — is convicted of the most open falsehood by the mere repetition of my own words by which I am judged to have so written. For thus the words of my Letter written to Scultetus run:

I for my part take it upon myself in turn to require and solicit you, most distinguished Scultetus — you who have solicited me about many things and obtained my assent — that both you and the venerable Calixtus may judge the sincere and clear mind of the Reformed in this cause to be that which one of you adduced from blessed Calvin's Institutes, Book IV, chapter 17, section 9, in these words: Whatever can serve to express the true and Substantial Communication of the Lord's Body and Blood, which is exhibited to the Faithful by the Sacred Symbols of the Supper, I gladly receive — and that in such a way that they are understood to perceive it not with imagination alone or the intelligence of the mind, but to enjoy it in very deed as food of eternal life. Reconcile the harder voice of Calvin commonly Beza, thrust out precipitately in the Consensus with the Zurichers as Doctor Calixtus says — that the Body and Blood of our Savior are at that time, when the Sacred Eucharist is administered, distant from us by as great an interval of places as heaven is situated from earth — with the immediately recited words of the same Calvin, so that there he may be held to have spoken of the Crucified Body of Christ, and here of the Glorious. The Glorious, or Glorified, Body of Christ, according to the Sentence of Calvin and the Reformed, is in the heavens, sitting there at the right hand of the Father, to return thence to judge the living and the dead; but the Crucified Body of Christ is most present in the Eucharist. For this is the sincere and clear Sentence of the Reformed concerning the Lord's Supper which I dare to weigh in the name of them all: that All Believers who receive and manducate the blessed Bread receive and manducate the Crucified Body of Christ; and that the same account holds of the consecrated Wine; but that the Mode by which it comes about that Christ's crucified Body and His shed Blood are really present to Believers in the Sacred Supper and are in very deed received, eaten, and drunk by them, we do not know, and that that Mode is Hyperphysical.

Did I then truly assert that Christ's Body is farther distant from the Holy Supper and the blessed bread of the Holy Supper than the heaven of heavens is from the terraqueous globe? When, namely, I asserted: (1) that the Crucified Body of Christ is most present in the Supper; (2) that this is the sincere and clear Sentence of the Reformed concerning the Lord's Supper — that All Believers who receive and manducate the blessed bread receive and manducate Christ's crucified Body, and that the same account holds of the consecrated wine; (3) that the Mode alone by which it comes about that Christ's crucified Body and His shed Blood are really present to Believers in the Holy Supper, and are in very deed received, eaten, and drunk by them, we do not know; and that that Mode is Hyperphysical.

Let it be permitted to add now: even if perhaps the Lutheran Doctors universally all hold which nevertheless I would somewhat doubt that Christ's Body which is now present in the Supper is Christ's glorified Body, and therefore, as to qualities, other than that which was present to the disciples in the first Supper — that is, humbled and near to Crucifixion, or about to be crucified — called by Christ Himself given didomenon (Luke 22:19), and by Paul broken klomenon (1 Corinthians 11:24) — contrary to what I hold, who have asserted that Christ's Body, as crucified more than as glorified, is present in the Holy Supper Substantialiter nevertheless, though Spiritualiter; by that very fact, because I most clearly maintained in one and the same place that Christ's crucified Body, as crucified, is present in its Substance Spiritually, that is, and therefore Sacramentally in every Holy Supper — by what face, I ask, can I be said to have opined that Christ's Body is farther distant from the blessed bread of the Holy Supper than the heaven of heavens from the terraqueous globe? Nor does it obstruct that I meanwhile believe, led by the Apostles' Creed, that Christ's Body ascended into heaven, sits there at the right hand of God the Father, and will someday return thence to judge the living and the dead. For I believe all this, with very many Lutherans, concerning the Corporal, Local, and Dimensional Presence of Christ's Body in Heaven, having never denied the Spiritual and therefore Sacramental Presence of the same Body of Christ in the Holy Supper, but most sincerely, with God granting, ready to confess it to the last breath of life.

translator_notes.text: Strimesius quotes his own Irenic Letter to Daniel Severinus Scultetus; the harder heaven-from-earth voice is the Calvin/Beza wording from the Consensus Tigurinus, distinguished as about the Glorious Body locally in heaven versus the Crucified Body most present in the Eucharist.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit didomenon citation for the first-Supper body.

title: Prefatio Crimina II J.VII opening: The anthropophagy charge answered from the Disputation on the Supper
english: J. VII.

There follows the SECOND CRIMINATION impacted on me by the Adversaries, by which I am said to have agitated the Eucharistic Doctrine of the Lutherans as Anthropophagy and Haematoposia — abominable to God and to men — in my Disputation on the Lord's Supper, and to have traduced it impiously and profanely, as Architect of a sly Union; which very thing is judged fit to be vindicated by no goose-quill style, but by a Tartarean spear. Even this imputation itself — to be held utterly foreheaded, and scarcely to be expected in that manner from a barbaric Tartarus — I will nevertheless never vindicate by any injurious word against the Author; I must dissolve it by the allegation of my own most innocent words, which run thus:

A third kind of arguments to be opposed, namely, to the CORPORAL AND ORAL Manducation of Christ's Body, which, the Lutherans themselves confessing, is not Scriptural flows from the nature of the Manducation itself to be instituted in the Holy Supper: which, if it is stated as a CORPORAL AND ORAL Manducation of Christ's Body, is found to be of such a kind that it could not have been instituted by Christ, because it induces Anthropophagy and Haematoposia, abominable to God and to men (Leviticus 7:26; 17:14).

From these words it is conspicuous: (1) that I carefully guarded not only lest anyone attribute Anthropophagy and Haematoposia to the Lutherans, but also lest I call the Lutherans' Eucharistic Doctrine — even concerning the Corporal and Oral Manducation of Christ's Body and Drinking of His Blood — a saving Anthropophagy and Haematoposia, and that for this sole cause, that they deny it to be such; while nevertheless holding that this Doctrine of the Lutherans concerning the Corporal and Oral Manducation of Christ's Body and the corporal and oral Drinking of His Blood contains Anthropophagy and Haematoposia, provided that, on the one side, the Body and Blood of Christ are the body and blood of a true man, and on the other side, Corporal and Oral Manducation and Drinking complete a true and proper Manducation and Drinking. (2) that I said only this: that the Manducation of Christ's Body if it be held Corporal and Oral is found to be of such a kind that it could not have been instituted by Christ.

translator_notes.text: Strimesius quotes his own Disputation de Coena Domini; the charge turns his reductio of corporal-oral manducation into an accusation that he branded Lutheran doctrine anthropophagy.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit citation against blood-drinking in the Disputation quotation.
Explicit paired citation with Leviticus 7:26 in the same Disputation quotation.

title: Prefatio Crimina II remainder: Anthropophagy reductio, Capernaism, and the reverse charge of making God author of sin
english: From these words it is conspicuous — completing what was begun above under (2) — that the Manducation of Christ's Body, if it be held Corporal and Oral, is found to be of such a kind that it could not have been instituted by Christ, because it would induce Anthropophagy and Haematoposia; and that every Anthropophagy and Haematoposia without distinction, without any limitation anywhere made in the Holy Scriptures, is held abominable to God and to man (Leviticus 7:26; 17:14).

So then it would scarcely be lawful for a Reformed man to draw any consequences — even those contained in the most evident manner in explicit propositions — if those consequences should happen to press upon the Lutheran Doctrine; nor indeed without adding the imputation of consequences not acknowledged by the Lutherans, which imputation I have warned again and again in what precedes to be otherwise less lawful. And therefore I have also judged that not even a Partial Capernaism, likewise contained in the Corporal and Oral Manducation of Christ's Body, ought to be attributed to them.

Conversely it will be free for the Lutherans to elicit anything from anything, and to transcribe upon the Reformed with impunity whatever blasphemies they please — and among them all the greatest, that God is the Author of sin (a charge the Reformed hold abominable, detest in the highest degree, and never cease to execrate) — blasphemies never to be vindicated from them even by a goose-quill style, much less by a Tartarean spear (from which kind of revenge all the Reformed justly abhor)?

translator_notes.text: Capernaism recalls the John 6 Capernaum hearers who took eating Christ's flesh carnally; Partial Capernaism is Strimesius's label for a corporal-oral reading short of full cannibalism.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit citation that unrestricted blood-drinking is abominable.
Paired with Leviticus 7:26 in the same reductio.

title: Prefatio Crimina III §.VIII opening: The Sandomierz cruelty charge and the Synod's clash with a single contradictor
english: §. VIII.

But we hasten on to the THIRD and greatest of all the CRIMINATIONS — belonging almost solely to my first and most vehement Accuser — who, alas!, indulges too much his envy and his unjust and tumultuous zeal, by which he is rather often carried off into various things less becoming a Christian man, especially a theologian, so that not seldom he appears to have laid down his shield even in the most manifest distortions. He takes it ill that I set forth and recommended the Sandomierz Consensus as an Example of the Ecclesiastical Union of Evangelicals — than which none more excellent is given, and by which the Polish Evangelicals once coalesced so closely that they all but held every sacred thing in common, and neither Reformed living among Lutherans nor Lutherans living among Reformed feared, when occasion was given, to use and enjoy one another's sacred Sermons and Administrations of the Sacraments, while for the rest they proposed to one another, where need was, the most modest discriminations of beyond-fundamental Doctrines, without any party detractions, through charitable informations and conferences — persisting most amicably in such Consociation for more than half a century (as we proved by a just computation of the time from when the Consensus began to when it was afterward disrupted by certain well-known Firebrands, in the Preface vindicating the Consensus and prefixed to its repeated Edition).

Accordingly, that he might hurt me, the Adversary arraigns both the Sandomierz Consensus and me its Herald as guilty of utterly monstrous Cruelty and Tyranny, on this sole ground: that when a certain Contradictor interposed against this Consensus — and after the Synod had dealt with him both publicly and privately, as one reclaiming against the Consensus and unwilling to foster Concord with the other Churches — a certain tumult arose (as Hartknoch reports), and he experienced the threats of a certain Polish Politician, made with the scimitar after the manner of the Nation.

Yet even without my reminding him, anyone sufficiently understands that nothing can fall away from or be detracted from the Consensus of so many Evangelical Churches, unanimously entered, and from its just praises, merely because one sole Pastor reclaimed against it; nor can the whole Synod, otherwise peaceably agreeing, justly be charged with cruelty because, when a large enough handle had been given by the obstinate contradiction of one man shouting against all, some one of the Nobles — especially of the Poles, among whom liberty sometimes degenerates into Polish license — threatened him with the scimitar beyond the mind and will of the Synod.

translator_notes.text: Christoph Hartknoch's Polish church history is Strimesius's cited narrative source for the Synod tumult and scimitar threat; Gericius the contradictor is named in the next defense section.

title: Prefatio Crimina III defense: Ignorance of the threat, praise for Consensus itself, and abhorrence of violence
english: Nevertheless (that, for Conscience before God Most High who searches hearts and kidneys, I may here defend even my innocence in the face of the whole Protestant Church) this must be said by me in this place:

(1.) That concerning that threatening accident which happened in the Sandomierz Synod, I knew nothing before I was preparing an Edition of that Consensus and prefacing it; nor had I read Hartknoch's History so attentively as to take account of that threatening deed — and that because, in vindicating the Sandomierz Consensus, I had to dispute not against Hartknoch, a mere Historian, but against Hornbeck's Lutheran theological Opponent, who in particular neither mentions those threats nor alleges Hartknoch or his Ecclesiastical History in a single word. Nor, if I had read and observed the fact, could I have stood safely enough on the man's credit (since more than once he has been caught by others writing from mere affections and disordered love of his Sect); nor, even if I had been free to rest securely on that Man's relations, would I have needed to attend to that accidental deed in this place, since — that very thing being left intact, posited, and even conceded — it would still remain open to me for the rest to honor the Sandomierz Consensus with due praises for many other excellent things. Just as it is also praiseworthy on this account: that by the unanimous votes of both Evangelical Parties it brought it about that Gericius, the importunate Disturber of the Consensus, was suspended from his office — Peace no less than Truth commanding him — and was also to be coerced by other Ecclesiastical penalties. So Hartknoch (p. 905): Gericius remained of his opinion, and because he would not let himself be moved either by entreaty or by threatening words, he was, with the consent of all present (Lutherans equally with Reformed), suspended from office, and it was resolved that he should be taken into custody and excommunicated. That this itself was decreed by the suffrages of all present — Lutherans as well as Reformed, Clergy as well as Politicians — apart from that Man's grave insolence having merited such a censure, can seem probable to no one.

(2.) That I celebrated and raised with due praises the Sandomierz Consensus under no other name than that of the Consensus itself and of the various circumstances and qualities of this Consensus, set out in express words in my Preface — not under the name of certain intervening threats of one Noble, and he perhaps a Lutheran (since the Lutherans present in the Synod urged that Consensus no less than the Reformed). Those threats meanwhile, if they happened (let the credit rest with Hartknoch), I grieve from the heart; so far am I from approving them, much less from judging that any praise can accrue to the Synod from their having arisen.

(3.) All who know me know that I so abhor every violence and truculent mode of proceeding — even by the very nature and temperament of my body — that there is nothing I detest and turn from with my whole breast more. Especially in Christian Ecclesiastical business, which I have sufficiently understood to rest on the authority and revelation of God alone, and so not to be thrust upon an unwilling man's Conscience; and most of all in the Dissensus of Lutherans with Reformed, which I (unlike the adversary, who for that reason rushes upon all else and sacrifices me together with all Calvinists even to Satan's most cruel violence and Tyranny) hold by fully convinced conscience to be beyond-Fundamental, and toward which not merely common but fraternal love is to be kept. Hence I may Christianly boast that, having lived among Lutherans for the greater part of my life, I never had to be reconciled with any of them, but have conversed hitherto most amicably with many, both Doctors and Hearers, and as fellow-members with me of one Christian Religion may by their own right, from Christ's own law, demand of me. I invoke as witnesses both the present Inhabitants of this whole City and, by name (one who has since migrated elsewhere), the celebrated and never-suspected-by-anyone of even the least neglect of Lutheran Orthodoxy Most Rev. Dr. Wegner, most deserving Professor of Theology at Königsberg, after he already nearly three years ago wished his testimony of this kind concerning me to be copied out even in public types, through express letters written to me — to be read in the Acts of the Jubilees of our University, Part 3, pp. 79–80.

So that from all these things, with best conscience, it is open to me, with truth itself voting, to weave the following argument to oppose to the Reviler's argument: Whoever of the Reformed detests with his whole breast every violence in any Christian Ecclesiastical matter — most of all that which touches the Evangelicals' Dissensus held by him only as beyond-Fundamental — never fell out with any Lutheran, but has lived most amicably with all who became known to him, the Lutherans themselves being witnesses, and for these causes set forth and praised with many praises the Sandomierz Consensus insofar as this Consensus was most amicable, not insofar as one Man contradicted it and one Polish nobleman's threats (whether he was Reformed or Lutheran is uncertain) — that man, so far, sought the Protestants' Ecclesiastical Union by no violent Counsels, nor had it in mind to seek it so. But Strimesius etc. Therefore.

translator_notes.text: Hartknoch p. 905 German is quoted in the Latin lock: Gericius remained obstinate and was suspended with Lutheran and Reformed consent, with custody and excommunication resolved.

title: Prefatio Crimina III close: Prayer for the adversary, Cassmann's rule for disputers, and Meldenius against self-appointed judges
english: As for what remains: I humbly beseech God that He would deign to pour into this adversary of mine (than whom no one ever experienced a more hostile man — irritated by not so much as a little letter, nor even by mention of his name anywhere) the Spirit of proving himself, by which he may understand and attain how great the sins with which he loads himself by the most petulant tearing of the fame both of me and of so many other excellent and pious Men devoted to the Lutheran Society — whether through most imprudent zeal, or through a hunt for his own fame, truly quite infamous, sought from men like himself — and may timely unload himself of them by serious repentance, lest Satan — not indeed a Calvinistic one (whom the Sacred page utterly ignores), but the infernal and first author of calumnies and contumelies — be able any longer to harm him and his soul, redeemed by the precious Blood of Christ, and be forever severed from the Evangelicals' Union, otherwise still most hateful to him.

Meanwhile let him note the following Rule spoken by someone to unjust Disputers: Not by reviling, but by entreating; not by fulminating, but by demonstrating; not by condemning, but by confirming; not by execrating, but by praying; not by striking, but by admonishing; not by dooming with dire imprecations, but by interceding with pious vows; not by attacking with curses, but by earning favor with good deeds; not by hateful windbags of words, but by unmoved testimonies of Holy Scripture; not by truculence, but by tolerance; not by agitation of minds, but by moderation of affections; not by force, but by gentleness; not by inhumanity, but by mildness; not by desire of revenge, but by will to gain the erring; not by clamor, but by love of the right — emerging from every Fanatics' Sophistry and fraud as from dense darkness, conquering Truth at last triumphs as victor, and will triumph forever, altogether to triumph at last. In Otto Cassmann, Schol. Tentat. I, p. 374.

And also the Admonition of Meldenius, a Lutheran Theologian, addressing all such Dictator-Theologians in these words: You have constituted yourselves not only Adversaries but Judges; you rashly condemn other Churches dissenting from You; you arrogate to Yourselves censure over any Theologians whatsoever, however well deserving of the Church, and over their pious labors; without blush you publicly arraign them as guilty of the foulest heresies; and thus most manifestly you affect a certain dominion over the Lord's inheritance, so that your πολυπραγμοσύνη (meddlesome busyness) becomes conspicuous to the whole World, and to all good men is rendered hateful and intolerable. Who designated You Judges of nearly all Controversies? who Censor of all books? who Aristarchuses even of all Theological phrases? as if you alone were wise, and all the rest wandered about like shadows? as if You, ignorant of every error, had been destined by God and the Universal Church to that office, that you should examine all others' sayings and writings most rigidly and with Lyncean acumen! Who finally permitted You more Right over others than others over You? why did you publicly provoke those by whom you had never been injured? If you had kept silence, you would not have betrayed yourselves like the hamster, and would have consulted best for your fame. And indeed you urge these Controversies with such bitterness of words, hauling wagons of insults from both sides and from every side, that no Apostolic gentleness can be found in you. Nay — what is far graver and least to be borne — you often violently twist even things spoken aptly, piously, and rightly into an alien and perverse sense, and thence boldly snatch occasion for shameless calumny, and fasten upon the innocent monsters of opinions of which they had never dreamed. If this license of cavilling should obtain, who at last will be innocent, who at last will be orthodox under these fault-findings? Christian Charity always hopes better things; your suspicion always thinks worse. Votive Exhortation for the peace of the Church, p. 34.

translator_notes.text: Meldenius is the Lutheran irenic voice behind the famous maxim often summarized as in necessariis unitas, in non necessariis libertas, in utrisque caritas; Strimesius cites his Paraenesis Votiva for church peace.

title: Part I Protheoria: Cassel consensus on Christ's Person, Baptism, and baptismal ceremonies
english: III. As to the Article concerning the Person of Christ, both sides agreed (pp. 13–16): 1. That the Divine and Human Nature are truly and personally united, so that Christ is God and Man in the unity of Person; and that that Union was made ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως — without confusion, without change, indivisibly, and inseparably. 2. That the Names of the Natures are truly predicated of each other, and in the proper signification of the words: God is Man, Man is God; and that the Properties also of each united Nature are truly and really predicated of the whole Person in the concrete, but according to that Nature to which those Properties or Attributes truly belong — which the Theologians have been pleased to call the Communication of Properties (Communicatio Idiomatum). 3. That the Human Nature is not intrinsically omnipotent, nor omniscient; thus in the Union the united Natures remained distinct, and the essential Properties of each safe; that the Principle which acts is the Person, the Principle by which, each Nature, and so on. 4. That the Human Nature has truly been raised to the highest glory, sitting also itself at the Right Hand of God. 5. That on both sides the Heresies of Nestorius, Eutyches, Marcion, Arius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Socinus (they place them in this order), and the like, are rejected.

There remained a dissent, and one not acknowledged as essential by those Men: 1. Whether to the Human Nature in the abstract there was communicated the divine Majesty, or All power, which it would exercise through the Omnipotence everywhere present and hypostatically joined to it? 2. Whether of the same Human Nature, in the abstract, there could be predicated the divine Properties that are fitted for operating — Omnipotence, and so on.

IV. As to the Article concerning Holy Baptism, both sides consented to this (pp. 17–18): That Infants are to be baptized; that the end of Baptism is that they be grafted into Christ and spiritually regenerated; that Baptism is necessary, yet not absolutely, so that only contempt of Baptism damns; that Infants are capable of regenerating grace: and both Parties established that these things belong to the essentials of that Sacrament. Controversies remained, yet acknowledged on both sides as not essential: 1. Whether Infants are at last grafted into Christ and regenerated through Baptism by the necessity of a means — namely an ordinary means? 2. Whether, because of the danger from neglect of Baptism, in a case of necessity, even a Layman may administer Baptism if a Minister's supply is denied?

V. As to Ceremonies — for example Exorcism in the Baptismal formula — there was consent on both sides: 1. That it is not to be thought the infant is corporally possessed by Satan. 2. That that rite can be employed no otherwise than to signify the habitual inherence of Original Sin. 3. That those formulas of Exorcism can be omitted and changed into express Prayers.

And according to the norm of this Agreement, the said Theologians judged that the Academies and Churches of Germany — especially (as nearer) the Brandenburg and Brunswick ones — ought to be invited into the same fellowship. And that truly Christian Mars of Germany, Assertor of Liberty as well as of Religion, FREDERICK WILLIAM, Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, most Invincible alike in mind and in arms — as Europe is witness, and as we too once were, and not long before his death, admitted into so great a Prince's sanctuary and conversation — had for many years wholly devoted himself to this most praiseworthy zeal, according to those fires of piety and charity with which he was kindled.

translator_notes.text: The four Greek adverbs are the Chalcedonian adverbs for the hypostatic union; Strimesius reports Cassel's shared confession before noting remaining abstract-majesty disputes.

title: Part I Protheoria: Obstacles — any error turned into heresy; verbal and private dissent
english: They went as far as they could! It belongs to pious Theologians of every sort to lend a helping hand — not by words or writings only, but also by deeds; that is, with hearts and tongues and pens kindled by true charity, and with domestic discords composed among the partners of the same Faith and of the same Token. That latter point, as concerns all or most, is more to be wished than hoped for, so long as there is still room for human affections and infirmities.

There are already in the rank of Protestant Men those who turn any Error into Heresy, or any Dissent into something Fundamental or Essential, as their passion wills! Nevertheless that dissent has very often been merely verbal, and has turned on phrasing or on the manner of stating a thing — for example in the words realiter, oraliter, sufficienter, efficaciter, and so on. Often it has turned on the mode of the thing — for instance the manner of presence or of being-present in the Eucharist. Or on the circumstances of the thing — for instance the Breadth of Redemption, whether also for the reprobate, while the thing itself and its substance remain unmoved. Often too the dissent is not in what was truly handed down, but in things fastened on by consequences not born in the teaching but brought in from outside — and certainly rejected; for example, that the Reformed deny God's Omnipotence, that they make God the author of Sin, that they assert a Stoic necessity, and so on. Finally, the private quarrel of Theologians more than the public quarrel of Confessions has pulled Brethren apart in more than one question: as in the Supralapsarian question, now nearly laid to sleep, and in very many others of that kind.

translator_notes.text: Margin cue Obices: the obstacles that keep Protestants from concord — verbal disputes, mode-vs-substance fights, and private theologians' quarrels rather than Confessional public dissent.

title: Part I Protheoria: Sacred majesty, royal power, and private blemishes made into church marks
english: I will add also that dispute concerning the Power of Majesty about Sacred things — more restricted by some, turned by others into an Architectonic power; or even concerning the limits of Royal Power and of passive obedience. On that argument a recent Theologian of Copenhagen has, with little modesty, branded the whole Reformed Church — twisting certain sayings or assertions of a few into whatever sense he wished — as adverse and hostile to the rights of Kings and Princes, and even to their divine origin, and indeed to their security: and with no other design than that he might shut out the French Exiles, fled into the bosom of the Most Powerful King, if not from a roof, at least from the Temple and from the liberty of Sacred things. Far be all your fury from my House! So there are sometimes brother Men who, with little Christian spirit, most eagerly snatch sayings — often spoken in the heat of disputation, often hesitatingly or as opinion, often sound in sense but awkward in wording, such as fell in countless numbers from the Writers and Fathers of the early Church — into matter for contention and for battles about words (λογομαχίαι)! There are those who abound in certain private thoughts of their own, or in their own sense, to the prejudice of Ecclesiastical tranquillity and against the laws of Christian prudence! There are those who transform the blemishes of private men into public marks of the Churches: thus taking certain sayings, for example of Zwingli, Calvin, Martyr, Beza, and others, as the judgment of the Reformed Church, and understood in a harsher sense!

translator_notes.text: Theologus Hafniensis: a Copenhagen Lutheran controversialist Strimesius charges with twisting private Reformed sayings to bar Huguenot exiles from worship under the French crown.

title: Part I Protheoria: Adiaphora made necessary; charity's defect; joining hands with moderate Evangelicals
english: There are those who of themselves order things indifferent (ἀδιάφορα) to become necessary, or order what belongs to the pattern of external discipline or of order — variable of course with the variety of Places, Nations, and Customs — to pass over into the very substance of Christianity, and as it were its soul! There are those who, theoretically immune from fundamental error (as we are ready to judge gently, ἐπιεικῶς), yet distinguish themselves practically by something far heavier: namely by a defect of charity (Matthew 5:23-24; 1 Corinthians 13:1, and so on)! It is already certain that all these things are done when our Savior's mandate, example, character, and last words are set aside (John 14:27), and when the rules and warnings of the holy Apostle of the Gentiles are despised (Ephesians 4:2-3; Philippians 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:4, and so on). The dignity and Office of their own Order are neglected as well; the pious efforts of the Greatest Princes, the most ardent vows of Theologians of either Party, and the groans and sighs of all the Good are tossed up and down as of no account; and no attention is paid to the weight of restoring Evangelical Peace.

We for our part do not cease either to lament in spirit and to grow sick at heart over the most unjust affections of men — with so great a loss to Evangelical truth, harm to the Church, joy to Enemies, offense to the Pious, and increase of Antichristian tyranny — or also to join right hands with those for whom the Divine Majesty has shaped the heart of better clay, who think more fairly and moderately of us and of our Churches, and who understand the fundamental consensus. Such men there are, by God's kindness, here and there through nearly all Germany and the Northern world; especially in these most mournful times, when the Church is already oppressed by the common Enemy and will be oppressed still further unless, with forces and minds joined under the auspices of the highest Powers, she has repressed that fury. And already we hear with joy that in the ample Dominions of the Most Powerful Brandenburg Elector studies are gradually coalescing, hatreds are departing, eristic strife is being barred, common counsel is being taken, and there are being recalled to minds formerly more stirred what men of proven piety, moderation, and prudence urged in this matter in the last century and in ours — Capito, Bucer, Melanchthon, Strigelius, Peucer, Pierius, Himmel, Palladius, Donauer, Chytraeus, Pelargus, Osiander, Calixtus, Meyfart, Matthias, Dilher, Dreier, Conring, Musaeus, Heinich, the Helmstedt men, and others.

translator_notes.text: Margin cue Officia: Strimesius's own duty — mourn unjust passions and join hands with moderate Evangelicals who grasp fundamental consensus; he cites Brandenburg coalescence and a roll of Lutheran/Reformed irenic names.

title: Part I Protheoria: Origins of the Sacramentarian schism — Luther, Carlstadt, Zwingli (1524)
english: And would that men went back to the first Origins of the dissensions, understood at length from the History of the Diffidence — first the Sacramentarian schism, born in the year 1524 between Luther and Carolostadius, otherwise Bodenstein of Carlstadt, with Huldrych Zwingli soon about to move into a middle opinion: namely, Carolostadius referring the This (τοῦτο) in the words of Institution not to the Bread but to the Body of Christ, and so removing every presence of the Body in the Eucharistic Bread; Luther on the contrary asserting a corporal presence, by the letter of the text (τοῦ ῥητοῦ); but Zwingli and Oecolampadius a Sacramental presence, under the figure of Bread and Wine. The origin of the discords is to be understood especially from the temperaments of those who were a great part of these contests. Luther, to be sure, was fervid, and did not easily bear an equal in doctrine or authority; Carolostadius was less prudent, led by impulse more than by doctrine and judgment; Zwingli was constant in his opinion and yielded neither to Luther's commands nor to his name; Oecolampadius was unmoved, by the authority of Augustine and of the whole early Antiquity; Melanchthon, of the gentlest temper, would so assert the proper sense of the words of Institution that he departed from Luther, not acknowledging a local coexistence or inclusion of the Body, nor an oral manducation of it. But soon there came after them the sons of Bellona — bitter and eristic tempers — that would enlarge the suits and the Controversies:

translator_notes.text: Margin cue Motibus ex Historia: Strimesius traces the first Sacramentarian split to 1524 Luther–Carlstadt, then Zwingli/Oecolampadius, before the later Ubiquitarian and Concord-Formula escalations.

title: Part I Protheoria: Degrees of the schism — Ubiquitarians, Flaccians, and the Formula of Concord
english: Such were Johann Brenz, father of the Ubiquitarians; Jakob Andreae, from the carpenter's craft called Schmidlin, who would add much to the Brentians; Tilemann Heshusius, fire and flame of so many tumults; Johann Marbach, marked by new portents and calumnies against Pezel, Zanchi, Tossanus, and others; Samuel Huber and Aegidius Hunnius, restless tempers, swollen with new births even concerning Predestination: and above all Flacius Illyricus with his party, the most unjust persecutor of Philip and of the Augsburg Confession as Melanchthon had emended it — though Luther himself had encouraged that work — from whom the Flaccians, and the Flaccio-Brentians, are most noted for their furies: and at last the Authors of the Book of Concord, or Bergen Formula, with Jakob Andreae, Selnecker, Chytraeus, Chemnitz, and others as chief captains. Concerning its Authors, Writing, Scope, Articles, Reprobation, Approbation, Apology, Sequels, and so on, Hospinian treats at length in his work Concordia Discors, and the Palatines in the Neustadt Admonition; also Heinrich Alting in his manuscript History of the Palatine Reformation, and others.

From these things it will easily be plain that a Schism of this kind was born among Evangelicals, to which rivalry between Luther and Carolostadius first gave occasion, and soon rivalry between Luther and Zwingli — men equal in learning and in zeal for reform, yet discordant in one point, the mode of Eucharistic presence. Hence first arose the unhappy Schism, a dissent about the Holy Supper lighter in its beginnings; lighter, I say, both from the Marburg Colloquy, in which Luther had enjoined silence, and from comparing Article X of the Augsburg Confession with the Elucidation Melanchthon afterward added, in which the disapproval of those who teach otherwise was omitted. But soon the sharp anger (ὀξυχολία) and vehemence of certain men fostered the divorce of minds and opinions — such as men's tempers were — and not last in that order Jakob Andreae, truly a Schmidlin or smith of contentions; Tilemann Heshusius, who somehow could not bear the fortune of General Superintendent of the whole Palatinate at the age of thirty-two; then the notorious Johann Marbach, Flacius Illyricus, and others. Soon the dogma of Ubiquity was brought to birth — asserted indeed at first on the occasion of the Eucharistic Controversy, but afterward left silent by Luther and dropped altogether, as also in the Augsburg Confession. Yet it broke out again after Luther's death, poured out by Brenz, but interpolated and promoted by Jakob Andreae, the Flaccians, the Bergen men, and others. Hence came their divorce from the Augsburg Confession as Melanchthon had reviewed and emended it, especially at Article X, and the distinction they produced between the Confession as varied and as unvaried. Hatreds, fury, force, and exacerbation followed on every side.

translator_notes.text: Margin cue Varii ejus gradus: degrees of the schism from a lighter Supper dissent (Marburg; AC Art. X) through Ubiquity and the Formula of Concord (Bergen), with Flaccian furies named as escalators.

title: Part I Protheoria: Formula of Discord — Frederick III, Predestination ulcer, hardening causes
english: through Germany — so far that they rose even against the best and most pious Princes: as when a fierce tempest was stirred against Frederick III of the Palatinate, with Jakob Andreae, Heshusius, and Bidenbach as chief firebrands, that they might shut pious Frederick out of the Peace of Religion and the Society of the Augsburg Confession — though they would fail at the Augsburg Diet of 1566. At last the Formula of Concord finished the work — first the Torgau Formula, afterward the Bergen — of which we have just spoken: in truth a Formula of Discord, and the complement of a lasting Schism. Elector Ludwig of the Palatinate protested at once, though most devoted to the Lutherans, and other Princes with him, and also the weightiest Theologians — Hospinian, Alting, and the rest already praised at length. But the unhappy Controversy concerning Predestination and its annexed Heads, born chiefly through Samuel Huber and then through Aegidius Hunnius of Wittenberg around the year 1580 — or so Georg Calixtus testifies below on the Confession of Thorn, p. 14 — drew the ulcer wider and rendered it incurable.

And at last they have hardened that Evangelical dissent down to this very day: Satan's malign craft (κακοτεχνία); the hidden arts of the many-scheming Jesuits (τῶν πολυμηχάνων); the calculations of Politicians who serve Rome or their own advantage; and among Theologians for the most part a spiteful rivalry (κακοζηλία), pride, hatreds, calumnies, prejudices, eristic and virulent writings, and private ambitions in very many cases — as it happens — and it will have no end until, by the authority of the Most Serene Princes and by a greater force if one ever intervenes, they are coerced.

translator_notes.text: Continues Varii gradus: Formula Concordiae as Discordiae Formula; Predestination controversy via Huber/Hunnius ~1580 (Calixtus on Thorn) hardens the schism until princes coerce.

title: Part I Protheoria: Digression — Lutheran concord not Remonstrant or Pontifical syncretism
english: But in the matter of mutual Tolerance and of fraternal Concord sought among the Churches of Protestants, the cause of those called Lutherans must not be confused — as some would wish — with that of today's Remonstrants, concerning whose Schism the Reformed judgment was not the same, and whose Dogmas were reviewed at length above. Still less is the cause of the Augsburg Brethren, in the irenic business, to be set beside that of the Pontiffs, though today's Roman Methodists may try to compose both. Hence both parties — Remonstrants and Pontiffs alike — have long solicited us toward Syncretism in Religion, with an eye to the communion offered to the brethren of the Augsburg Confession. And the Pontiffs have done so in that Method they call Richelian, which the Gallican Clergy lately revived, as Method 1: leading us by their Missionaries into Communion with the Roman Church. In particular the same Bishop of Condom, now of Meaux, pressed it in Chapter II of his Catholic or Tridentine Exposition.

translator_notes.text: Margin cue Disparatio / Communionis: do not confuse Lutheran mutual-tolerance cause with Remonstrants or with Richelian/Gallican/Bossuet (Condom to Meaux) methods toward Rome.

title: Part I Protheoria: Bossuet's pretenses answered in the 1681 Strictures
english: The pretense was, first, that the Lutherans defend the so-called real Presence of Christ's Body in the Eucharist, from which would follow the Adoration of the Body present in the Eucharist — which we so greatly flee. Second, that they defend the dogma of Ubiquity, from which would follow altogether the destruction of Christ's Humanity: and yet the Reformed are ready to offer them their communion, because they deny that consequence of a destroyed Humanity — why then not also to Pontiffs who equally refuse the Consequences drawn from Tridentine Doctrine? But we went openly and at length against this vainest Method in our Strictures against the then Bishop of Condom, published in 1681.

There we treat at length: (1) of the reason of tolerance and of the communion offered to the brethren of the Augsburg Confession — with a retort upon Pontiffs who know nothing of tolerance, indeed of humanity, while they still deny that dissent from the Roman Church is Fundamental; (2) of the dogma of Ubiquity, how far it is held to overthrow the foundation or not — compared with the contested dogmas of the Pontiffs and with their practice, which destroy the essence of Christianity by a far other reason; (3) of real Presence in the Lutheran sense, and of the adoration they approve in the Eucharist — narrating in a long series the difference from the dogma of Transubstantiation, from the Mass Sacrifice, and from Latria of the Host shown even outside the use of the Sacrament, besides other idolatrous and intensely superstitious acts in the Pontiffs' Mass rites; (4) finally of the Consequences which the Bishop of Meaux charges the Reformed with eliciting from Tridentine doctrine not without the stain of calumny — treated by us at length in those Strictures.

translator_notes.text: Obtentus: Bossuet's Cap. II pretenses (real presence to adoration; ubiquity to destroyed humanity) answered in Strimesius's Stricturae adversus Condomiensem (1681), distinguishing Lutheran communion offer from Tridentine Mass/latria.

title: Part I Protheoria: Remonstrant cause unequal to Lutheran — Luther De Servo Arbitrio
english: Nor indeed is the Remonstrant cause and the Lutheran on equal footing, even in the business of Predestination and its annexed Heads. The points above already teach as much, where the Rinteln Theologians explained their own mind and their party's, afterward defended by them in their Apology. And in this cause we appeal to the Leipzig men, to Gerhard, to Calixtus, even to Calov in his Consideration of Arminianism, and others — but before all to Luther himself. For there was no controversy with Luther concerning Predestination, or the total Impotence of the bound Will, or God's Providence about evil actions: he strongly asserted Augustine's doctrine — which is also Paul's — in the Book on the Bondage of the Will, issued against Erasmus toward the end of 1525. For in it there occur even more dreadful things concerning the Divine Decrees and the necessity of sinning than in Calvin himself — as all candid men confess, whatever escapes Luther's grandsons may have tried to seize.

translator_notes.text: Margin Dispar longe causa Remonstrantium & Lutheran. De Praedestin. Controv.: Rinteln/Leipzig/Gerhard/Calixtus/Calov, but above all Luther's De Servo Arbitrio (1525) vs Erasmus — candid men admit harsher decree/necessity language than in Calvin.

title: Part I Protheoria: No Predestination quarrel until Hunnius — Formula, Montbeliard, Marbach-Zanchi
english: And afterward Luther confirmed it in a lucid Preface to the Epistle to the Romans and in other writings, even German ones. Nor was any Controversy on this argument moved against the Reformed — neither in the Torgau Formula or Book of Concord of 1577, nor in the Montbeliard Colloquy published in 1587. On the contrary, Synergists were marked in the Formula of Concord: namely those who set a certain synergy (συνεργία) of Free Will, and held the Causes of Conversion to be the Holy Spirit, the Word, and Man's Will — which error was imputed to Melanchthon. So when contention arose at Strasbourg in 1562 between Johann Marbach and Jerome Zanchi, and Zanchi's doctrine was most bitterly harassed, there was no serious remonstrance on the Predestination argument. In that doctrine the Arbiters — among them Schmidlin summoned from Tubingen — judged there was no great diversity.

Nor, Calixtus himself warns in his Animadversions on the Thorn Confession, was a sentence different from that received Augustinian view — to which the Theologians of the Unaltered Augsburg Confession had clung — brought back into Churches and Schools before Aegidius Hunnius, then teaching at Wittenberg in 1580, and Georg Mylius of Jena.

translator_notes.text: Completes captave-rint: Luther Romans preface; no Reformed Predest. fight in Formula Concordiae 1577 or Montbeliard 1587; Synergists marked; Marbach-Zanchi 1562 without serious Predest. remonstrance; Calixtus: divergent view returns only with Hunnius 1580 and Mylius.

title: Part I Protheoria: Disparitas — ten points Lutherans still confess against Remonstrants
english: Therefore even now today the Theologians named from Luther confess: (1) that certain persons are elected from eternity, not because of foreseen faith, but elected in faith, or through faith in Christ; (2) that Election has no impulsive cause in us, but the whole business of salvation hangs upon God; (3) that faith is foreseen in some, yet as from the grace of the Holy Spirit, as God's gift, as to its beginning, progress, and perseverance; (4) that we are dead in sins, and that there are no residual powers in fallen man toward spiritual good, toward the supernatural acts of Conversion; (5) that God's Grace truly precedes every operation of man, and that in him there are no powers toward Conversion except those prevented, excited, and moved by Grace — so that toward the first reception of Grace they have themselves only passively, as Calixtus expressly says;

(6) that that grace is not given except from a decree of giving efficacious Grace for believing; nor does God foresee anything except dependently on Himself as first cause, still less foresee spiritual good in us; (7) that Faith is trust in divine grace, or in the remission of sins, through and on account of Christ, already contradistinguished from works in the business of Justification; and that a subjective certainty of salvation is given; (8) that the Election of certain Persons is eternal and immutable, and so the Elect according to foreknowledge (κατὰ πρόγνωσιν) cannot finally fall away, on the hypothesis of divine Foreknowledge, which is infallible; (9) as to Reprobation, although they want no other than according to foresight of final Impenitence, yet they do not deny that in this way it is eternal — that the distinction of elect from reprobate is eternal, that the cause of this comparative distinction is God's good pleasure, and that Foreknowledge of the reprobate also is infallible; (10) finally that they condemn every Pelagianism and Semi-Pelagianism. So genuine grandsons of Luther appear to have stood far from the aim and mind of the Remonstrants.

translator_notes.text: Margin Disparitas: ten current Lutheran confessions (election through anti-Pelagianism) showing genuine Luther heirs far from Remonstrant aim; Ulterius confirmatur (Dordrecht/Socinian contrast) left for next contiguous slice.

title: Part I Protheoria: Ulterius confirmatur — Augustana not Remonstrant; no Socinian commerce
english: From which things it is plain how no necessity binds together the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession with the Remonstrants, and how the men of Dordrecht had nothing to do with brethren of that sort, while these latter barred recocted Pelagianism together with us. It is also plain how ready it would be for Lutherans in the common sense to conspire fraternally with the Reformed, if from the pulpit — dropping quarrels, and dropping also unjust delations before Princes and Magistrates — those men would keep within bounds. Add that dissent in the cause of Predestination gave no cause to the Schism, nor was there contention with Luther on that matter, from what has just been said. And above all, the Brethren of the Augsburg Society have no commerce with the Socinians, as today's Remonstrants do from the history above, from page 242.

So likewise among those called Lutherans there is no palliation of Fundamental errors, nor excuse, nor diminution, in the Heads concerning the Holy Trinity, the eternal Divinity and Generation of the Son, the adoration of the Holy Spirit, Original Sin, the Satisfaction of Christ, Justification by faith alone, and so on.

translator_notes.text: Margin Ulterius confirmatur: further confirmation that Augsburg Theologians are not bound to Remonstrants; Dordrecht shared the anti-Pelagian bar; Predestination dissent did not birth the Schism; Augsburg Society lacks Remonstrant Socinian commerce.

title: Part I Protheoria: Remaining dissent from Dordrecht — six heads; easy consociation
english: So that if any consensus of the Brethren with the Quinquarticularian Theologians remains, the dissent from the men of Dordrecht consists chiefly in these: (1) In phrase, where Lutherans speak of election or reprobation (yet not from Luther) as from foresight of faith, or from foresight of unbelief — although the Formula of Concord did not distinguish πρόγνωσις from προορισμός, as Peucer long ago observed in the Confession set out by Hospinian. (2) In reviewing the order of the Decrees; namely with a conditional Decree set first — concerning the salvation of all, redemption, calling to faith, and so on — provided they are not wanting to it. (3) In the object of Christ's Death, which is all and every human being, elect as well as reprobate. (4) In asserting the mode of the operation of Grace, which with respect to all is even internal, and efficacious from God's side, yet which men resist and against which they set an obstacle — although elsewhere they confess the impotence of Free Will for the work of Conversion.

(5) In the asserted possible apostasy of the saints, which the Reformed also do not deny if the saints are considered in themselves: yet the same Brethren deny it if they are considered elect according to God's infallible foresight. (6) Finally in the Reformed sentence now and then twisted or taken in a sinister sense, and in the Predestinarian Heresy affixed to them — such as was once affixed to Augustine, to Gottschalk, and to those of like mind (ὁμοδόξοις). But once that inequity of judgments and suspicions is hereafter ordered to be of no force, in the remaining things that leave a difference either in phrase, or in the method of conceiving the Decrees, or in the mode of the matter, or its extent, or its circumstances — the substance being safe on both sides (for example Christ's Death, or preventing and confirming Grace, or justifying Faith, or Holy Baptism), overturned by the common Adversaries of Protestants — easy association will follow. Nor will anything be wanting to the complement of either party's vows, except the longed-for peace, that God the perfecter of all may complete it — who daily also fills even what is beyond oath and beyond hope, as I may speak with the Lyric poet.

translator_notes.text: Margin Qualis remaneat dissensus Lutheran. a Reformatis, aut Consensus cum Armin.: six remaining heads vs Dordrecht (phrase, decree-order, death's object, grace-mode, possible apostasy, affixed Predestinarian heresy); if unjust suspicions drop, consociation is easy.

title: Part I Protheoria: Two classes of controversy — Melanchthonian AC vs Bergen Formula party
english: Of the Controversies with the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession, two various Classes are to be set up. For some are with the genuine Disciples of Luther, and with those who profess the Augsburg Confession even as Melanchthon recognized it after the Wittenberg Concord, and as it was often explained, especially as to Article X. And now almost the only contested head remaining is the Lord's Supper — Melanchthon expressing the presence of Christ's Body in these words in the later Confession, which others call the Variata by Philip's private authority: That with the bread and wine the Body and Blood of Christ are truly exhibited to those who eat in the Lord's Supper. The prior edition, of the year 1530, had: That the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat in the Lord's Supper, with the disapproval of those who think otherwise added. That one thing was, while Luther lived, an apple of discord (μῆλον ἔριδος) — first with Carolostadius, from what was said before, and then also with the Swiss, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and those who joined them in the order of the Reformers.
