english: ANNOTATION II. On the Augsburg Confession associates' fundamental consensus and their praeter-fundamental dissent — and on that dissent's origin, progress, and outcome. To the Author's pp. 332–333.

§. I. The associates' fundamental consensus looks to the foundation of the Christian religion — Christian doctrine, theoretical and practical — of which some doctrines are fundamentals and others are built on them (fundamentata).

The former, taken in the scriptural sense, are the doctrines concerning Christ, our only Saviour, God and Man: the highest, first foundation for everything else ([[1 Cor. 3:11 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 3:11]]: "For other foundation can no man lay," &c.).

Here "Christ" means chiefly the doctrine about Christ, not only his person — clear from what precedes and what follows. Paul as wise architect is said to have laid the foundation (Christ); what he laid was not Christ himself but the gospel-doctrine about Christ, the base on which other Christian doctrines are built.

What follows confirms it: others are to build on that foundation gold, silver, wood, stubble — many things founded on the fundamental doctrine of Christ, some precious and useful, some cheaper and futile.

[[Eph. 2:20 >> Bible:Ephesians 2:20]] says the same in one verse: Apostles and Prophets (i.e. their chief doctrines, not their persons) are called foundation, and Christ the cornerstone — that is, the doctrine of Christ is named the principal and most fundamental.

title: Annotatio II §.I cont: Theological sense — doctrines necessary to faith and salvation; God alone fixes necessity
english: Or take fundamentals in the theological sense: doctrines wholly necessary both to constitute Christian religion or faith and to reach faith's end — the salvation of our souls.

Hence they are commonly called either fundamentals of faith (toward the object: the intrinsic, essential thing founded) or fundamentals of salvation (toward the end: the thing founded partly intrinsic/essential, partly extrinsic/extra-essential).

God alone in Holy Scripture fixes all that necessity — explicitly or implicitly, by a consequence open to anyone — and in an exclusive sense no less than a positive one: so God both names which doctrines are necessary and, by not naming others as necessary (explicitly or implicitly), exempts them from faith-and-salvation necessity, though not from usefulness of every degree.

It is neither likely nor admissible that God, sole author of all Scripture — where necessities for faith and salvation are mixed with lesser matters, and some necessities are at times marked openly — either failed to define all necessities at all (and so failed to distinguish them from the less necessary) or left that definition and distinction to human whim; especially since he handed down everything needed for salvation promiscuously, and as such. See this taught more fully in the Inquisition into the Arminians, Annotation XVII.

title: Annotatio II §.II: Who fundamentally consents or dissents — Socinians(juris)/Pontificii(facti); Protestants agree except domestic-necessity urgings
english: §. II. Those finally are said to agree fundamentally in Christian religion and faith, in the theological sense, who agree in everything God has called necessary to faith and salvation — and who count as necessary neither other things, nor more, nor fewer, than God has commanded to be such in his word.

Those dissent fundamentally who either diverge from the necessaries of faith and salvation so named by God, denying all or some of them as to truth or as to necessity; or who, beyond the divine necessaries, forge and push other things as necessary apart from God's word.
Of these dissents the former is more a matter of right; the latter more of fact. Socinians dissent fundamentally from Protestants in the former way; Romanists in the latter.

Protestants, or Evangelicals, are understood to agree fundamentally among themselves in both ways — except those who still press as necessary certain house-dogmas of their own, founded neither in Scripture as to truth nor (still less) as to necessity, and who cut off and damn those who refuse them: thereby falling from the foundation, if not of faith strictly so called (Christian theory), then of charity or practice (the other part of the Christian religion, and of Christian faith in the wider sense).

title: Annotatio II §.III (1)-(2): A posteriori necessary heads — Scripture sole principle; Elements (Symbol, Decalogue, LP, two sacraments)
english: §. III. That Protestants agree fundamentally among themselves has already been shown a priori; the same can be confirmed a posteriori by running through the general necessary heads of Christian doctrine.

(1.) They agree on the first and only adequate principle for knowing all Christian dogmas — at least all the necessary ones — namely Holy Scripture: held by Protestants with one voice as a rule and norm, both sufficient and perfect and clear enough, for everything Christians must believe and must do.

Other so-called Christians (synonymously or only equivocally) differ here: they either set something beside Scripture as co-principle — Traditions, the unwritten word — or put Scripture under something else, native light (reason) or fictitious light (enthusiasm).

Protestants, by contrast, explode enthusiasm and the unwritten word as hostile to Scripture; and they treat reason, however illuminated, not as a principle of proof but as a bare instrument of apprehension.

(2.) They agree in an honest, unvarnished reception and profession of the elements of Christian religion in all their parts: the Apostles' Creed, the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and only two sacraments — which not only signify their significates but also exhibit and seal them.

title: Annotatio II §.III (3)-(4): Sincere AC Invariata incl. Art. X (Lutheran species); Formula Concord except two Coena/Person modes
english: (3.) They agree in sincere adhesion to the Augsburg Confession — and to it as Invariata — even on Article X, whether the German or the Latin is read here, provided the "species" of bread and wine in the German edition are taken not in the Roman sense (as accidents) but in the Lutheran sense (as symbols of Christ's body and blood).

Hence the Reformed colloquists at Leipzig testified they would always be ready to subscribe the Invariata Confession and cling to it with their whole heart — as we already said in Annotation I, and will quote their words below.

(4.) They agree in admitting the Formula of Concord strictly so called — both the Epitome of certain disputed articles and the Solid Declaration and Repetition of the same — as to substance and as to modes, except only two modes: one on the Holy Supper, the other on the Person of Christ.

Even that twofold modal diversity, we shall show in due place, does not touch the foundation of the Christian faith even from afar. See meanwhile our German tract on the Protestants' fundamental consensus, §§. 10–24.

title: Annotatio II §.IV open: All Protestant dissent praeter-fundamental — Coena words: Luther, Carlstadt, Zwingli
english: §. IV. So every dissent among Protestants is rightly called praeter-fundamental. Its origin, progress, and peak (akme) may be sketched here in brief.

That dissent begins in the controversy over interpreting the words of the Supper — which the three first Reformers, Carlstadt, Luther, and Zwingli, each framed differently as a counter to Roman abuses, and not equally handy in every respect (Calixtus, Judgment of Controversies §. 47).

Luther kept the line drawn from his former teacher Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, and still held by the fewer and better Romanists: that Christ's body is predicated of the bread so that, the bread remaining, Christ's body is joined with the bread in the Supper's use (Wittenberg Latin Tom. II, fol. 70 B) — predicated of the bread as contained in the bread, by a proposition unusual yet proper, and empty of any rhetorical trope.

Carlstadt, pressing the Romans harder, invented an identical proposition: driving the bread of the Lord's Supper out by Christ's body (much as the more common Roman view), as if Christ had given his disciples only the received, blessed, broken bread, and while giving, pointing to his own body, had said of that — not of the bread — "This is my body."

Zwingli, midway between them, meant to keep both bread and Christ's body in the Supper — the bread corporally, the body spiritually — and taught that Christ's body is improperly predicated of the bread by the impropriety common to all sacramental propositions: by metonymy the significate is said of the sign, which signifies it and exhibits it spiritually.

title: Annotatio II §.IV close: Carlstadt fades; Upper/Lower Germany split; corporeal presence+ubiquity vs spiritual session — stop before §.V
english: Carlstadt's middle reading — fabulous, and dragging in a little story forged outside Scripture, not unlike the Socinian fable stitched onto [[John 1:3 >> Bible:John 1:3]] "And the word was with God" (by which Socinians hostile to Christ's deity press their case) — found very few backers and soon vanished.
The other two remained, taught with all the more heat — one in upper Germany, the other in Lower — the more they first seemed to clash.
The one: a corporeal or local presence of Christ's body in the bread. The other: at first glance seeming to admit no presence at all, not even a spiritual one.
The former called in aid the ubiquity of Christ's body, unheard of in past ages; the latter, that body's session at God's right hand in the heavens into which it had ascended.

title: Annotatio II §.V open: Dissensus on Coena words/presence grows via Ubiquity controversy — Luther in dispute heat (Greater Confession)
english: §. V. That same Protestant split — begun over how the Supper words are read and over the mode of Christ's bodily presence in the Holy Supper's use — then grew through the controversy on the ubiquity of Christ's body.
Luther himself, once and again in the heat of debate, had drawn it in, chiefly from two places in his Greater Confession — the ones Calixtus cites at loc. cit. nos. 41–42.

title: Annotatio II §.V: Ubiquity drawn to ease corporeal Coena defense — afterward neglected
english: He brought ubiquity in so he could defend a corporeal presence of Christ's body in the Holy Supper more easily — then later let it drop.

title: Annotatio II §.V: Brentius & Jacob Andreae resume ubiquity — Heshusius contradicts though sharing Coena view
english: Brentius and Jacob Andreae took it up again (as we noted in the preceding Annotation, §.14) — even though Tillemann Heshusius, who shared their Supper view, contradicted them (see Hospinian, Historia Sacramentaria, p. 40).

title: Annotatio II §.V: Marbach Senior confirms with harsher theses — human nature called God; Fechtius reports
english: Marbach the Elder then confirmed and defended it with further like — and even more absurd — propositions, daring to say Christ's human nature can rightly be called God Himself.
So Fechtius reports in his Supplement to Ecclesiastical History, p. 30 (cf. Hospinian, Concordia discordans, ch. 55).

title: Annotatio II §.V: Torgau prior Convent 1574 Art. 4 rejects ubiquity again
english: The Torgau assembly of 1574 rejected it again in Article 4.

title: Annotatio II §.V close: Torgau 1576 silent; Philippist Corpus out, Formula Concord body in; Bergen Fathers explain as potential — stop before §.VI
english: In the later Torgau meeting of 1576 it went silent — the year the Philippist Corpus Doctrinae was set aside and today's Formula of Concord body of Lutheran doctrine took its place.
At last the Bergen Fathers explained it as potential, in the Solid Declaration and Explanation of the Controverted Articles (my copy p. 754; 4to ed. 1580).

title: Annotatio II §.VI open: Dissensus reaches Fastigium — Hunnius attacks Predestination sentence nearly universal since Augustine, received by first Reformers of both parties
english: §. VI. Not long after the Formula of Concord came into print — a story already more than familiar — the Dissensus hit its peak.

Aegidius Hunnius struck at the Predestination teaching that, from Augustine onward, had been all but the rule of the Western Church, and that the first Reformers on both Protestant sides had taken over: Luther and Zwingli, as pupils of Augustine and of Thomas Aquinas.

title: Annotatio II §.VI: Hunnius urges embracing the opinion of Fathers older than Augustine
english: He pressed for taking up the view held by the Fathers who came before Augustine.

title: Annotatio II §.VI: Most Lutherans follow Hunnius; Reformed mostly keep insisting on Augustinian doctrine
english: From then on the greater part of the Lutherans went with Hunnius, while most of the Reformed held fast to Augustinian teaching on this point.

title: Annotatio II §.VI: Calixtus — our men once approved Absolute Decree, then retreated to first-four-centuries foreknowledge sentence; Hunnius labored much
english: As the often-praised Calixtus puts it: many of our own once approved the Absolute Decree as well, then by degrees fell back to the teaching of the first four centuries — a decree framed according to foreknowledge — and Aegidius Hunnius did a great and distinguished work in that change:

title: Annotatio II §.VI: Hard to state without Pelagian tinge — Tossanus and Tanner accuse Hunnius; Calixtus Thorun/Gratia refs
english: Still, it is hard to set out that teaching without seeming to shade toward Pelagianism — and Daniel Tossanus the Calvinist and Adam Tanner the Jesuit both charge Hunnius with Pelagianism (cited place, no. 22).
See also the same Calixtus, Consideration of Reformed Doctrine according to the Thorun Confession, on Grace, p. 62.

title: Annotatio II §.VI close: Neither this nor prior Dissensus judged Fundamental — Tractatus prior refs; stop before Annotatio III
english: And they still did not count this split — or any of the earlier ones — as Fundamental: see the earlier Tractate, nos. 23–35, no. 45, and nos. 76–82 inclusive.

title: Annotatio III open §.I: Landgrave Philip of Hesse tries to smother Dissensus in the bud — letters to Luther, Melanchthon, Brentius
english: ANNOTATIO III. On the Attempts Made toward Consociation (pages 334–341).
§. I. The moment the Dissensus first broke out, Landgrave Philip of Hesse — a prince hard to praise enough — tried to choke it off in the bud.

title: Annotatio III §.I: Letters urge Concord and fraternity with Zwinglians before and at Augsburg — theologians refuse fundamental consensus
english: He wrote again and again to Luther, Melanchthon, and Brentius, pressing hard for Concord — both before the Augsburg Diet and while it sat — and for fraternity with the Zwinglians that would actually be kept.

Those letters are still in Chytraeus’s Acts with the Zwinglians; and the named theologians, for their part, were angry and would not admit that the Zwinglians shared with them a fundamental consensus of faith.

title: Annotatio III §.I: Philip’s letter for the Zwinglians — shared articles; Coena by faith; response too hard — Chytraeus / Buddeus Luther replies
english: So the Most Illustrious Prince argues for the Zwinglians in one letter (Chytraeus, History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 652): since they agree with you in the other articles, confess Christ as you do, grant that Christ is eaten in the Supper by faith — and that eating is needed for salvation — and do not strip God of omnipotence, but read the words by the analogy of faith according to Scripture as they take them; and since Christ’s glorified body cannot feed a stomach, so He can scarcely be eaten except by believers and through faith — your sentence and reply look harder than they need to be, and I hope God will bring you to a truer view.
For Luther’s answering letters, see the recent Buddeus Supplement, Epistle 122, pages 1024 and 102.

title: Annotatio III §.I: Landgrave brings both parties to Marburg 1529 — Universal Consensus except the Article on the Lord’s Supper
english: By all of this the Landgrave at last got the theologians of both sides to come out to him at Marburg, and there in 1529, with him present, they entered a Universal Consensus — one article excepted: the Lord’s Supper.

title: Annotatio III §.I: Chytraeus on Zwingli/Oecolampadius follow Luther elsewhere; interim Christian love; Buddeus Luther to Agricola; wish bitterness eased
english: On that outcome Chytraeus writes: Zwingli and Oecolampadius gladly followed Luther’s teaching in everything else; only on the Sacrament they would not follow (p. 643).

Though they had not yet agreed whether Christ’s true body and blood are corporally present in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, each side would still show the other Christian love as far as conscience allowed, and both would pray God to confirm them by His Spirit in the true teaching (p. 646).
Buddeus, the noted Halle professor, adds in his Supplement Luther’s Epistle 98 to Johann Agricola, urging that harsh words and writings stop from then on (pp. 71–72).
Chytraeus himself, opening his History of the Acts with the Zwinglians, says he and all the pious wish the bitterness of these splits and hatreds softened and eased (p. 636).

title: Annotatio III §.I: MARPURGENSE — first of the more perfect Consociation attempts, though lowest grade (all dogmas but one; Luther refuses right hand of fraternity)
english: I would call this Marburg attempt the first of the more complete Consociation efforts — though still of the lowest grade.
More complete, because they agreed on every dogma but one; lowest grade, because Luther would not give the right hand of fraternity (Chytraeus, p. 647).

title: Annotatio III §.I close: Luther calls Zwinglians heretics; Zwingli weeps for Wittenberg unity; spiritual presence offered — stop before §.II Bucer/Wittenberg
english: Worse: Luther called the Zwinglians heretics — Epistle 103 in Buddeus’s Supplement, p. 105, to Jakob Probst, Licentiate of Theology: they were treated most unfairly in being denied the name of brothers and forced to leave as heretics, yet so that peace might hold for a time by mutual writings, if God should open their heart.

On that footing Luther became the first author of the Protestant schism — and the more out of season, the more carefully the other side had sought Concord, as Luther himself admits in Epistles 98 and 123 in Buddeus.
He records that Zwingli, weeping openly before the Landgrave and the Estates, begged and cried out: there are no people on earth with whom I would rather be one than with the Wittenbergers (p. 105).
And again: the Zwinglians had promised they would say with the Lutherans that Christ’s body is truly present in the Supper, but only spiritually — if only they might be called brothers. Same place.

title: Annotatio III §.II open: More perfect Consociation attempt owed to Bucer — vies with Melanchthon for palm of theological moderation; still presses Concord after Marburg
english: §. II. Next comes a more complete Consociation attempt — one owed to Martin Bucer, who could even vie with the gentlest Melanchthon for the palm of theological moderation and modesty.

Chytraeus tacks it onto the Marburg effort in these words: when the Landgrave’s intercession could not get the Saxons to receive the Zwinglians as brothers, Bucer still did not quit — even after our Confession had been shown — but kept pressing every path to conciliation and Concord (pp. 658 and 679).

title: Annotatio III §.II: Bucer to Luther at Coburg, then to Oecolampadius and Zwingli — delays stretch to the sixth year; Concord finally set at Wittenberg
english: Still, a little later — before the diets closed, and with the Elector of Saxony and Bucer’s own magistrates knowing — Bucer went to Luther at Coburg to work out godly ways of settling the controversy.
For the same cause he soon went on to Oecolampadius and Zwingli.
One delay after another pushed the close of that business out to the sixth year; Concord was finally constituted at Wittenberg.

title: Annotatio III §.II: Second Consociation attempt ranked WITTENBERGENSE — Formula explains Coena consensus; eleven Reformed and six Lutheran subscribers; almost Interim-like pending wider approval
english: On that account I rank this second Consociation attempt higher — the Wittenberg one — because of the Wittenberg Formula of Concord, which even spells out agreement on the doctrine of the Supper.
Eleven Reformed and six Lutheran theologians subscribed it; read it in Chytraeus, pp. 680–681.

Call it almost Interim-like if you like: those theologians (Chytraeus’s words) would not finish the Concord until they had also referred it to the other theologians and magistrates for their approval.

title: Annotatio III §.II: From the Lutheran side — Luther himself urges Bucer toward Concord (1535); then presses Strasbourg and Swiss approvals (1536–1538)
english: From the Lutheran side, another mark of the Wittenberg Concord’s completeness is this: Luther himself spurred Bucer to seek it — letters to the Strasburgers, 1535 (Buddeus, Epistle 120, p. 248).
After the Formula was set, Luther pressed Strasbourg’s approval in 1536 (Epistle 223, p. 257), and the Swiss as well — 1 December 1537 (Epistle 231) and 1538 (Epistle 232).

title: Annotatio III §.II: From the Reformed side — Wittenberg Formula never revoked, only declared; Helvetian approval; Zurich reply dated 4 May 1538 (not 1539 typo in Werenfels)
english: From the Reformed side: the Wittenberg Formula of Concord was never revoked — only declared (Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 162).
The Swiss approved it point by point (Crocius, pp. 100 and 107).

Because some have doubted that approval, we must call the Helvetians’ own reply letters from Zurich to Luther as witnesses — written a little later, yet not as late as 1539 (the year a Berlin printing of Werenfels’s sermon assigns them, perhaps by typographical error, in this very year of my writing).

They were drawn up on 4 May 1538 — about half a year after Luther’s letter reached them — as Selneccer, Kirchner, and Chemnitz, the three most celebrated Lutheran historians of the Augsburg Confession, recount when they cite the letters in these words:

title: Annotatio III §.II: Zurich reply (German) — joy at Luther’s answer; Capito and Bucer’s report; Basel Confession accepted; unity on Word, Baptism, and Supper without empty signs — Hucusque Tigurini
english: The Zurich letter opens: Honorable, highly learned friend in Christ — we received with highest joy your kind answer to the writing we sent you toward Schmalkalden, thanking our heavenly Father.

From your letter and from Capito and Bucer’s faithful report while they were with us, we can only take it that you mean this holy unity well, and that you gladly accept our Basel Confession with the Declaration that followed.

On the outward Word and Baptism you find no misunderstanding; on the holy Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood we gather you have never taught — and do not teach — a descent or ascent from the Father’s right hand that would set a presence or eating in the Supper contrary to the true incarnation and ascension.

We for our part refuse bare empty signs in the Supper: the Lord’s body and blood are received, yet truly grasped only by the believing mind, as our Confession and Declaration sent to Schmalkalden still hold.
So we now see nothing else than that — God be praised — we are one in understanding and right substance, at peace, with no dispute left between us. (Full page Hh.) Thus far the Zurichers’ words.

title: Annotatio III §.II close: Werenfels votes to renew the short-lived 1536 Concord; Luther’s 1 Dec 1537 letter; Strimesius joins the wish — Concord later ruptured; Luther’s bitter Jan 1546 letter before death on the Feast of Concord — stop before §.III Francofurtanum
english: Those Zurich words seem to move Werenfels — once chief theology professor at Basel — to end his sermon with this wish, adding the Luther letter that had drawn the Zurich replies: would that the Concord made in 1536 between the evangelical theologians of both sides — alas lasting no more than three years — were renewed.

Of that Concord Luther wrote to the evangelical Swiss on 1 December 1537 (Jena Works, Tom. 6, f. 507): take me for one who means it from the heart; so far as I can, nothing that furthers Concord shall be lacking in me.

We join Werenfels’s wish — the more warmly because, alas, it is surer still that for merely carnal causes (Calixtus the Elder, Jud. Controv. nos. 72 and 75) the earlier Luther broke the Wittenberg Concord.

Worse: by his letter to Jakob Praepositus in the month before he died — 18 February, the holy day of Concord — Luther can seem to have died into the schism (we hope at least beside his intention and knowledge): Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the Sacramentarians, nor stood in the way of the Zwinglians, nor sits in the chair of the Zurichers. You have what I think. (17 January 1546; Buddeus, Supplement, Epistle 255, pp. 287–288.)
Stop before §. III — the third, Frankfurt attempt after Luther’s death.

title: Annotatio III §.III open: Third Consociation attempt FRANCOFURTANUM — after Luther’s death, Melanchthon still living; Estates and Otto Henry call twenty-five theologians (1557–1558)
english: §. III. The third Consociation attempt of this Reformation century is the Frankfurt one.
It came after Luther’s death, while Melanchthon was still alive — in 1557 and 1558 — undertaken by the Imperial Estates and their leader, Otto Henry the Palatine.
Twenty-five theologians were called to Frankfurt; among them Johann Pistorius, Andreas Hyperius, and Nicolaus Rhodingus, Marburg professors commonly counted as rigid Calvinists.

title: Annotatio III §.III: Prior year — assembled theologians tell the Papists none among them foster opinions alien to the Confession; consensus stands in the foundation
english: In the prior year, the assembled theologians tell the Papists with whom they were to confer: none among them fosters erroneous opinions alien to the Confession, and they stand in consensus on the foundation.

title: Annotatio III §.III: Later year — they also agree a Sacred Supper Formula (summary at p. 335): teach per Augsburg Confession that Christ is truly, vivifically, and substantially present
english: In the later year, after comparing reasons, they also agree on a Formula for the Sacred Supper (our author summarizes it at p. 335).
On this article, they say, our churches must teach according to the Augsburg Confession: in the Lord’s ordinance of the Sacred Supper, Christ is truly, vivifically, and substantially present.

With the bread and wine he has so ordained, he exhibits his body and blood for Christians to eat and drink, testifies that we are his members, gives himself with the promise of grace, and works efficaciously in us — as Hilary says: what is taken and drunk makes Christ to be in us and us in him.

title: Annotatio III §.III: Formula words speak of action or use — Paul’s ‘bread we break’ is communion of Christ’s body, not bread outside the use
english: The words clearly speak of action or use — as Paul says expressly of use or action: the bread we break is the communion of the body of Christ.

That cannot mean bread outside the use; take it this way: this bread is the thing by which communion of Christ’s body is exhibited to us — and so speak the older writers and chief Fathers in the Church.

title: Annotatio III §.III close: Fathers on earthly and heavenly Eucharist — substance remains; later ‘bread changed like Moses’ staff’ phrases — Crocius; stop before §.IV
english: Irenaeus says the Eucharist consists of two things, earthly and heavenly; Epiphanius and Theodoret clearly say the nature and substance remain, yet with the bread gifts are given — namely Christ’s body and blood.
Later new phrases came in: that the bread is changed, as Moses’ staff was changed into a serpent (Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 204).
Stop before §. IV.

title: Annotatio III §.IV open: Fourth Consociation attempt HEIDELBERGENSE — Otto Henry & Frederick III (1559) pursue Protestant Concord; Heshusius opposes; Melanchthon restores ancient Coena speech
english: §. IV. To the Frankfurt attempt, by the link of years, one may join the Heidelberg one.

Its authors were Electors Palatine Otto Henry and Frederick III, in the Palatinate in 1559 — pressing hard for Protestant Concord, and opposing the very turbulent Heshusius (so Schmidlin in Hospinian, Concordia Discordans ch. 46 near the end, new Geneva ed. p. ~409).

From Philip Melanchthon’s counsel they restore the Fathers’ ways of speaking about the Sacred Supper. That counsel, given about half a year before Melanchthon’s death, stands in the later part of his Theological Counsels and Judgments supplied to Elector Frederick III (p. 378ff).

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Melanchthon to the Elector — silence quarrelers; keep one Forma of Paul’s κοινωνία words; declare the Supper’s fruit; the Son is present for man, not for bread
english: Some of Melanchthon’s words to the Elector are worth keeping: he approves the Elector’s counsel that both sides’ quarrelers be silenced, lest the tender church split and the weak nearby be troubled — and he wishes such quarrelers gone from either party.

Second, once the contentious are removed, the rest should agree on one Forma of words; best here is to keep Paul’s: the bread we break is the κοινωνία of the body — and to speak richly of the Supper’s fruit so people love this pledge and use it often, declaring what κοινωνία means.

Melanchthon inserts: the Son of God is present in the ministry of the Gospel and efficacious in believers — present not for the bread but for the man ("Abide in me…"; "I am in my Father, and you in me…"). By these consolations he makes us his members and promises to vivify our bodies.

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Some call this fruit-doctrine ‘Cothurnos’ and demand body-in-bread formulas — then invent inclusion, conversion, transubstantiation, ubiquity unknown to learned antiquity
english: Yet some brand this true, simple fruit-doctrine as Cothurnos (inflated tragic boots) and demand a yes/no: is the body in the bread, or in the species of bread — as if the sacrament were instituted for the bread and that papistic adoration.
Then they invent how to shut it into the bread; some invent Conversion, others Transubstantiation, others Ubiquity.
All these portentous inventions are unknown to learned antiquity.

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Heshusius refuses Origen’s σύμβολα and Clement; the same stroke would hit Augustine, Ambrose, Prosper, Dionysius, Tertullian, Bede, Basil, Nazianzen, Theodoret (pp. 379–380)
english: Heshusius refuses assent to Origen, who calls bread and wine σύμβολα of body and blood; he calumniously rejects Clement of Alexandria.

The same verdict would fall on Augustine, Ambrose, Prosper, Dionysius, Tertullian, Bede, Basil, and Nazianzen (who speaks of an ἀντίτυπον body), and on Theodoret, who says of the bread φύσιν and μεταβαλών (pp. 379–380).

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Frederick III’s Testament (via Grynaeus) warns sons against turbulent ministers who spawn logomachies against churches agreed on the foundation in Christ
english: Also worth remembering is a passage from Elector Frederick III’s Testament to his sons, taken from Johann Jacob Grynaeus and joined to his pious admonition on the duty of godly men who must live beside the cataract of anathemas against sound eucharistic teaching (pp. 47–49).

Third and above all, he warns his dearest sons to watch most carefully against turbulent ministers of churches and schools who, in religion and faith, spawn every kind of contention, word-fight, and deadly condemnation against pious churches and schools that still agree on the foundation and the chief heads of Christian religion and place their salvation with us in Christ alone.

From ambition and crooked zeal, under pretext of a ministry by which they claim the Spirit should convict the world, they introduce this without declared cause and not without scandal — trying, no less than in the cursed Papacy, to dominate magistrates’ and subjects’ consciences and raise a new primacy for themselves everywhere.

title: Annotatio III §.IV close: Turbulence breeds political and church division and Papal opening — princes must remove the unamendable, yet not strip pastors of moderated correction; stop before §.V Sendomiriense
english: From such turbulence follow not only political and church distraction and ulcerated minds — disturbance and ruin of both governments — but also an opening for the Pope and his retinue to persecute our true Christian religion with iron, flame, exile, and countless other punishments, and so to fix their tyranny.
How great and miserable the resulting divisions and calamities are, even our own age shows too many examples in Electors’ and other German princes’ lands, and among neighboring peoples.

Christian princes, churches, and schools should therefore take the lesson: guard hard against these turbulent enemies of public peace; do not let them seize posts, inflame parties, or tear people apart; avoid and flee them; and if no hope of amendment appears, remove them outright — as Frederick says he and other Electors and princes have more than once agreed for these and other pious, weighty reasons.

Yet nothing in that counsel should strip godly church ministers of due daily reproof and correction of vices, or of error-refutation drawn from God’s word with Christian moderation and equity — aimed at building up, not tearing down.
Stop before §. V.

title: Annotatio III §.V open: Last and most perfect Reformation-century Concord attempt — SENDOMIRIENSE in Poland, 1570 (Consensus Sendomiriensis)
english: §. V. The last Consociation attempt at Protestant Concord in that first Reformation century was not in Germany but in Poland in 1570.
It is the most perfect of all — the Sendomir attempt, celebrated under the name Consensus Sendomiriensis.

title: Annotatio III §.V: New Latino-German edition plus Prefatio with nine arguments prove its perfection — no need to linger on cause or praise
english: Of this Consensus we have not only prepared a new Latino-German edition, but in a special Prefatio set out nine clearest arguments for the perfection by which it leaves every other Protestant consensus many parasangs behind — and we have answered all the usual objections.
So there is no need to linger further either stating its cause or praising its excellence.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Rather pray imitation across Germany, neighboring northern kingdoms, and all Europe wherever both Protestant parties are found
english: Better to pray with whole heart that Protestants in our Germany, in the neighboring northern kingdoms, and throughout Europe — wherever either party’s Protestants are found — imitate so wholesome, clear-headed, and thoroughly Christian a deed and example.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Rest in Hornbeck’s judgment — no better, more august, or more perfect Confession ever made; approved politically and ecclesiastically; confirmed by joyful sacramental communion
english: For the rest we rest in blessed Hornbeck’s judgment on this Consensus — and we will always make it ours — when he says: no better, more august, or more perfect Confession than this was ever made.
It was approved politically and ecclesiastically, and they confirmed it mutually by a most joyful and illustrious communion of the sacraments.

title: Annotatio III §.V close: Both sides repeatedly acknowledge each other’s Confessions and churches as true and Orthodox — Bohemica/Helvetica and Augustana Socii (Misc. Sacr. I p. 703); stop before §.VI
english: From both sides they more than once acknowledge each other’s Confessions and churches as true.

We have agreed: just as the Augsburg Confession’s associates testify that we, our churches, and our Confession published in this synod of the Brethren are Orthodox — so the Bohemian Confession’s associates speak of themselves and of the Helvetic Confession’s associates — so also we will pursue their churches (the Augsburg associates’) with the same Christian love and confess them Orthodox (Hornbeck, Miscel. Sacr. Part 1, p. 703).
Stop before §. VI.

title: Annotatio III §.VI open: Two famous post-Reformation Consociation attempts — LIPSIACUM (1631) and CASSELLANUM (1661); the prior distinguished three ways
english: §. VI. After the Reformation century come two most famous Consociation attempts at reconciling Protestants with one another.
One is the Leipzig attempt — Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian theologians, 1631; the other the Cassel attempt — Hessian collocutors alone (Marburg and Rinteln), 1661.
The prior (Leipzig) is marked out in three ways.

title: Annotatio III §.VI (1): Reformed at Leipzig ready to subscribe the Invariata — Variata not rejected; Nauenburg 1561 precedent; Brandenburg/Hessian Relation confession
english: (1) Right at the start the Reformed theologians did not hesitate to bind themselves to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, and were fully ready to subscribe it whenever the other side asked — without rejecting or repudiating the Variata (Philippica), which they defended as the Imperial Estates had admitted it at the Nauenburg Convention in 1561.
Since this Leipzig Reformed act has been remembered before, it helps to bring in their own words from the German Relation of the Leipzig Colloquy.

There the Brandenburg and Hessian theologians voluntarily confessed with mouth and heart the 1530 Confession delivered to Charles V at Augsburg, and said they would subscribe it — even the Saxon Elector’s exemplar in the Augapfel — whenever and wherever asked, because they and their lords already bound themselves to it in church and school.

title: Annotatio III §.VI (2): Colloquy end — both sides measure Augsburg-article agreement and hope closer union; mutual Christian love stipulated
english: (2.) At the colloquy’s end both sides signal why they met: to see how far they agree in the Augsburg Confession’s articles, and what hope remains of a closer union later — to enlarge Christ’s true church and quench the papists’ confidence drawn from Protestant division — while stipulating Christian love to one another in the meantime.

Their Relation words put it thus: the colloquy was meant first to learn, in summary, whether and how far both parties are one in the twenty-eight Augsburg articles, and whether further conferences of peace-loving theologians, with Christian high authority, might raise a nearer holding-together; and both sides’ theologians would show each other Christian love going forward, faithfully and without deceit.

title: Annotatio III §.VI (3): Frankfurt Estates (third year after) approve the Leipzig Colloquy and decree Saxony and Brandenburg continue the Protestant peace work
english: (3.) Finally, in the third year afterward the Imperial Estates gathered at Frankfurt am Main not only approved the Leipzig Colloquy, but — judging they would not be cheated of the Leipzig theologians’ hope — sanctioned by a special decree that Electors Saxony and Brandenburg be asked in the Estates’ public name to keep the Protestant peace business begun at Leipzig going through more moderate theologians’ work, and to bring it to a happy end.
Because few know that decree, we set it out here in the words printed in John Dury’s Prodromus Irenicorum, p. 1.

title: Annotatio III §.VI Decretum: Dury’s union proposal heard; six Circles call the work grateful and necessary, yet many lack instructions — so they will report home
english: Decree of the Evangelical Estates made at Frankfurt.

John Dury again laid before the Evangelical Estates’ convention (Circles present, and absent princes’ legates) the business of union and fraternal reconciliation among Evangelicals inside and outside the Empire on the fundamental heads of Christian evangelical religion — a matter floated before — and in a notable deputies’ sitting he was heard by all confederated Estates, citing many leading theologians and academies of either party in Germany, France, England, and Transylvania on how that Christian unity-aim might be reached.

The six Circles unanimously judged the work grateful to the God of peace, praiseworthy, most necessary, and useful to evangelical churches — yet also a heavy business for which many deputies present had no instructions. So the present legates and deputies undertook to report home faithfully the proposal and the theologians’ opinions shared with them.

title: Annotatio III §.VI Decretum close: Continue the Leipzig collation; keep Christian moderation in teaching and writing; public prayers; Act Frankfurt 14 Sept. 1634 — stop before §.VII Cassellanum
english: Some legates also offered friendly proposals: that the Circles forward at once a declaration on Dury’s proposed procedure and on a peaceable theologians’ colloquy — modeled on the Leipzig collation three years earlier among Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian-Cassel electoral theologians — and that the Electors invite foreign princes and kings by letters.

Others usefully proposed that, saving each Elector’s, prince’s, and Estate’s rights, Electors Saxony and Brandenburg be asked to continue that Leipzig-friendly collation and call a convention where other peaceable theologians of either party can sit or send judgments — aiming at a modest Christian consensus-confession on every salvation-foundation head, while parking scholastic fights on the rest.

Several also agreed that meanwhile both sides should use Christian moderation and mildness in teaching and writing, and that public prayers for the work be framed in both parties’ churches, committing the business to God Most High.
This recess was made in witness of that. Done at Frankfurt am Main, 14 September 1634.
Stop before §. VII (Cassellanum).

title: Annotatio III §.VII open: POSTERIUS — CASSELLANUM (this century’s second Protestant-peace molimen) claims three peculiarities
english: §. VII. This century’s later Protestant-peace Consociation attempt — the Cassel one — claims three peculiarities of its own:

title: Annotatio III §.VII (1): Careful weighing of disputed dogmas; consensus and dissent marked without varnish; modest judgment on weight more than bare truth — consciences unhurt
english: (1.) It carefully weighed the force of the special disputed doctrines, marked consensus and dissent everywhere without varnish,
and only then gave a modest judgment on the weight of that consensus and dissent more than on bare truth — leaving both sides’ consciences unhurt.

title: Annotatio III §.VII (2a): After full examination — Evangelicals agree on the Foundation of Faith and Salvation; disputed questions do not overturn that foundation
english: (2.) After everything was duly examined, it candidly and heartily judged that Evangelicals agree on the Foundation of Faith and Salvation:
the disputed questions touch that foundation less — and still less tear it up or overturn it;

title: Annotatio III §.VII (2b): Remaining controversies — not for pulpits, or only with utmost modesty; schools and academies likewise without persecution or personal naming (Autor p. 330)
english: and lest either side next tear or damn the other for some leftover dissent, they judged it wise and agreed:

remaining controversies should not be handled from church pulpits — or if necessity plainly forced it, only with utmost modesty, naming no dissenters, using no harsh words, forging no consequences, declaring truth from Scripture alone;
and in schools and academies likewise with great moderation, without persecution, personal attacks, or name-pointing (Autor p. 330).

title: Annotatio III §.VII (3) close: Defense of the charitable colloquy; Rinteln Epistola Apologetica; Maresius/Hornbeck/Heidegger — stop before §.VIII
english: (3.) Both colloquy sides vigorously and learnedly defended their charitable colloquy against detractors and every hater of Protestant peace, and won near-universal applause from foreign Protestants.
Even the Rinteln Epistola Apologetica — by that pair of high-judgment, many-sided theologians Peter Musaeus and John Hennichius — was translated into other languages.
Compare the Cassel Colloquy defenses of Maresius, Hornbeck, Heidegger, and others.
Stop before §. VIII (fruits of Lipsiacum and Cassellanum into the present age).

title: Annotatio III §.VIII open: Fruits of Lipsiacum & Cassellanum not small — reach into the present century
english: §. VIII. The fruit of both those Consociation attempts — Leipzig and Cassel — was not small.
It reaches not only the age in which they were begun and finished a few years back, but even our present century, itself not long under way.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: Better theologians grow milder; magistrates filled with desire for ecclesiastical peace
english: For besides this: the better theologians on both sides grew used to thinking more mildly and kindly of one another and of their own parties, and by example led their hearers to do the same;
so they filled their magistrates more and more with love and desire for reconciling church peace.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: After Leipzig — Charles Louis Palatine’s pacific institute blocked by Dannhauer (Autor p. 335)
english: After the Leipzig Colloquy, Charles Louis of the Palatinate had a pacific project in hand — one our Author celebrates —
though Dannhauer’s virulent writings then overturned it (Autor p. 335).

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: After Cassel — Frederick William the Great’s many peace attempts hindered by Dannhauer’s circle
english: After Cassel, the many peace attempts of Frederick William the Great, Elector of Brandenburg — whom our Author (p. 341) rightly calls Germany’s Mars and upholder of liberty and religion — are even publicly known;
yet other theologians near the March, Dannhauer’s disciples or fellow-initiates, blocked them out of deadly hatred of the Reformed,
and all but blasphemously prayed God to fill them ever more with hatred of Calvinists — not knowing what they asked.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: David/Solomon parallel — Great Elector’s peace zeal; Differtatiuncula / Dorothea; inheritance to Solomon our King
english: So the same seems to have befallen that prince of immortal glory — famed no less for piety toward God and sincerity of heart than for warlike fortitude, a strenuous emulator of St. David on both sides — as befell that Hebrew:
David burned to build Jehovah a stone temple, yet was barred from the work for set causes, and the building passed to his son Solomon, for whom God had also destined it;
likewise the most glorious Achilles of the Marchers, kindled with zeal to advance day by day the Evangelical peace once sought at Leipzig with him as persuader and author,

even with tears attested as much to us when we humbly offered our little Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Peace (which by his special order was soon to be put into the vernacular and dedicated to his most serene consort Dorothea, worthy of so great a hero),
and was about, as often before, most kindly to open his then thoughts on that peace and press perpetual peace-zeal upon us with all his force —
yet God so disposing, for reasons known to the All-wise alone, he was drawn off from raising the sanctuary of Protestant peace,

and transmitted by inheritance to his son — our Solomon, everywhere pacific, now crowned by God with the royal diadem — both richer furniture collected for finishing that sanctuary and his own desire for peace.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII close: Prayer for the Sacred Peace building; Royal Rescript to Bishop Ursinus introduced — stop before Rescript body
english: This is what we vow and pray from the heart for our Most Pious King:

that, with the Most High God of Peace blessing him, he may carry the building of Sacred Peace as happily as possible to its very summit — last year he again strove to lay its foundation, most kindly using our slight labor —
other kings and princes also helping as tireless promoters of kindly church peace, for God’s glory and the comfort and joy of all Evangelicals.
We judge the Royal Rescript in this business — given to his first bishop, the Most Reverend Lord Benjamin Ursinus, and turned from German into Latin — should be set before our reader here,
so anyone may judge the most sincere intention of our August King and his most fervent zeal to promote ecclesiastical peace.
Stop before the Rescript body (Nos Dei Gratia Fridericus Rex Borussiae…).

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript open: Frederick King of Prussia to Bishop Ursinus — greeting
english: It runs thus:
We, by God’s grace, Frederick King of Prussia, etc.
Our greeting and clemency!
Most Reverend Bishop, beloved and faithful.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript: Peace among Evangelicals our chief care; pulpits nearly free of mutual condemnations
english: You know how, especially under Our reign, promoting peace among Evangelicals has been Our highest care —

and with God’s grace helping we have come so far that in the Kingdom and Our other subject provinces those public bitternesses, charges of heresy, and Protestants’ mutual condemnations are scarcely heard any longer from the pulpit.
So a sure hope shines on us that Our peace-counsels, God blessing them, will reach a happy end.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript: Printed union/tolerance counsels; Collegium Theologorum erected; Ursinus named Praeses
english: But since Evangelicals of both sides have here and there put into print various counsels on closer union — or at least on mutual and greater tolerance —
and We, moved by such public writings and by everyone’s unanimous desire ahead of other princes, have been stirred to set hand to this salutary work of restoring peace,
We have most clemently resolved to erect in Our very capital a College of Theologians who love both peace and Our salutary intent, for God’s greater glory and the increase of Christ’s kingdom.
By these presents We name You Our Bishop its President.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript: Assessors — Strimesius, Jablonski, Lütkens, Winkler
english: joining to You for now these Assessors:
Samuel Strimesius, Our man for sacred sermons and Ordinary Professor of Sacred Theology in Our Frankfurt Academy, and Daniel Jablonski;
also Francis Julius Lütkens, councillor of Our Consistory and Provost of Cölln; and Winkler, Archdeacon of the Magdeburg Basilica.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript: Private colloquies and letters abroad; procure church peace at least in Our realm
english: Yours, then, as Bishop and President of this whole assembly, will be to make those Assessors sure of Our most clement will declared in this Rescript.
Meet and confer with them first inside private walls, without noise.

See that — by colloquies and by letters to foreign theologians — solid means are found by which the church peace all Evangelical Protestants long for may be procured and settled, if not elsewhere, at least in Our Kingdom, Electorate, and other lands.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript: External theologians by royal approval; Proto-Notary F. H. Ursinus; trust in earnest labor
english: If You and Your Assessors judge foreign theologians should also be brought into this College and convention, invite them with fitting courtesy — yet only after Our prior most clement approval — and report to Us by word and writing all that is done among you.

And so that everything in this charitable College or convention may be recorded in better order, We join to you Our intimate secretary and librarian Frederick Henry Ursinus as Proto-Notary, and for this business most clemently free him from the ordinary library duty that binds him.

As we do not doubt this irenical work will please God and that Our royal Christian intent will share divine blessing, so we most clemently trust you all, from true zeal for truth and peace, will gladly take up this care and strain every nerve.
Then we may obtain Our most ardent vow — the long, anxiously desired peace among Evangelicals made firm.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII Rescript close: Royal clemency; Cologne on the Spree 25 March 1703 — stop before Annotatio IV
english: As for the rest, take security from Our royal clemency.
Issued at Cölln on the Spree, 25 March 1703.
Frederick, King.
The Count of Wartenberg addresses Lord Bishop Ursinus.
Directed to Benjamin Ursinus, our Most Reverend First Bishop, beloved and faithful.
Stop before Annotatio IV (Obices Consociationis Ecclesiasticae).

title: Annotatio IV open: De Obicibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae (Autor pp. 341–343)
english: ANNOTATION IV.
On the Obstacles to Ecclesiastical Consociation (Autor pp. 341–343).

title: Annotatio IV §.I open: After frustrated peace attempts — inquire into OBICES; general vs special
english: §. I. After so many frustrated attempts to compose church peace, the Author not without cause turns to the OBSTACLES set against such pious efforts (p. 341ff.).
He points only at the special ones, passing the more general sources in silence — yet it is worth at least summarizing those generals too, mainly so they may be more carefully guarded against.

title: Annotatio IV §.I: Divide obstacles into Externos and Internos
english: We divide them, first, into Externals — placed outside the person — and Internals — at home in the person.

title: Annotatio IV §.I: External obstacles — Devil’s instincts and arts; neither over-blame nor exempt him
english: The external sort fall under the Devil’s varied instincts, tricks, and wicked arts — he being the first parent of lies, quarrels, and slanders.
We must neither exaggerate with the crowd that dumps nearly every misdeed on the Devil, nor, with the author of this fascinated world, exempt him from the community of human things and deeds.

title: Annotatio IV §.I: Scripture — Devil father of dissensions; lion; Judas; diabolical quarrels; tares in the wheat
english: For the Holy Spirit Himself names the Devil father of dissensions no less than of slanders and of the murders that sprout from them (John 8:44).

He does not only gape after people like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5) and spur them to his works (James 4); God permitting by just judgment, he also works in the sons of unbelief and through them (Ephesians 2:2 with 5:6), and even entered a Judas, betrayer of Christ (John 13).

Moreover he stirs up, feeds, and pushes quarrels of that kind — so, from their first spring, they are rightly called diabolical (James 3:15) — sowing tares of lies and dissension in the wheat of truth and peace.

title: Annotatio IV §.I close: Who wrecked the peace molimina? The wicked / common enemy (Matt. 13:28) — stop before §.II
english: So to anyone who asks who wrecked the peace attempts recounted above, you may aptly answer with Christ’s words:
the wicked one — our common enemy — did it (Matthew 13:28).
Stop before §. II (internal fountains: pravity of will and error of intellect).

title: Annotatio IV §.II open: Internal obstacles — fountains from will’s pravity and intellect’s error; many rivulets
english: §. II. The later obstacles you may call other fountains — arising from two common vices in the first principles of human action, intellect and will: pravity and error.
From those fountains spring still more rivulets, greater in number.

title: Annotatio IV §.II: First fountain — free-acting pravity of will precedes intellect-error; sacred strife by free choice
english: Of the two fountains, the first is the free-acting pravity of the will — which, under the covenant of grace no less than of works, runs ahead of intellect’s error.
For any divine covenant with man presupposes enough light in the mind to restrain or repel malicious will-pravity.

So whoever has gone on to needless sacred quarrels and church splits — even with the Devil prodding — should know he rushed in not unwillingly, nor merely by intellect’s mistake or the Devil’s talk, but by his own free choice and προαίρεσις.
Three larger rivulets from will-pravity, well marked by the Apostle John, promote that work of dissension; we list them here in reverse order:

title: Annotatio IV §.II (1): Ambition / pride of life — hostile to truth and peace; Arius couplet
english: (1.) Pride of life — or ambition — which usually clings even to the sacred order (as in the Pharisees, Matt. 23:5–7).
It is most hostile to truth and peace (John 5:44; 7:18) and most fertile of quarrels (2 Tim. 3:1–3).
That common couplet on quarrelsome Arius makes the same point: ask why the heretic (schismatic) Arius became what he was — the ready answer is, he was ambitious.

title: Annotatio IV §.II (2): Lust of the eyes — excessive sacred curiosity; multiplies dogmas and unhealthy novelties
english: (2.) Lust of the eyes — meaning spiritual lusts of the soul; in a word, excessive curiosity in sacred things, born of ambition — against Romans 12:3: do not think beyond what you ought, but think unto sobriety.
For the puffed-up man languishes among questions (1 Tim. 6:3–5) that a bishop must flee (2 Tim. 2:23–24; Titus 3:9).
This breeds two evils most hostile to church peace: an extraordinary multiplication of theological dogmas, and an unhealthy doting on novelties.

title: Annotatio IV §.II (3): Lust of the flesh — φιλαργυρία with φιλαυτία; alien to Christian teachers
english: (3.) Lust of the flesh — craving carnal and worldly goods — plus the love-of-money the Apostle rebukes as the mark of Pharisees and false teachers (Luke 16:14).
It sticks close to self-love (φιλαυτία, 2 Tim. 3:2), which Peter insists Christian teachers must keep far from (1 Pet. 5:2).

title: Annotatio IV §.II: Second fountain — Error of intellect when will-pravity is loosed; near sources of error
english: The second fountain is error of intellect — which anyone who loosens the reins to will-pravity is apt to fall into; conversely, whoever hates malice draws nearer the truth (Ps. 25:14; Matt. 5:8; John 7:17).
Error is born nearby from prejudices, passions in the saddle, warped schooling and teaching, the reading of slanderous books, and the like.

title: Annotatio IV §.II close: How error is perfected — bad grasp, false reconciliations, confusions, inept inferences — stop before §.III
english: It is finished either by grasping theological things badly and weakly and measuring them by earthly standards — with Nicodemus (John 3:12) and the Capernaites (John 6) —

or by twisting apparent contradictions into harmony outside Scripture: for example Christ’s two sayings in Matt. 26:11 and 28:20, reconciled by inventing a double body of Christ, visible and invisible, though the biblical distinction of Christ’s two natures (Paul, Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5; Peter, 1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1) does it far more easily.
Or by confusing what differs and not distinguishing enough — e.g. any theological truths whatever versus the fundamental and more necessary ones;

or by inferring clumsily — e.g. that God’s omnipotence is denied when his will and revelation in some dogmas are debated; or that a dissenter holds as sure everything rightly or wrongly drawn from his opinion; and so on.
Stop before §. III (further rivulets from either fountain, noted by our Author).

title: Annotatio IV §.III open: Further rivulets from either Obex fountain — noted by our Author
english: §. III. From either fountain of these obstacles still other rivulets run down, drawing the same kind of water — ones our Author notes.

title: Annotatio IV §.III from Prior (1): Stretch any error into heresy, or lesser dissent into fundamental
english: From the first fountain: (1.) Stretch any error into heresy at will, or turn a lesser dissent into a fundamental one.
“Fundamental,” I mean, when the dissent is wholly feigned and so none at all, or only verbal, or at most about the mode of the thing.

title: Annotatio IV §.III from Prior (2): Practical heresy — no room for charity’s judgment; worst-part reading
english: (2.) Labor under practical heresy — leave no room for charity’s judgment, and take everything dissenters say in the worst possible sense.

title: Annotatio IV §.III from Posterior [1]: Abound in one’s own sense; instill novelties to the church’s hurt
english: From the second fountain: [1.] Swell with your own sense, and in good faith drip your novelties into others — to the hurt of the church and of church peace.

title: Annotatio IV §.III from Posterior (2): Obstinate adiaphora — even into sin and open disobedience
english: (2.) Cling stubbornly to church adiaphora from long habit, even where sin is a real risk,
and even with open disobedience to the higher magistrate, under a zeal that is really owed to ignorance.

title: Annotatio IV §.III close: More in Stregensis’s Northern Olive-branch — stop before Annotatio V Limites
english: Gather more from the Northern Olive-branch of Johannes Matthiae, Bishop of Strängnäs — berries four, six, seven, and eight.
Stop before Annotatio V (Limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae).

title: Annotatio V open: De Limitibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae (Autor pp. 347–352)
english: ANNOTATION V.
Concerning the bounds of church Consociation — Autor pages 347 through 352.

title: Annotatio V §.I: Limits opposite Obstacles — by right (jure), not merely de facto
english: §. I. Limits stand opposite Obstacles: limits are understood of right, obstacles of fact.
An unjust boundary acts like an obstacle; a just obstacle acts like a limit.
So here the limits of church consociation are not whatever happens to obtain in practice, but what by divine and church right can and ought to be set.

title: Annotatio V §.I: Limits taken Materially (articles) or Formally (the act of limiting)
english: Taken that way, limits are either Material — the things or articles of the Christian religion that justly bound church consociation and keep it inside those bounds —
or Formal — the limitation itself, the act of limiting in its various degrees.

title: Annotatio V §.II open: What sets just bounds — Fundamental faith-dogmas, not every Christian truth
english: §. II. What sets just bounds for church consociation is not every Christian truth whatever, but the Fundamental dogmas of the Christian faith (described in Annotation 2).

That such fundamentals exist, distinct from less fundamental dogmas, has been shown elsewhere — by our Author’s Tract on Fundamentals (Disp. 1–2) and his Specimen against the Bishop of Condom (pp. 63–70), and by us in the Dissertation on Church Peace (ch. 7) and the Inquiry into the Arminians (Annot. 17) —
and all Protestants reckon the same way, even against the Roman party,

title: Annotatio V §.II: Against making all dogmas hang on Roman authority — Constance / papal council can inflate the least
english: who own no fundamentals in themselves — neither by immediate divine authority nor by their nature as founding the Christian faith —
but hang every dogma of the faith, great or small, as to truth, necessity, or fundamentality, on the authority of the Roman Church.
So what barely touches the Christian faith, or even runs against it, can still, through some Constance or papal council, become essential to that faith — even the greatest point.

title: Annotatio V §.II close: Tridentine anathema if one affirms bread and wine remain (1 Cor. 11) — stop before Eph. 4 proof
english: Thus someone who affirms with Paul that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine remains (1 Cor. 11:26–28) is treated no milder than if he had trampled the whole foundation of the Christian faith:

Trent, Session XIII, Canon II, launches a terrible anathema in these words — if anyone says the substance of bread and wine remains with Christ’s Body and Blood, and denies that marvelous conversion of the whole substance of bread into the Body and of wine into the Blood (species alone remaining), which the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation, let him be anathema (pag. m. 130).
Stop before the proof that true divine Fundamentals make the limits — from Ephesians 4 (authoritative and ratiocinative).

title: Annotatio V §.II cont open: True divine Fundamentals make the limits — proved Autoritative and Ratiocinative
english: That the same true, divine Fundamentals set the limits of church Consociation is proved two ways — by authority and by reason.

title: Annotatio V §.II Autoritative (Eph. 4): Keep the Spirit’s unity in the bond of peace — one body and one Spirit
english: By authority: take Ephesians 4 as a standing commonplace for the point — covering the whole foundation, theoretical (vv. 1–17) and practical (v. 17 to the chapter’s end).

There the Apostle bids us keep the Spirit’s unity in the bond of peace (v. 3), and affirms one body and one Spirit — one spiritual body — where there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, above all, through all, and in all (vv. 4–6).

title: Annotatio V §.II Autoritative (Eph. 4): One Lord, faith, baptism, God — yet diverse gifts for building the body
english: Yet afterward, and for what remains, grace is given to each — even in different measures — according to Christ’s gift (v. 7).
Some are set as apostles, others as prophets (v. 11), and that for the building up of Christ’s body (v. 12).

title: Annotatio V §.II Autoritative (Eph. 4): Unto the unity of the faith and the perfect man — truthing in love
english: The aim is that we all arrive at the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a full-grown man (v. 13) — not tossed by every wind of teaching (v. 14) —
meanwhile speaking truth in love, studying truth in charity (v. 15).

title: Annotatio V §.II Ratiocinative: Unanimous in fundamentals — one spiritual body more than not, though lesser dissent remains
english: By reason: those agreed on the fundamental — and so necessary and chief — dogmas of the Christian religion, though they still differ on lesser points, yet press on toward fuller unity in charity.
They are more one spiritual body than not.
Or, what comes to the same, they are more held in the Consociation of one Christian church than they are shut out of it — for we name a thing from its greater part.

title: Annotatio V §.II Ratiocinative close: Church members who keep essentials — even amid many non-overturning errors — stop before §.IV
english: Just as people with a body and a rational soul still count as human and as members of one society — even when the soul’s force is weak and some bodily members are badly misshapen —
so those who keep the church’s essentials, theoretical and practical, should be counted sharers in the same church Consociation,
even while they wrestle with many errors and sins that do not overturn the Christian religion.
Stop before §. IV (consensus and Consociation judged from the same fundamental principle).

title: Annotatio V §.IV open: From the same fundamental principle — judge both Consensus and Consociation
english: §. IV. From that same principle of the Christian religion’s fundamental dogmas we must judge both Christians’ Consensus and their Consociation —
that is, both unity of mind (or Spirit) and unity of body (or Church).

title: Annotatio V §.IV: Else no catholic Christian consensus or Catholic Church — vain hymn of all Christendom
english: Otherwise there will never be any catholic Christian consensus, nor any Catholic Church joined by that consensus.
Then we would believe that Church in vain, and sing falsely: “All Christendom on earth holds quite evenly in one mind.”

title: Annotatio V §.IV: Orthodox self-claim to the Catholic title alone — ridiculous, not even at one with itself
english: Unless those who today brandish the Orthodox name try — how ridiculously — to claim the Catholic Church’s title for themselves alone, or snatch it without thinking.
They cannot even be reconciled with the kinds among their own people, still less with each person in those kinds — not even with one individual, that is, with none of their own at one with himself —
once you allow for shifts of place, time, and other externals that greatly change internals.

title: Annotatio V §.IV: Consenters in all Fundamentals (Annot. 2) constitute one and the same Christian Church
english: So, as in Annotation 2 above we rightly called consenters in the faith only those who agree in all Fundamentals, though they differ elsewhere,
here we hold that all who keep the same Fundamentals make up one and the same Christian Church.

title: Annotatio V §.IV: Exiles from Consociation — Socinians (theoretical) and Pontificii (practical anathemas)
english: By that measure we count as exiles from church Consociation only those who fail in the Fundamentals —
theoretical failures such as the Socinians, or practical ones such as the Pontificians, who under anathemas bind any Christian conscience to their extra foundation,
against all Christian charity, which is most essential to the Christian religion.

title: Annotatio V §.IV close: Evangelicals Reformed and Lutheran already one by fundamental consensus — stop before §.V
english: Conversely, Evangelical Protestants — Reformed and Lutheran — though they dissent in some points, are already held in the same Christian Church and joined by church Consociation because of fundamental consensus.

At least those who treat the modes of dissent in about three dogmas (both sides keeping the substance) as less essential and less fundamental — and who not only refuse but abhor damning dissenters on that account.
On Arminians strictly so called we long ago gave a like judgment (Inquiry into the Arminians, Annot. §. 1. 3).
Stop before §. V (Hannekenius on truth and charity at the end of the Preliminary Questions).

title: Annotatio V §.V open: Only of Fundamental Truth understood — Hannekenius at end of Preliminary Questions
english: §. V. So those remarks apply only where Fundamental Truth is understood and laid out.
Toward the end of the Preliminary Questions on the Theological Declaration for a true estimate of the Augsburg Confession, Hannekenius (cited above) treats the point this way:

title: Annotatio V §.V Hannekenius: No sound mystical-Body union when Truth is wounded — Charity the bond from Truth
english: Wound Truth, and the mystical Body with its members cannot stay in sound union.
Charity — the very bond of that union — is violated the moment it loses the Truth from which it springs.

title: Annotatio V §.V: Vain charity with wounded Truth; empty Truth without charity — no confessor who splits Union
english: Charity with injury to Truth is vain; Truth without the exercise of Charity is empty.
No one shows true charity without a solid profession of Truth.
Nor is anyone heard as a faithful confessor of saving doctrine who, having broken Charity, splits the Union.

title: Annotatio V §.V: 1 Cor. chain; epiphonema — If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, anathema Maranatha
english: He points to a long run of 1 Corinthians (chs. 1–3, 8–10, 12–14, and 16:13–14).
The letter’s strongest closing cry is: anyone who does not love the Lord Jesus — the one true Salvation and saving Truth — is anathema, Maranatha.

title: Annotatio V §.V: Salvation in knowledge of Truth so that Jesus must be loved — cannot be loved in broken Synaxis
english: On that reading, salvation sits in knowing the Truth, and that knowledge teaches us to love Jesus.
Where the synaxis of union is already torn, that love cannot go deep.

title: Annotatio V §.V close: Pestilent charity without Truth; cursed Unio that does not love Jesus in Truth — stop before §.VI
english: Charity without Truth is pestilent, and every church union that does not love Jesus in Truth is cursed (1 John 4:10–12ff., p. m. 39).
Compare our German tract: Short Sketch of the Unity of the Evangelical-Lutheran and Reformed, §. 4, pages 21–25.
Stop before §. VI (limits of Consociation considered formally — Tolerance vs perfect Union).

title: Annotatio V §.VI open: Limits so far Material; Formaliter — the act of limitation in two grades
english: §. VI. So far we have treated the limits of church Consociation on the material side.
Taken formally — as naming the act of drawing that limit — they show up in roughly two degrees.

title: Annotatio V §.VI: First grade — Tolerance alone = Consociatio partialis
english: One degree reaches only as far as Tolerance.
That grade is rightly called partial Consociation.

title: Annotatio V §.VI: Second grade — perfect Union = total Ecclesiastical Consociation
english: The other stretches out to perfect Union.
There it completes total ecclesiastical Consociation.

title: Annotatio V §.VI: Two grades from vulgar opinion — Political vs Ecclesiastical Tolerance confused
english: I mark those two grades chiefly because common opinion mixes Political Tolerance with Ecclesiastical Tolerance.
That confusion is what makes the double ladder look sharp to the crowd.

title: Annotatio V §.VI: Ecclesiastically tolerable only if agreed with Foundation and Fundamentals
english: Otherwise, anyone to be tolerated in the church must already agree with the Foundation of the Faith and the Fundamentals of the Christian religion.
Without that agreement, ecclesiastical tolerance does not even begin.

title: Annotatio V §.VI close: Agreed in Fundamentals = already to be / coupled in Consociation — stop before Annotatio VI
english: But whoever does agree with the Fundamentals is, by that very fact that he is tolerable, also to be joined — and already joined — in the same church Consociation.
Stop before Annotatio VI (Classes of controversies among Evangelicals).

title: Annotatio VI open §.I: Two major classes by Authors, Number, and Mode of treating controversies
english: ANNOTATION VI. On the classes of controversies that stand between Evangelicals (pp. 353–356).
§. I. Our author quickly splits them into two major classes, marked off by a nearly threefold difference: authors, number, and the mode of handling the disputes.

title: Annotatio VI §.I Prior Class: Genuine Luther disciples admitting Melanchthon’s varied Augsburg Confession (Art. X)
english: The prior class, on his account, has as disputants Luther’s genuine disciples.
They admit Melanchthon’s milder, declared and explained Augsburg Confession — even Article X on the Sacred Supper — if not from the start, then afterward (see Annot. I. §.6).

title: Annotatio VI §.I Prior Class Number: Almost one point — in/with/under bread and oral manducation, not conceded spiritual presence
english: The disputed number shrinks almost to one point.
Both sides already concede a real supernatural and spiritual presence and manducation of Christ’s body and blood in the supper.
What remains is presence in, with, and under the bread, plus oral eating by unworthy and worthy communicants alike.

title: Annotatio VI §.I Prior Class Mode: Peaceful treatment; less-fundamental controversy so fraternal charity remains
english: The mode is peaceful — the kind that fits a theological fight.
Both parties treat the controversy as less than fundamental, so fraternal Christian charity still has room.

title: Annotatio VI §.I: Same kind as intramural Lutheran or Reformed disputes — does not derogate Ecclesiastical Union
english: As to the matter, this class between Lutherans and Reformed is no different from disputes that still run inside each camp — Lutheran fights over the body’s omnipresence and multipresence, or Reformed fights over universal and particular grace.
While it lasts, it takes nothing away from church union.

title: Annotatio VI §.I: Recognized Fraternity — Marburg/Rinteln/Cassel; Sendomir; Reformeds profess; Lutherans held by fear of schism
english: So there is no doubt: the Reformed once recognized fraternity with these Lutherans — in Germany at Cassel among Marburgers and Rintelners, and in Poland at Sendomir among Augsburg, Bohemian, and Helvetic confessionists.
They still openly profess that Christian fraternity with such Lutherans.
These Lutherans have joined heart and mind to the Reformed in brotherly love, even if more secretly — held back from an external profession by fear of schism with the rest of their own.

title: Annotatio VI §.I close: No fundamental error either side — stop before §.II (Posterior Class / Formula of Concord)
english: They have long held that the Reformed differ from them by no fundamental error at all.
The Reformed, for their part, have long acknowledged and celebrated these Lutherans as free of every fundamental error.
Stop before §. II (Posterior Class — Brenz, Andreae, Hunnius, Flacius / Formula of Concord).

title: Annotatio VI §.II open: Posterior Class authors — Brenz, Andreae, Hunnius; Flacius mode; Formula of Concord swearers
english: §. II. The posterior class has, for the hottest points, Brenz on the ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ’s body, Andreae on oral manducation of that body added on top, and Hunnius on predestination from foreseen faith.
For the harsher style of fight it has Flacius Illyricus’s disciples — a most restless ingenuity.
In a word: those who (if not all, then most) bind themselves to the Formula of Concord’s words — even the damnatory ones — as tightly as to Holy Scripture itself.

title: Annotatio VI §.II Number: Ternary principals — Supper, Person of Christ, Predestination; innumerable lesser
english: As to principal controversies the number is a ternary: first the Sacred Supper; then, sprung from it, the Person of Christ; and third, Predestination.
The lesser ones are countless, and they grow daily by intemperate zeal — sometimes by bare authorial whim.

title: Annotatio VI §.II: Triple difference — nude confictae, adiaphora, and real heads (German Einigkeit tract)
english: Our author therefore sorts this class into a threefold difference.

Some items are bare fabrications — questions of fact, not of right — that never entered any Reformer’s mind (Is God the author of sin? Is He omnipotent in bodily supper-presence? Is He merciful in the doctrine of grace?).
Others are lesser adiaphorous rites, where Lutherans would easily find the Reformed compliant.
Others again are more real and touch the three principal heads (see our German Short Sketch of Unity, §.XIII ff.).

title: Annotatio VI §.II Mode: Acerbic treatment — odious; prostitutes sacred order and the Protestant cause
english: The mode of treatment is usually more acerbic.
Pious Christians and the more sober theologians alike hate it.

It foully prostitutes sacred things, the sacred order, and the Protestant cause — and nearly brands them with the worst infamy — sunk even below the quarrels, calumnies, and shameless abuse of the crowd and of old women.

title: Annotatio VI §.II: Damnationes of non-fundamental opinions in the Epitome — against Lutheric brethren and Reformeds
english: It is also promiscuously joined to damnations of opposing opinions — however harmless, whether true or false, and certainly not fundamental.

In the Epitome of articles on controversies among Augsburg Confession theologians, such damnations abound — against some opinions of Luther’s own-named brethren, and against more on the Reformed side — for example these:

title: Annotatio VI §.II close: Epitome samples (faith/works, Supper, humanity’s capacity) — stop before §.III
english: That faith does not justify without good works (i.e. solitary faith does not justify); that good works are necessary to salvation; that faith in Christ is not lost and the Spirit still dwells even when someone sins knowingly in act only.

That Christ’s body is not taken corporeally with the bread but only bread and wine by mouth, the body spiritually by faith; that the faithful must look to heaven rather than seek the body in the supper elements; that unbelieving communicants receive only bread and wine.
