That Christ according to the humanity is incapable of divine omnipotence and the other infinite properties; that the greatest power given to His humanity still has no communication with God’s omnipotence (Epitome antitheses to Arts. 3–4, 7–8).
Stop before §. III (if Lutherans dropped this acerbic mode / swapped damnations for bare rejections, the door to fraternity would stand open).

title: Annotatio VI §.III open: If Lutherans dropped acerbic mode or swapped damnations for bare rejections
english: §. III. If today’s named Lutherans would drop this harsher way of handling controversies — or at least trade their damnations (not unlike Tridentine anathematisms) for bare rejections of opinions they judge false —

then even if those opinions may perish on their own view, the authors and favorers of them (erring, if at all, in good faith) are above all to be saved, and spiritual fraternity is to be kept with them.

title: Annotatio VI §.III: Reformed desire and open door to one Church — fraternity with all keeping the Foundation
english: The Reformed would then desire it, and the door into one church with them would be judged wide open.
The condition is simple: they stand most ready to give the right hand of spiritual fraternity to everyone who keeps the Foundation of the Christian faith — practical and theoretical alike.

title: Annotatio VI §.III: Bergen Fathers already — Rejicimus (non damnamus) four election errors (Art. XI Negativa)
english: The Bergen Fathers already did something like this in the Negative of Article XI.

They write: We therefore reject (but do not damn) all the errors we shall now list — that God does not will all to repent and believe; that His call is not serious for all; that some are doomed by bare counsel apart from their sins; that election’s cause lies partly in us, not only in God’s mercy and Christ’s merit (p. m. 591).

title: Annotatio VI §.III: Easy to do likewise on other Antitheses — none damned in Scripture; opposites asserted
english: Today’s doctors would be led most easily to do the same on the other antitheses named above.
They need only recall that none of those antitheses — nor many like them — is read damned in Holy Scripture, either expressly or by ready consequence.
Rather, the antitheses of those antitheses are asserted in God’s word, if not in the same words, then by legitimate consequence.

title: Annotatio VI §.III: Scripture for the Antitheses’ antitheses — James, Paul, Psalms, John 6, Rom. 1/9, 1 Pet.
english: For example: solitary faith does not justify (James 2 entire); good works are necessary to salvation (1 Cor. 7:19; Gal. 5:6; Heb. 12:14).
Faith in Christ and the Spirit are not wholly lost by every partly voluntary act of sin (Ps. 51:13; 2 Sam. 7:14).
Christ’s body is taken spiritually by the mouth of faith, not corporeally with the bread by the body’s mouth — sought from heaven, received by the faithful only (John 6:35, 47–59, 63).
Omnipotence does not belong to Christ according to the humanity (John 10; Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5; 1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1).

title: Annotatio VI §.III close: Faxit Deus — end mutual hatreds; return to full καταλλαγή — TANTUM before Coena Hexas
english: May Almighty God grant that, as I now end these Annotations on the Author’s Historical and Catallactic Protheoria of controversies with the Lutherans, so an end may at last be put to Evangelicals’ mutual hatreds.
Then every handle for a history of these fights may be cut off, and they may return to a full and perfect καταλλαγή — glued more and more to their common Head, Christ.
TANTUM. Stop before HEXAS Annotationum on the Prior Protestant Controversies De Coena Domini (Annotatio I).

title: HEXAS De Coena Domini Annotatio I open §.I: Why Priores — unde Schismatis initium
english: Here begins the Hexad of Annotations on the earlier Protestant fights over the Lord’s Supper — the place where the schism took its start.
ANNOTATION I asks whether the Institution words of the Sacred Supper are to be taken properly or figuratively.
§. I. Our author himself shows why he calls those Supper controversies Priores when he adds the clause: whence the beginning of the Schism.

title: Annotatio I §.I: Not priority of Dignity or Order (Sennert) — but of Time and Acerbitas
english: They are not “prior” by dignity — as if they alone were some fundamental article of the faith, or the chief matter Protestants hammer out among themselves.
Nor by order — as if a methodical theological system would have to put them first.
Even some Lutherans deprecate those kinds of priority (Sennert, Exercises on fundamental articles §§. 64–65, fasc. pp. 430–431).

title: Annotatio I §.I Time: First mutual dissent after egress from papal Babylon was on Supper questions
english: They are prior partly by time.
Once out of papal Babylon, Protestants first began to dissent from one another on some questions about the Lord’s Supper.

title: Annotatio I §.I Acerbitas: That dissent erupted into the foul beginning of the Protestant schism
english: They are prior partly by acerbitas.
That dissent at last erupted into the nerve and gave a foul beginning to the Protestant schism.

title: Annotatio I §.I Calixtus: Eucharist deformed by papal abuses — reformers right, but weak foresight at the start
english: Calixtus notes the occasion of that first priority without tastelessness: among the Pontificians the Eucharist had been deformed by foul abuses and superstitions — scarcely any other head of religion had suffered equal calamity.
They adored the blessed bread as the very Body, set it out for adoration, and offered a propitiatory sacrifice; solitary Masses without communicants were frequent.
The first Reformation leaders rightly meant to abolish those errors — yet human ingenuity is weak, and not all foresaw at the start how it would be done rightly (Judic. §.47, Dutch ed. pp. 69–70).

title: Annotatio I §.I close: Chytraeus — Luther at Marburg 1529 refused Zwinglians as brothers; Landgrave still sought peace — stop before §.II
english: Even the Lutheran David Chytraeus records the cause and author of the second priority.

In his full account of the 1529 Marburg colloquy he adds: after Luther refused to acknowledge Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bucer and their associates as brothers — because they taught differently on the true and essential presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Supper —
the Landgrave and other peace-seekers still did not stop laboring that the Supper dissent might be piously softened and Christian peace and fraternity set between both sides (p. mihi 647).
Stop before §. II (first controversy: interpretation of the Institution words Hoc est corpus meum — literal/κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν vs proper/improper).

title: Annotatio I §.II open: First prior Supper controversy — Institution words Hoc est corpus meum needlessly split in two
english: §. II. Of the earlier Protestant Supper controversies, the first is how to read the definitive Institution words: This is my body.
One party has needlessly torn that question in two: whether literally / κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, and whether the propositions This is my body / This is my Blood are taken properly or improperly.

title: Annotatio I §.II: Taking κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν three ways — retain words; follow native sense; want the sense proper
english: That one fight should not be counted as two is plain once you see that taking a proposition κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν can mean three things.
First: keep the words — formally, or by formal equipollents that do not even differ in concept.
Second: follow the words’ genuine native sense.
Third: want that sense to be proper.

title: Annotatio I §.II: No Protestant fight on the first two; only the third remains — is the literal sense proper or improper?
english: On the first two meanings Protestants have no lawsuit: both sides hold the formal (and equipollent) words, and one genuine sense that fits Christ’s mind.
Only the third stays doubtful and contested.
So the disputed “literal” sense of the words in the proposition reduces to this: is that literal sense proper, or improper?

title: Annotatio I §.II: Literal sense wider than proper/improper — Scherzer on literal/logical sense and figures
english: A biblical proposition’s literal sense is wider than proper vs improper, and stretches equally to both with equal clarity.
An improper predication does not make the sense less literal, less true, or less matched to the speaker’s intent — the letter is open to impropriety no less than to propriety.

Scherzer puts it best: the literal or logical sense is what the Spirit first and proximately intends, whether in proper words or figurative speech; otherwise many biblical sayings would have no literal sense at all (Syst. Theol. I.§.24).

title: Annotatio I §.II Schmidius: τὸ ῥητόν includes tropic acceptance — Matt. 16:16 and John 6:51 both literal; no Calvinist quarrel so far
english: Sebastian Schmidius agrees for the Supper proposition itself: the literal sense / τὸ ῥητόν is what the words immediately yield when all circumstances are weighed.
He gladly allows that τὸ ῥητόν covers not only words taken properly but also words taken tropically.

So Peter’s You are the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16) and Christ’s I am the living bread (John 6:51) are both literal — though only the second is a trope — and thus far there is no quarrel with the Calvinists (pp. 18–19).

title: Annotatio I §.II close: Real dispute — propositions proper (Lutherans) or improper (Reformed/Gomarus) — stop before §.III
english: After needless talk of word-propriety outside the proposition — which the Reformed never refuse — Schmidius himself grants that the whole Protestant fight over a retained or less-retained “literal” sense of the Supper words comes back to one question: as they complete Christ’s proposition, are This is my body taken properly or improperly?

For Lutherans the ῥητόν of This is my Body / This is my blood (as one whole proposition, not the several words stripped of their own proper sense) is when every word stays in its proper signification and no trope is admitted.

The Reformed deny only that those propositions, taken in their genuine literal sense, are proper (Gomarus, Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 10); Lutherans contend they are — otherwise the two sides would not differ here at all.
Stop before §. III (Reformed proofs that the definitive Supper propositions are improper — generic/specific arguments).

title: Annotatio I §.III open: Reformed prove Hoc est corpus meum improper — GENERICA and SPECIFICA genera
english: §. III. The Reformed argue that the definitive Supper propositions — above all This is my body — are not proper but improper.
They reduce the proofs to two genera: the GENERIC and the SPECIFIC nature of the proposition taken materially.

title: Annotatio I §.III GENERICA remote: Disparatum de disparato — Carlstadt Identica out; Gomarus / Bellarmine
english: As remoter genus, the GENERIC nature shows a disparate predicated of a disparate — whether τὸ hoc is bread alone, or bread with Christ’s body besides — once Carlstadt’s Identica This Body is my body is exploded as a novel fiction both Protestant sides hate.

Body predicated of bread is disparate of disparate; disparates force improper predication and shut out the proper — otherwise no improper speech would remain, and no metonymy or metaphor could exist except among disparates.

Gomarus builds this sharply (Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 14–20), ending with Bellarmine: common sense suffices — if disparates may be affirmed properly of disparates, one may as well affirm nothing of something, darkness of light, Belial of Christ (p. 139).

title: Annotatio I §.III: Personal predications no help — Vorstius concrete-of-concrete vs sacramental abstract-of-abstract
english: Objecting “personal” predications does not help here.
Vorstius notes that in those, a concrete is predicated of a concrete — not abstract disparate nature of abstract disparate nature.
In our sacramental saying, by contrast, abstract is predicated of abstract: body of bread, hence disparate of disparate.

title: Annotatio I §.III vs Musaeus: Eucharistic bread still abstract; body of composite; synecdoche / improper
english: Musaeus (§.99 vs Vorstius) claims the sacramental line somehow predicates concrete of concrete — this Eucharistic bread / Eucharist of two things is Christ’s body — citing Bajer on Impanation.
But blessing does not turn bread’s abstract nature into a concrete; and he conflates Eucharistic bread with the Eucharist itself.

Even then an abstract body is still predicated of a composite of body and bread — unlike personal propositions — so abstract of concrete remains disparate of disparate, a synecdoche, and thus improper.

title: Annotatio I §.III GENERICA nearer: Signatum de signo — metonymy/synecdoche when sign ≠ thing; sacramental induction
english: (II) As nearer genus, the GENERIC view shows the sacramental proposition predicating the thing signified of the sign.

That can be proper only when sign and thing are materially the same; when they differ, the predication is metonymic or synechdochic — sign for thing, container for content, or part for whole — and so improper.
Induction from Old and New Testament sacramentals in the Supper’s own Institution confirms that a horistic sacramental proposition is improper by nature.

title: Annotatio I §.III close: Circumcision and Passover institutions predicate improperly — stop before Baptism/Cup
english: (a) In circumcision’s Institution (Gen. 17:10–11) God’s covenant is predicated of circumcision only improperly — circumcision is the sign of the covenant, God Himself explaining in the next verse.

(b) In the Passover Institution (Exod. 12:11, 21, 27) passover / passage is predicated only improperly of the lamb and of its slaughter and eating — the same species of trope by which Christ is our passover (1 Cor. 5:7) and the desert rock was Christ by signification, not substance (Augustine, Quaest. Lev. 57).
Stop before §.III continuation (Baptism and Cup Institution inductions; SPECIFICA genus).

title: Annotatio I §.III cont: Passover instance applied to Hoc est corpus meum — same tropic hearing for the disciples
english: Tighten the consequence by applying that Passover instance to This is my Body.
Christ was instituting the Supper right after Passover for disciples still raw in the divine mysteries.

He cannot have meant This bread is my body to be heard differently from This lamb is the passover / passage — especially with broken for you and This cup is the N.T. in my blood poured out for you — or else He would have spoken obscurely and opened John-14-style puzzles.

title: Annotatio I §.III (y): Baptismal definitives — signata of the sign; metonymy or synecdoche
english: (y) In some baptismal definitives — Baptism is putting on Christ (Gal. 3:27); it is the appeal of a good conscience toward God (1 Pet. 3) — the Spirit predicates only Baptism’s signified things of the sign.
Whether the sign is bare external baptism or the whole exhibitive rite, the predication is metonymic or synechdochic; that cannot be denied.

title: Annotatio I §.III (d): Cup is the New Testament in Christ’s blood — many tropes; Valencia / Cajetan
english: (d) In the other half of the Supper Institution — Luke 22:20 and 1 Cor. 11:25 — The Cup is the N.T. in Christ’s blood.
No one easily denies that one line breathes several tropes — not even Cajetan.

Gregory of Valencia grants the necessity: the cup must be taken for the contained blood, and testament/promise is predicated of that blood only figuratively (as Matthew and Mark’s blood of the New Testament shows).

title: Annotatio I §.III: Scultetus grants tropum in the Cup words but denies consequence for the rest — Strimesius replies
english: Scultetus, in his recent Discussion of Reformed Universalism, grants a trope in those second-part Institution words, yet denies the consequence for the rest of the Eucharist Institution.
Proper sense, he says, is kept everywhere unless a grave cause blocks it — and in This is my body, he claims, there is none.
Strimesius notes he already agrees the Cup proposition is built of more than one trope, and all the more once Heb. 9:17, 20 shows it emulates Moses’ This is the blood of the N.T.

title: Annotatio I §.III close: Not all Institution words tropic from the Cup; yet sacramentals do not abhor impropriety — Disparatum as grave cause
english: So Strimesius consents on two points: admitting Cup impropriety does not make every other Institution word tropical; and proper sense stays unless a grave cause blocks it.

(1) He does not infer from This cup is the New Testament that all Supper Institution words are improper — only that definitive sacramentals so little abhor impropriety that from all the rest (This is my body set aside for now) one may most probably infer these too are improper.

(2) That impropriety must be written onto This is my body as well, because the gravest cause blocks propriety: otherwise a Disparate would have to be predicated properly of a Disparate against nature and sound reason.

title: Annotatio I §.IV open SPECIFICA: Testimonies acknowledging impropriety — Fathers explicit; stop before Picherellus catalog
english: §. IV. Arguments for the specific nature of the proposition under debate are drawn chiefly from those who acknowledge its impropriety in species — expressly, or implicitly by their interpretations.
EXPLICITLY figurative: the more ancient Church Fathers (collected by Oecolampadius and Melanchthon), the Reformed Jonstonus, and the Pontifician Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 28).
Stop before the Picherellus / Tertullian catalog and further SPECIFICA testimonies.

title: Annotatio I §.IV cont: Picherellus — Tertullian’s quasi vere; Origen, Augustine, Cyril on figurative eating
english: Picherellus is worth quoting: few own his Opuscula, and a Pontifician witness carries extra weight when his own side presses Christ’s words as proper.

On John 6’s Unless you eat the flesh… he reads Tertullian as taking the eating not truly — i.e. improperly — because the hearers treated the sermon as hard as if He had truly set His flesh to be eaten (quasi vere → non vere).
Origen, Augustine, and Cyril likewise mark figurative speech for that hard saying.

title: Annotatio I §.IV (2): Reformed doctors — Est as significat (Zwingli) or Est signum (Oecolampadius)
english: (2.) The Reformed doctors as one interpret the Est in This is my body either with Zwingli as significat, or with Oecolampadius as Est the sign or figure of my body.

title: Annotatio I §.IV: Do not confuse proposition-propriety with real supernatural presence and manducation
english: Do not mix the propriety of Christ’s Eucharistic proposition with the question of real substantial presence and manducation in the Supper.
Deny propriety of the words, and you still have not denied real presence or eating — the first fight is logical (words/terms); the second metaphysical (the thing).

This bread is my body can be improper while Christ’s body is truly present and eaten supernaturally and spiritually (John 6; 1 Cor. 10) — just as asserting propriety alone does not prove that presence.

title: Annotatio I §.IV (3): Many Lutherans concede tropic speech — Marbachius vs Pezelius
english: (3.) Not a few Lutherans concede tropic speech in genus, or metonymy / synecdoche in species.
Marbachius against Pezelius allows that This is my body does not shut out every figure — only the kind that forces us off each word’s proper signification.
On that the Reformed easily rest, pressing tropic locution while caring less whether the trope sits in the words or in the predication.

title: Annotatio I §.IV: Synecdoche Grammar vs Rhetoric; Mansfeld’s Calvinian vs Lutheran metonymy
english: On synecdoche, Selneccer, Luther, and countless others distinguish Grammatical from Rhetorical synecdoche — a distinction that sins against Grammar for anyone not still wet behind the ears.
Call it Grammatical or not: synecdoche remains a trope, like metonymy, metaphor, or irony.

Mansfeld grants metonymy in both halves of the Institution, yet under a rather ridiculous split between Calvinian sign/thing-signified metonymy and Lutheran effect-for-cause / container-for-content metonymy.

title: Annotatio I §.IV close IMPLICITE Pontificii: Double trope under the species — stop before Lutheran IMPLICITE
english: IMPLICITE, whoever interprets the proposition otherwise than the Reformed also make it tropical — Pontificians and Lutherans alike — even while both fight explicitly for word-propriety as for hearth and altar.
The Pontificians’ That which is contained under the species of bread and wine is my body embeds a double trope: synecdoche (this → accidents) and metonymy of container for contained.

Swap This is my body for under these accidents is my body and you deny proper hearing in the act — subject and attribute seats flip, and This is falsely traded for under these species (Gomarus, p. 142).
Stop before Lutheran IMPLICITE readings (Luther’s in/cum/sub; Flacius’s duplex mass).

title: Annotatio I §.IV IMPLICITE Lutheran: Luther’s duplex — in/cum/sub hoc pane (Schwärmer sermon)
english: The better-known Lutheran reading of This is my body is twofold.
Luther’s: This / this bread is my body means in, with, and under this bread is my body (Wittenberg Tom. II vs the Fanatics, p. 98).
Let the Schwärmer go — his nickname for those not ὁμοψῆφος with him on the sacrament — and stay with the words as they sound: IN THE BREAD Christ’s body, IN THE WINE His blood truly.

title: Annotatio I §.IV IMPLICITE Lutheran: Flacius’s complexum / duplex mass — both readings tropical
english: Flacius Illyricus’s other reading: This complex / this mass of two things is my body.
Both readings are openly tropical — Luther’s as metonymy of container for contained; Flacius’s as synecdoche of part for whole.

title: Annotatio I §.IV: Schmidius’s exception — Hoc as complexum plus demonstrative
english: Sebastian Schmidius tries to save Flacius’s more famous reading (or its propriety): τὸ Hoc names a complex and is demonstrative at once, so the proposition cannot turn tropical.
Strimesius will not let that exception stand.

title: Annotatio I §.IV: Replies (1)–(2) — complexum unproven; Luther vs King of England on hoc = bread
english: Reply (1): the Complex is not yet proved.
Reply (2): Luther himself rejects it — hoc means nothing but bread.

Against the King of England he threads the Institution verbs (took, blessed, broke) onto the bread: This is my body = this bread is my body; the pronoun shows the subject, not the predicate — the King hid those clear words and pressed the naked proposition onto the body.

title: Annotatio I §.IV: Captivitate Babylonica + Paul — panis is participation; not in pane est
english: In On the Babylonian Captivity Luther believes not only that Christ’s body is in the bread, but that the bread is Christ’s body — the Words keep him: This = this bread He took and broke.

Paul likewise: the bread we break is participation of Christ’s body — he does not say (NB.) it is in the bread, but the bread itself is that participation; common speech proves the demonstrative subject is bread when He says this is my body.

title: Annotatio I §.IV close IMPLICITE Lutheran: Replies (3)–(5) — part/whole, demonstration, Carlstadt; stop before §.V
english: (3.) Grant the Complex only for argument: then a part is predicated of the whole, and the proposition is tropical.
(4.) A demonstrative does not cancel the complex — therefore not the trope either.

(5.) Sense can only point to what senses reach: the sitting body (Carlstadt), the bread in Christ’s hands (Reformed sign-for-signified metonymy), or an invisible second body — which cannot be shown to sense, doubles Christ’s bodies, and drags back both the unproved Complex Luther rejected and a propriety hardly to be conceded.
Stop before §.V (Bucer / Lutheran tropus-limits).

title: Annotatio I §.V open: Lutherans exclude only the tropus that exterminates substance — Bucer & Chytraeus
english: Weighed more deeply: the Lutherans themselves want only one tropus shut out of This is my body — the kind that drives Christ’s true substance out of the Eucharist.
Bucer (Opera Anglicana p. 704 §26) and Chytraeus (p. 660 mid) attest that limit at length.

title: Annotatio I §.V: Bucer — Luther rejected our reading as if it removed presence; nostri deny absence-sign
english: Bucer: Luther rejected our interpretation, so far as his writings show, because he thought it removed Christ’s presence from the Supper.
Our doctors deny that bread is a sign meaning the body is absent or not taken — and they have said so in many books.

title: Annotatio I §.V: Augustine’s signum corporis; contention de verbis not de re — Epist. Buceri ad Pontanum
english: Calling bread a figure and sign of Christ’s body does not prove the body is absent — else Augustine too would be read as teaching bare bread, though he wrote against Adamantus: Christ did not hesitate to say this is my body when giving the sign of His body.

Our doctors never meant to deny presence; they only press that bread is not substantially the body, to lead people from visible bread to invisible Christ — so the fight is about words, not the thing (Bucer to Pontanus).

title: Annotatio I §.V: Calixtus Senior — Reformed metonymy as admissible ecclesiastical phrase
english: Calixtus Senior points the same way (Judgment on the Controversies §81, p. 136): the Reformers’ metonymic proposition is an ecclesiastical phrase that could be admitted.

title: Annotatio I §.V: Hoc pacto the controversy vanishes — tropus that keeps presence vs tropus that ejects it
english: On that pact the whole controversy ceases and vanishes.

The Reformed defend a tropus that will not let Christ’s body be absent from the Supper — still less make it so; the Lutherans fight a tropus that is less shy about moving the body out and stripping presence from the meal.

title: Annotatio I §.V close: Morton’s figurative proofs vs Pontificii — stop before Annotatio II
english: For the rest, see Morton (sometime Bishop of Durham), On the Eucharist II Class 1 chs. 2–4, for figurative Institution proofs against the Pontificians.
Stop before Annotatio II (Consubstantiation history).

title: Annotatio II open §.I: De Consubstantiatione — from verbal fight to real-presence debate
english: Annotatio II opens On Consubstantiation — a short history at Author pp. 34 and 36 fin.
§.I: the Eucharistic war has moved from the verbal fight over whether This is my body is proper or improper to a real debate on Christ’s bodily presence in the Supper — or rather its mode.

title: Annotatio II §.I: Three opinions — corporal with bread / transubstitution / spiritual to the faithful
english: Three camps: some join a corporal presence to the bread; others put Christ’s body in place of annihilated bread-substance; others deny the corporal and credit a spiritual presence to the spirits of the faithful.
All three hunt antiquity to prove their side.

title: Annotatio II §.I: Triple denomination and history — Consubstantiation, Transubstantiation, Spiritual Presence
english: From that triple opinion came a triple name and a triple history: Consubstantiation, Transubstantiation, and Spiritual Presence.
Strimesius will run them in a short compendium.

title: Annotatio II §.I close: Order of treatment — consub first, spiritual last, transub middle (Spanhemius); stop before §.II
english: Order: start with Consubstantiation — the part chiefly opposed to us in this Elenchus; end with ours (Spiritual Presence) as its antithesis.
Insert Transubstantiation in the middle only for kinship with the first, as Spanhemius notes.
Stop before §.II (Consubstantiation crassior vs subtilior).

title: Annotatio II §.II open: Consubstantiatio — crassior vs subtilior; crass local inclusion / physical mixture
english: §.II: Consubstantiation, by etymology, is the joining of two substances kept apart in themselves — considered in act or in state.
It comes in a crasser and a subtler form. The crasser means either local enclosure of Christ’s natural body in the bread, or an interior union like a physical mixture of altered elements.

title: Annotatio II §.II: Adversaries pin crassior on Luther — Carlstadt’s Gott im Brod
english: Adversaries say Luther taught that crasser mode after he rejected Transubstantiation.
Carlstadt pins local enclosure on him: You will not long persuade me that God is in the bread — and How can one bring Christ into bread and wine?

title: Annotatio II §.II: Becanus’s personal/perichoretic union; In/Cum/Sub + Verborgen → Impanation suspicion
english: Becanus (Manual Controv. II.2.2 p. 330) charges Luther with a personal, intimate, perichoretic union of body with bread.

Luther’s own speech feeds the suspicion: In, With, and Under this bread is my body, plus his hymn line hidden in the bread so small / He gave us His body to eat — ample handle for Impanation and Companation labels.

title: Annotatio II §.II: Babylonian Captivity Deus est homo parallel; Musculus absolves personal union
english: In On the Babylonian Captivity he compares bread–body union with the hypostatic union (Deus est homo), which looks personal.

Yet his Greater Confession on the Supper denies a personal mode, and the Captivity comparison is only bare Disparate-of-Disparate predication — so Musculus (among ours) absolves him from personal union of body and blood.

title: Annotatio II §.II: Lutherans — coexistence only; In/Cum/Sub together; Verborgen = imperceptibility; crassior not owed
english: Lutherans say the crasser-sounding formulas only mark inexplicable coexistence — hence In/Cum/Sub used together, never apart (though Annotatio I §§.3–4 showed the contrary).
Verborgen in the hymn means only that the mode of presence is imperceptible — hidden, incomprehensible, secret.
However forced the excuses, Strimesius will not rightly pin that crasser Consubstantiation on Luther or today’s Lutherans.

title: Annotatio II §.II close: Subtilior coexistence; Kronmayer/Suicer; Becanus — any consub kills proper predication; stop before §.III
english: Subtler Consubstantiation: bread and Christ’s body coexist in the Supper with an exterior, παραστατική union — substantial/corporal/local materially as to the things united, not formally as to union-mode; each keeps its own place.
Lutherans own the definition and the name Consubstantiation / συνουσία (Kronmayer; Bayer) — yet Suicer would call them ἐνουσιάσται, not συνουσιάσται.
Becanus’s sharper point: grant any Consubstantiation, even the Lutheran subtler kind, and proper predication of Christ’s words has nowhere left to stand.
Stop before §.III (history: conception / nativity / duration).

title: Annotatio II §.III open: Consubstantiation history — CONCEPTIO, NATIVITAS, PERDURATIO
english: §.III: both kinds of Consubstantiation get a short history in three moments.
CONCEPTION, then NATIVITY, then DURATION.

title: Annotatio II §.III CONCEPTIO: Triple error of consubstantiation-pressers — PRIMUS starts in early Fathers
english: CONCEPTION sits in a triple error of those who finally pressed either Consubstantiation.

FIRST error: early Fathers badly read — as if the Eucharist were two substances (earthly + celestial), or one earthly substance plus some celestial accident of external holiness or intrinsic divine virtue.

title: Annotatio II §.III (1): Irenaeus — Eucharist of earthly and celestial; restricted to use
english: (1) Irenaeus (A.D. 160) is the stock witness for two things, earthly and celestial, in the Eucharist after invocation.

But bk. 5 restricts the saying to use: celestial souls feed on celestial substance; earthly bodies on earthly — the creature-cup and creature-bread confirmed as His blood and body when they receive God’s word.

title: Annotatio II §.III (2): Justin & Gregory Nyssen — earthly substance with external holiness
english: (2) Justin (near Irenaeus’s senior) describes deacons giving bread and wine called Eucharist — not taken as common bread or cup.

Gregory of Nyssa: bread starts common, then consecrated is called Christ’s body — both mean bare external holiness (set apart by word and prayer; like oil, baptismal water, temple stones), not a second metaphysical substance.

title: Annotatio II §.III (3): Clement/Theodoret, Victor, Mark liturgy, Cyprian — Spirit’s virtue; spiritual presence only
english: (3) Clement (via Theodoret’s Stromata epitome): bread and oil change by the power of the names into spiritual power — not same in appearance.

Victor of Antioch, the Liturgy of St. Mark, and Cyprian speak of the Spirit sending life-virtue into the species — yet all introduce only a spiritual presence of Christ’s body, by the Spirit’s authorship and effect.

title: Annotatio II §.III close CONCEPTIO error 1: Fathers twisted toward corporal union ante usum; stop before §.IV
english: Those Father-sayings meant legitimate use: the worthy receive earthly and celestial; 1 Tim. 4 sanctification; Spirit’s virtue toward communicants, not a changed bread-substance.
Rhetorical, not metaphysical — yet consubstantiation-pressers twist them as if the Fathers taught corporal bread–body union before and outside faithful use, ex opere operato to any eater.
Stop before §.IV (SECOND error — middle-ages Fathers after Chalcedon).

title: Annotatio II §.IV open: CONCEPTIO error 2 — middle-ages Fathers vs Eutyches absorption
english: §.IV: after the first error comes a SECOND — middle-ages Fathers after Chalcedon, read askew.
Fighting Eutyches they said Christ’s exalted human nature is not absorbed by the divine more than bread is absorbed by Christ’s body in legitimate Eucharistic use.

title: Annotatio II §.IV: Chrysostom & Theodoret — bread remains after sanctification (Burnet / Picherellus)
english: Burnet (39 Articles p. 330) and Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 176) stack the same loci.
Chrysostom to Caesarius: after sanctification the bread is worthy of the Lord’s-body name, yet the bread-signature remains.
Theodoret’s Dialogue II: the mystical signs keep prior substance, figure, and form — still bread to sight and touch, understood as believed.

title: Annotatio II §.IV: Gelasius & Prosper — divine thing, yet bread/wine nature; sacrament and res
english: Gelasius against Eutyches: what we take is a divine thing, yet does not cease to be the substance and nature of bread and wine.
Prosper: Eucharist = visible element-species + invisible Lord’s flesh and blood (sacrament and res), as Christ’s person is God and man.

title: Annotatio II §.IV: Primary anti-absorption intent twisted into ante-usum hypostatic-style union
english: Those texts first meant to block belief that after spiritual bread–body union the bread is abolished or absorbed.
Consubstantiation-seekers bend them instead: after consecration, even before use, they imagine union like the divine person joining Christ’s human nature in Mary’s womb into one ὑφιστάμενον.

title: Annotatio II §.IV close: CONCEPTIO error 3 — Bertram/Ratramnus & Berengar; embryo into public light; stop before §.V
english: THIRD error (9th–11th c.): crudely heard Bertram/Ratramnus on the figure of Christ’s body (to Charles the Bald), plus Berengar’s figure-sayings taken too raw.
Opponents denied figure so hard they urged corporal union — and so forced the long-fostered Consubstantiation embryo, crass or subtle, into public light.
Stop before §.V (Paschasius Radbertus as alleged first author).

title: Annotatio II §.V open: Burmann & Bayer name Paschasius Radbertus first Consubstantiation author
english: §.V: Reformed Burmann (Synopsis Theol. II p. 401) and Lutheran Bayer (Theol. Histor. p. 593) both cast Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie — Bertram’s coeval adversary — as Consubstantiation’s first author and father.
They point to his book under the same title as Bertram’s.

title: Annotatio II §.V: Bellarmine — conversion/transubstantiation propagator; Cave seconds; Rhadebert’s own sayings
english: Bellarmine is nearer the mark: Paschasius propagates Conversion, the seed of Transubstantiation (Eucharist Controversies; Ecclesiastical Writers).
Cave adds his vote; Paschasius’s own On the body and blood of the Lord ch. 20 props that reading.

title: Annotatio II §.V: Bertram knows only two opinions — spiritual vs corporal-by-conversion; no silent third
english: Bertram nearly settles it: in his day he knows only two opinions — spiritual presence (his own, with the Fathers of every age) versus corporal presence by conversion of the bread (Paschasius), which he attacks.
Had there been a novel third (consubstantiation), he would not have passed it in silence — least of all in his adversary.

title: Annotatio II §.V: Bayer concession — first oral reception of the proper body, yet for the faithful only
english: Concede to Bayer this much: Paschasius is first to teach oral reception of Christ’s proper body in the Supper without tooth-laceration.
Even then he restricts oral reception to the faithful alone — that food only for Christ’s friends and brothers.

title: Annotatio II §.V close: Burmann concession — spiritual manducation too; stop before Berengar-confuter inventors
english: Concede to Burmann likewise: Radbertus also teaches spiritual eating of the flesh and spiritual drinking of the blood in the Supper sacrament.
Stop before Berengar’s confuters as inventors of crassior/subtilior (Rupert of Deutz &c.).

title: Annotatio II NATIVITAS open: Inventors among Berengar’s confuters — PRIORIS Rupert of Deutz
english: Among Berengar’s confuters you easily find inventors of both crasser and subtler Consubstantiation.
Of the crasser: Rupert, Abbot of Deutz — Gerhard owns him; Forbes and Bayer list him only as insult — because Rupert’s own exposition brands him a crass Impanator.

title: Annotatio II NATIVITAS: Rupert’s Genesis gold/fire analogy — bread still bread, yet truly Christ
english: Genesis commentary (VI.32): how is visible bread Christ? Like gold in strong fire — still gold to sight, yet truly called and is fire.
So bread brought into Christ’s passion-mystery still seems bread, yet in truth is Christ — a similitude Augsburg brothers later use of iron.

title: Annotatio II NATIVITAS: Rupert’s Exodus — bread/wine substance joined, not destroyed, into body-unity
english: Exodus commentary (II.10): as God did not destroy human nature when joining it into personal unity from the virgin’s womb, so He does not destroy bread-and-wine substance when joining it to the Word into unity of the crucified body and shed blood.
What we take from the altar we truly call Christ, the Lamb of God — as we confess the virgin-born man on the cross to be God.

title: Annotatio II NATIVITAS: Cuno of Siegburg — accomplice and patron of Rupert’s sentence
english: Rupert names Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, accomplice and patron of his sentence.
In the Genesis/Exodus preface Christ stood by him through Cuno alone against those who roared at the work — Cuno a peg in a faithful place for the vessel of his hope.

title: Annotatio II NATIVITAS: Guitmund — PANI ET VINO COMMISCENTES; Impanent et Invinent heresy
english: Same eleventh century, the other way: Guitmund of Aversa calls the sentence a heresy to smother in the blade.
Beaten from denying Christ’s body in the Lord’s food, some mix Christ with bread and wine and found another heresy — Impanate and Invinate by their own authority.
No prophet, Christ, apostle, or world taught Impanation; the Lord kills Impanators with This is My Body — not In this lies My body.

title: Annotatio II NATIVITAS close crassior: Alger vs personal Impanation; stop before §.VI Ascelinus subtilior
english: Alger joins Guitmund: some erring readers make Christ personally Impanated as God is personally Incarnate — a new absurd heresy to root out by reason and authority.
Stop before §.VI (SUBTILIOR inventor Ascelinus).

title: Annotatio II §.VI open: SUBTILIOR first author — not Berengar but Ascelinus (Cave vs Bayer/Guitmund)
english: §.VI: first author of the subtler Consubstantiation is not Berengar — Guitmund guessed that from hearsay, and Bayer followed him blind.
It is Ascelinus, a monk Cave remembers and Bayer (with many) never knew.

title: Annotatio II §.VI: Ascelinus follows Paschasius on corporal presence, yet defends coexistence not conversion
english: Ascelinus’s letter to Berengar (Dacherius, from Casale Benedicti membranes) owns Paschasius on corporal presence of Christ’s flesh in the sacrament.
On consecrated bread and the mode of presence he writes far otherwise: not conversion of bread into body, but at least coexistence of the Body with the blessed bread.

title: Annotatio II §.VI: Letter to Berengar — altar bread/wine UNIATUR to the virgin-born body
english: His words: do not marvel that God can make altar-consecrated bread and wine, by Spirit and priest, be united to the body our Redeemer took from Mary.
Both are corporeal substance; both visible.

title: Annotatio II §.VI close: Union similitudes; Asceliniana egg-to-egg with modern Lutheran; stop before §.VII
english: Similitudes illustrate the union of two substances, not the mode: we are compacted of corporeal/incorporeal and mortal/immortal; in Christ divine and human meet in one person.
Letter at Dacherius on Lanfranc (Paris 1648); Otrokocsi cites it.
These Asceliniana — union of bread and body without pious/impious distinction — match modern Lutheran sentence as egg to egg.
Stop before §.VII (Nativitas summary / Lateran XIII).

title: Annotatio II §.VII open: Nativitas of both Consubstantiations reborn — Lateran XIII under Innocent III
english: §.VII: both Consubstantiations have their Nativity reborn in the 13th century — Lateran Council under Innocent III.
That council already treats Consubstantiation as an exploded, antiquated opinion, and names it thus:

title: Annotatio II §.VII: Lateran names Consubstantiation as already exploded — true accidents and true substance remain
english: Some said: after consecration, as true bread-accidents remain, so true bread-substance remains.
For a subject cannot stand without accidents, nor accidents without a subject.

title: Annotatio II §.VII: Under remaining substances — BODY AND BLOOD; sense proves bread/wine, faith the rest
english: With bread and wine substances still there, at Body and Blood of Christ those start to be under them.
Under the same accidents both are truly received — bread and flesh, wine and blood — sense proves one, faith the other.

title: Annotatio II §.VII close: After Berengar’s public censure; consub born from over-fighting him; stop before §.VIII
english: By then Berengar’s sentence had already taken public censure in his person.
Consubstantiators had openly fought him — and in over-fighting him had begotten their own Consubstantiation.
More on that in the Annotations that follow.
Stop before §.VIII (PERDURATIO / revival after apparent extinction).

title: Annotatio II §.VIII open PERDURATIO: Seemed extinct — Waldenses not consub; revived by John of Paris
english: §.VIII PERDURATIO: Consubstantiation looked extinct — short-lived, few teachers; Waldenses (some claim) keep a subtler line, but they actually teach something else (see Annotatio IV).
Yet it rose again near the end of the 13th century through John of Paris, Dominican.

title: Annotatio II §.VIII: Scotus and Durandus (1320) tolerate revival; Aquinas not to be dragged in
english: Some Scholastics did not reject the revival — Scotus early in the 14th century, and Durandus in 1320 (Otrokocsi, Irenicum VI.27ff.).
Aquinas is not to be dragged into this consent by Dorsche, even if he grants Transubstantiation is not proved from the Institution words alone.

title: Annotatio II §.VIII: Peter d’Ailly of Cambrai (1414) favors it — Luther admits drawing from him
english: Peter d’Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, at Constance (1414) began to favor it more openly — the same whose hand and counsel saw Huss and Jerome of Prague perish.
Luther himself confesses he drew that line from Cambrai (Babylonian Captivity, Jena Latin II fol. 263).

title: Annotatio II §.VIII: Luther’s Captivity — true bread and wine; Thomist opinions are not articles of faith
english: Luther: Cambrai’s Sentences IV gave him leave to think true bread and wine on the altar likelier than bare accidents — unless the Church had ruled otherwise.
Seeing that Church was Thomist/Aristotelian, he fixed his conscience: true bread and wine, with Christ’s true flesh and blood no less than under accidents.
Thomist opinions stay opinions, not articles of faith — even if an angel from heaven said otherwise; without Scripture or proven revelation, opinion is free, belief not owed.

title: Annotatio II §.VIII close: Bayer wastes oil proving Luther ≠ Cambrai; stop before §.IX Marburg
english: So Bayer wastes oil and labor trying to prove Luther both differed from Cambrai and shared a wider common opinion (Disput. de Impan. §50).
Stop before §.IX (Marburg determination; difficulties of corporal-in-bread presence).

title: Annotatio II §.IX open: Cameracensis opinion not charged to today’s Lutherans — they refuse it
english: §.IX: whatever one makes of Luther versus Cambrai, today’s Lutherans will not wear Cambrai’s opinion as theirs.
That refusal is enough — we do not impute it to them.

title: Annotatio II §.IX: Marburg determination does not free Luther from corporal-in-bread / subtilior consub
english: Marburg’s determination (we have not agreed whether the true body and blood are corporally present in the bread and wine) does not free Luther from corporal presence in or with the bread — nor from subtler Consubstantiation.
Those words confess not presence alone but a corporal mode in the bread itself.
Colophon: watch the difficulties that press corporal-in-bread presence for crassior or subtilior (at least Luther’s) Consubstantiation.

title: Annotatio II §.IX (1): Scripture — bread is called body, not body corporally present in the bread
english: (1) Scripture and Institution say the bread is Christ’s body — not that the body is present to the bread, less corporally present to it, least of all corporally present in it.
Call presence corporal and you import locality and inclusion; then the bread is not the body, because the body is only said to exist corporally present in the bread.

title: Annotatio II §.IX (2): First Institution — body at table, not in bread; else two bodies / self-eating
english: (2) At the first Institution Christ’s body was corporally at the table — so not corporally in the bread.

If it was in the bread while He Himself ate with the disciples (Matt. 26:29; Mark 14:25), He ate His own flesh in and under the bread — whole body and soul in His mouth — hence either multiplication of one body, or two bodies (one eating, one eaten).

title: Annotatio II §.IX (3): Sacraments are signs, not δοχεῖα containers — Augustine; baptism analogy
english: (3) No sacrament is a sign that contains the thing signified in its essence — sacraments are not δοχεῖα jars enclosing what they signify (cask, purse, cradle), though Luther and Maulbronn use such likenesses.
Augustine: visible signs of invisible grace — a sign signifies; it does not contain corporally.
Hence Lutherans dare not say Christ’s blood is corporally in baptismal water.

title: Annotatio II §.IX (4): Body corporally in one place — heaven now; Vigilius; Luther’s Bible preface
english: (4) Christ’s body is corporally in one place only — at the Institution at the table, not also in the bread in His hands; now corporally in heaven (Acts 3:21; Matt. 26:29; 1 Cor. 11:26).
Vigilius: as when on earth it was not in heaven, so now in heaven it is not on earth.
Luther’s Bible preface: we dwell on earth with the body before Christ seated in heaven, and are with Him only spiritually by faith — three points Strimesius marks.

title: Annotatio II §.IX close (5): Determination aporiae — spiritual presence in the believer’s soul, not in bread; stop before Annotatio III
english: (5) Consubstantiation cannot settle the body’s internal quality or external condition if it is corporally in the bread — emptied or exalted? with soul or without? bloody or bloodless? whole in each species or part?
The doubt ends only if we confess the body present in the Supper supernaturally and spiritually — not in the bread, but in the soul of the true-faith eater alone.
Stop before Annotatio III.

title: Annotatio III open §.I: Transsubstantiation — if not by name, by rem older than Consubstantiation; absurd rem, late apt term
english: Annotatio III opens on Transsubstantiation (to p. 36 end): a short History-compendium.
§.I: as rem (if not yet as name) it is older than Consubstantiation; the rem it names is most absurd; the term itself came late but fits the generic concept.

title: Annotatio III §.I: Definition — one substance into another under residual accidents; ORTUS / PROGRESSUS plan
english: Transmutation reshapes form; Transsubstantiation turns one substance into another while sense-exposed accidents of the former remain and those of the latter are absorbed — a mutation without precedent.
Plan: ORTUS (causes) then PROGRESSUS (modes and degrees), treated here only for kinship with Consubstantiation.

title: Annotatio III §.II: Occasional cause of Ortus — GENERALIOR = hyperbolic / catachrestic Fathers on Eucharistic symbols
english: §.II Ortus causes: also the Occasional (cause by accident).
GENERALIOR: hyperbolic — sometimes even catachrestic — Father-speech on Eucharistic symbols; mishandled, it leads the unwary into error.

title: Annotatio III §.II: Chrysostom samples — immolated Lord handled; teeth fixed in His flesh (Hom. Matt. / Cor. / John)
english: Chrysostom (Eastern Fathers’ most eloquent): in the Eucharist you behold the immolated Lord — seated with the Father yet handled, seen, touched, eaten; blood from His side stains the tongue (Hom. Matt. / 1 Cor.).
Again: He knits us into one mass with Himself; teeth are fixed in His flesh so that by the food given we are turned into His flesh (Hom. 45 on John).

title: Annotatio III §.II close: Augustine / Prosper ‘carried in His hands’; QUASI / QUODAMMODO; Picherellus; de Marca / Whitaker
english: Augustine (Serm. 1 on Ps. 33): Christ was carried in His own hands when He said ‘This is My Body’; Prosper parallels Him bearing His body in the sanctified bread.
Such hyperboles aimed to exalt the mystery and turn communicants from outward symbols to the things signified — yet some took them too properly, missing QUASI / QUODAMMODO softenings (Picherellus).
More samples: de Marca’s posthumous Eucharist dissertation (pontifical abuse) — vindicated by Whitaker.

title: Annotatio III §.III: SPECIALIOR ansa — Greek emphatic μεταβολή-terms for relative / mystic mutation, not substance
english: §.III SPECIALIOR handle: Greek emphatic change-terms (metabole, metamorphosis, metapoiesis, metastoicheiosis, metatyposis, metarrhythmismos, metaskeuasis) for a mutation relative to the thing signified and mystic for communicants — cited via our Author, Salmasius, Johnston.
Fathers meant moral and schetic (relative) change; later readers bred a substantial-mutation opinion from those words.

title: Annotatio III §.III close: Four reasons Fathers meant moral / σχετική mutation; Dunelm; stop before §.IV vera causa
english: Four proofs Fathers meant no mutation beyond that: (1) consecrated breads remain what they were; (2) they are still called signs/figures/symbols/types — so conversion into Christ’s body is implicitly denied (Johnston).
(3) Same terms describe the faithful’s union with Christ by due Eucharist use; (4) same terms on other things no one takes as substantial conversion — Dunelm on that metabole vocabulary.
Stop before §.IV vera causa (idolatry and tyranny of Papism).

title: Annotatio III §.IV open: From non-cause to VERA ORTUS CAUSA — Idololatria & Tyrannis of Papism
english: §.IV: leave the non-cause; the TRUE CAUSE of Transsubstantiation’s Ortus sits in Idolatry and Tyranny.
That pair is Papism’s true soul, and will win it Antichristianism’s highest disgrace.

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Sixth century — sacred image use and cult arise in temples; once unheard-of and hated
english: When the Apostolic / Episcopal / Patristic centuries were spent (or nearly ended), about the sixth century sacred-image use and cult began to strengthen in temples.
Earlier ages had never heard of it; Protestant public Confessions hate it still more.

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Constantinopolitanum IV (Leo Isaurus / Copronymus) — 380 Fathers ban temple images
english: Opponents of the new idolomania gathered in Constantinopolitanum IV (popularly ‘Seventh Oecumenical’) under Leo the Isaurian and Constantine Copronymus.
380 Fathers unanimously: tolerate no temple images — least of all figures of God and of Christ.

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Sole known figure of Christ — that given in the Sacred Eucharist / consecrated bread
english: Annexed reason, most express: the true Church never knew any other Figure of Christ than the one given in the Sacred Eucharist and seen in the consecrated Bread.
Sagittarius (council epitomator) reports the Constantinopolitans’ mind and constitution so.

title: Annotatio III §.IV: Sagittarius — painters’ insane opinion; flesh-image apology = Nestorian diabolic invention
english: Sagittarius’s quote: what insane painters’ opinion — for base gain they try to figure with impious hands what mouth and heart alone confess?
Condemned for painting Christ’s incomprehensible, uncircumscribable Divine nature, they invent a flesh-only image apology — impious, and a Nestorian diabolic invention.

title: Annotatio III §.IV close: True image = Eucharistic bread as type; substance commanded vs human-effigy idolatry; stop before §.V
english: The true image of Christ they honor is what the High Priest Himself handed at the passion as type and efficacious remembrance: blessed, broken bread — ‘This is My body’.

As the assumed humanity is material substance (lest Divinity get an addition), so He commanded bread’s substance as the whole chosen image — lest a human effigy breed idolatry; Eucharist bread, Spirit-sanctified true image of natural flesh, He willed a divine body (Sagittarius pp. 354–355).
Stop before §.V (Nicaea II overturn).

title: Annotatio III §.V open: Constantinopolitan judgment barely heard — image patrons’ rage ~30 years to Nicaea II
english: §.V: the Constantinopolitans’ salutary, Word-congruent judgment was barely heard before image-patrons grew angry.

After ~30 years their indignation forced Nicaea II — called Second Nicene from the city, but by pontiffs ‘Seventh Oecumenical’ (as the Orthodox had styled Constantinopolitanum) — and an adverse decree contradicted those Fathers.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Nicaea II (pontiffs’ ‘Oecumenical 7th’) — temple image use/cult not to be despised
english: Nicaea II: temple image use and cult are not to be despised.
In particular, images of Christ crucified for us revive His memory.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Eucharist-‘figure’ reason overturned — consecrated bread said to be the body itself, not a figure
english: The counter-reason from the Eucharist as image/figure was judged so false that consecrated supper-bread must be held not a Figure of Christ’s body but the body itself.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Implies Conversion — Transsubstantiation’s chick under the egg-shell, soon to be named
english: Taken properly that cannot stand: bread’s substance remains wholly diverse in species from Christ’s body, and neither disparate shares the other’s specific essence.
So it implicitly fostered Conversion — Transsubstantiation’s chick under the egg-shell, soon to break into light and after an octave be named.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Bellarmine — from Nicaea II Greeks often: Eucharist not figure but body; mode unknown ~200 years
english: Bellarmine: from Nicaea II (not sooner) Greek Fathers often — not always — warned the Eucharist is not a figure but Christ’s body (Tom. 3 de Eucharist. p. 579 Ingolstadt); they did not expressly inculcate it.
For ~200 years they still left the mode wholly unknown, in the middle.

title: Annotatio III §.V: Paschasius (IX) vs Bertram — conversion asserts; Otrokocsi on crassior substantial sense
english: Ninth century: Paschasius Radbertus rises against Bertram (who with the Ancients kept the bread a Figure) and expressly professes conversion — under visible bread-species only Christ’s flesh is offered; bread into flesh, wine into blood (De corp. & sang. Dom. 10 & 20).
Otrokocsi: Paschasius means a crasser substantial conversion, unlike ancients/Bertram’s sacramental-mystic speech.

title: Annotatio III §.V close: Paschasius nuances (faithful only; not by teeth) vs Lombard; Hucusque Otrokocsi; stop before §.VI
english: Paschasius quirks: flesh and blood under the species, yet received only by a true believer; not chewed by teeth — marvels that already distance him from later followers.
Hands may handle and mouth receive under bread-species, but teeth do not wear the flesh; he had not yet spun Lombard’s accident-only fraction/attrition subtlety. Hucusque Otrokocsi.
Stop before §.VI (public Ortus / Berengar XI).

title: Annotatio III §.VI open: Ortus gained but obscure/private — public light only in the eleventh century
english: §.VI: Transsubstantiation has its Ortus — but still obscure and private.
Public authority will push it into public light only in the eleventh century.

title: Annotatio III §.VI: Berengar follows Bertram’s orthodox Eucharist opinion — yet crudely, almost a naked figure
english: Berengar follows Bertram’s orthodox Eucharist opinion (with many allies).
Yet he seems to speak crudely: consecrated bread almost a naked Figure of Christ’s body.

title: Annotatio III §.VI: Lanfranc and doctors pierce him — Leo IX (1049) & Nicholas II (1059): judgment, prison, recantation
english: Private and public doctors — Lanfranc of Canterbury foremost — pierce him with their pens.
Leo IX (1049) and Nicholas II (1059) haul him to judgment, prison, and a forced recantation.

title: Annotatio III §.VI: Recantation publicly confirms Paschasius’s conversion — and solemnly introduces dental laceration
english: That recantation publicly confirms Paschasius’s conversion of bread into Christ’s body.
It also solemnly introduces the dental laceration of Christ’s body — which Paschasius himself had found most absurd.

title: Annotatio III §.VI: Ego Berengarius — sensualiter handled, broken, worn by the faithful’s teeth (Gratian)
english: Ego Berengarius: after consecration the altar bread and wine are not only sacrament/symbol/figure but the true body and blood.
And SENSUALLY — in truth, not only in sacrament — priests’ hands handle and break them, and the faithful’s teeth wear them (Gratian De Consecr. dist. 2 c. 42).

title: Annotatio III §.VI: Berengar revokes the forced palinode — Hildebrand/Gregory VII beats him into a new substantial-conversion formula
english: Berengar, conscience-struck, published a revocation of that forced palinode as absurd and impious, calling the council a church of the malignant and of vanity.
Hildebrand (Gregory VII) summoned him to Rome, beat him with rods, and after a three-month truce forced a new formula: mystic bread substantially converted into Christ’s true proper flesh.

title: Annotatio III §.VI close: Walden / Uspergensis / Ussher / Dunelm on Berengar; stop before §.VII (public monster / Lateran name)
english: Recantation formula: Thomas Walden Tom. 2 ch. 24; Abbot of Ursperg Chronicle at 1080.
Full Berengar history: Ussher De successione Ecclesiarum ch. 7 §§28–end, summarized in John of Durham’s Historia Transsubstantiationis ch. 7 §.4 ff. pp. 134–143.
Stop before §.VII (public monster seated by papal decrees / Lateran name).

title: Annotatio III §.VII open: Transsubstantiation’s monster thrust into public light — still unnamed; seated by papal decrees
english: §.VII: by this path the horrible Transsubstantiation-monster is thrust into public light — yet still without its proper name.
Papal decrees from Peter’s Roman seat plant it firmly enough on a throne.

title: Annotatio III §.VII: After Lombard and the Scholastics dispute the true Conversion-mode — subtle and sharp
english: That seating follows Scholastic dispute on the true Conversion-mode in the Eucharist.
Lombard (bk. 4 dist. 11 pp. 311–313) leads — subtle and sharp alike.

title: Annotatio III §.VII: Mid-XII — Transsubstantiation’s name invented (Peter of Blois / Stephen of Autun)
english: Mid-twelfth century: the name Transsubstantiation is invented.
Cave points to Peter of Blois Ep. 140; others to Stephen of Autun On the Sacrament of the Altar (Bibliotheca Patrum — author and date very uncertain).

title: Annotatio III §.VII: 1215 — Innocent III canonizes the name in his Lateran Council
english: Next century, 1215: Pope Innocent III canonizes that name in his Lateran Council.
So the invented term Transsubstantiatio becomes a canon of the faith under Lateran IV.

title: Annotatio III §.VII: Innocent’s allocution — Dunelm: rival of Christ, not mere Vicar, when the article is thrust
english: Innocent betrays the author of the canonization in his own sermons — ‘To me it is said in the Prophet: I have set you over nations and kingdoms…’ (as a shrew by its voice).
Dunelm (pp. 149–150): commemorate this already Rival of Christ, not mere Vicar, to see the Latin Church’s face when Transsubstantiation was thrust as an article of faith.

title: Annotatio III §.VII close: Firmiter canon — TRANS SUBSTANTIATIS bread into body; Sagittarius; stop before §.VIII
english: Firmiter (Extravag. De Fide & summa Trinitate): one universal Church; Christ’s body and blood truly under bread and wine species.
Key clause: bread TRANSUBSTANTIATED into body and wine into blood by divine power — only a duly ordained priest may confect (Sagittarius p. 495).
Stop before §.VIII (still on the Scholastic anvil after canonization).

title: Annotatio III §.VIII open: Even canonized — Transsubstantiation still on the Scholastic disputation-anvil
english: §.VIII: even after canonization, Transsubstantiation is not past concussion or overthrow.
Scholastic standard-bearers still hammer the genuine Conversion-mode on a licentious disputation-anvil — every part, every which way.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: Antesignani probe Conversion-mode every way — John of Paris joins; many opinions cited
english: John of Paris joins those Antesignani.
From his pages 30 and 50–77 a more copious heap of opinions is adduced.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: Werenfels reduces their opinions to a dozen (German Concio on the Sacred Supper)
english: Our Werenfels trims that heap to a dozen.
Source: his German Concio on the Sacred Supper, p. 30.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: XIV–XV reformers — Rupert/Ascelinus consub, or ancient supernatural/spiritual presence kept
english: Fourteenth- and fifteenth-century reformers of pontifical idolomania also rose.

Some restore Rupert of Deutz and Ascelinus on Consubstantiation (crasser or subtler); others restore the pristine Church’s supernatural and spiritual presence of Christ’s body in the Supper — and keep it to this day, undeterred by Trent’s brute thunderbolt.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: Not deterred by Trent Sess. XIII cap. 4 Can. 2 — TRANSSUBSTANTIATIO defined
english: Trent Sess. XIII cap. 4 Can. 2 (p. 130): because Christ said what He offered under bread-species was truly His body, consecration converts the whole substance of bread into His body and of wine into His blood.
That conversion the holy Catholic (Roman) Church conveniently and properly calls TRANSUBSTANTIATION.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII: Anathema if bread-substance remains — Pius IV profession/oath names Transsubstantiation
english: Anathema if anyone says bread and wine substance remain with body and blood, or denies that singular conversion with species alone remaining.

Nor do they delay the Pope’s definition and the Council’s unjust confirmation: profession and oath must follow this Transsubstantiation form — Ego N. … truly, really, substantially body and blood; conversion of whole substances — Pius IV’s bull on the Trent faith-oath.

title: Annotatio III §.VIII close: Pius IV bull curse (Rome, 13 Nov 1564); stop before §.IX Form from Lombard/Aquinas
english: That thirteenth Roman-Symbol article closes with Pius IV’s threat: none may infringe this page; presumers incur God’s and Peter and Paul’s indignation.
Dated Rome at St. Peter’s, 13 November 1564 (Ides).
Stop before §.IX (Form from Lombard / Aquinas / Hoc est corpus meum).

title: Annotatio III §.IX open: Historia’s Form — Lombard Sent. IV Dist. VIII and Aquinas ST 3 q.78 a.1
english: §.IX: so the History stands; they lodge its Form in Lombard Sent. IV Dist. VIII (p. 307).
Chief commentator: Aquinas ST 3 q.78 a.1 (p. 292).

title: Annotatio III §.IX: Form in Hoc est Corpus meum / Hic est sanguis — priest’s enunciation confects Transsubstantiation
english: Form = enunciation of Christ’s words: Hoc est Corpus meum; Hic est sanguis meus; or Hic est calix sanguinis mei.
By the priest’s speaking those words, they say, the Sacrament of Transsubstantiation is confected.

title: Annotatio III §.IX: Some require inserting causal ENIM (Matt. 26:28) under both Eucharist parts
english: Some insist on inserting the causative conjunction ENIM into those words.
It stands in Matt. 26:28, so they would have it understood under both Eucharist parts everywhere.

title: Annotatio III §.IX: ENIM partly aetiological, partly promissive — baptism parallel (Mark 16:16)
english: ENIM is partly aetiological — why what was offered was to be eaten and drunk.
Partly promissive — like Baptism’s own promise: whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved.

title: Annotatio III §.IX: Without ENIM some call the Form incomplete — Transsubstantiation not fully confected (Picherellus)
english: Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. §.8) is cited on this.
Others press the little word so hard that without adding ENIM they call the Form incomplete — Transsubstantiation not fully done.

title: Annotatio III §.IX close: Stillingfleet vs White before James II — Mass without Enim still latria = material idolatry; stop before §.X
english: Stillingfleet, disputing with Jesuit White before James II, used that to warn: standers at a Mass that omits Enim, adoring the ‘venerable,’ cannot escape even material idolatry on their own hypothesis.
By latria they would worship what — for want of enim — has not yet become Christ’s true body (Israel-in-the-desert parallel).
Stop before §.X (Transsubstantiation unworthy of Christ’s banquet; eliminate from the Church).

title: Annotatio III §.X open: Whatever of the Form — Transsubstantiation unworthy of Christ’s banquet; eliminate it
english: §.X: leave the four- or five-word Form fight — rashly pinned on without Scripture’s authority.
Transsubstantiation itself, taken in full scope, is utterly unworthy of Christ’s instituted banquet and most worthy to be wiped from Christ’s whole Church.

title: Annotatio III §.X: Else it turns the Church Antichristian — tyrannizing Revelation, Reason, and the Senses
english: Otherwise it remakes the Church truly Antichristian — especially by staking its own Necessity on many Anathemas.
It tyrannizes divine Revelation (belief and practice), human Reason, and all the Senses, trying to break and abolish their force.

title: Annotatio III §.X (1): Adversatur Scripture — Institution antithesis; Hottinger’s dozen-plus
english: (1) It is adverse to Holy Scripture — overthrown elsewhere and above all where the Sacrament’s Institution is given.
Hottinger (Eucharist Defense VIII, pp. 79–84) shows that from an antithesis denser than a dozen.

title: Annotatio III §.X (1) cont.: Forbes points to Picherellus and Spalatinus among Pontificians themselves
english: Forbes, with many learned Protestants, has shown the dogma adverse to Scripture.
He also begs readers to weigh Pontificians against themselves: Picherellus on the Institution-words and the Mass, and Spalatinus De Republ. Eccles. 5.6 (Fabricius p. 600) refuting it at length.

title: Annotatio III §.X (2): Adversatur Analogia fidei — body-nature articles; forged miracles worsen the clash
english: (2) It clashes with the divine Analogy of faith — Creed articles and Scripture on Christ’s body as substantially like ours.
Forged miracles here do not heal that contradiction; they worsen it, tearing also the analogy of faith about what miracles are for.

title: Annotatio III §.X (2) close: Daily Mass-‘miracles’ vs the senses; Tillotson; Melchior — credible only by Enthusiasm; stop before (3)
english: Miracles should be rare, not rash, to convince the senses of what is hard to believe; the papistic Mass instead commands the same ‘miracle’ daily in countless places against the senses’ clearest contrary witness (Tillotson Sermons 3, pp. 364–365).
Melchior of Herborn ingeniously showed Transsubstantiation credible only by Enthusiasm (Opera Theol. 2, pp. 467–840).
Stop before (3) Praxis Christiana (first table / latria; cup withheld).

title: Annotatio III §.X (3)(a): Praxis Christiana — first table; latria of what every sense calls bread and wine
english: (3)(a) Christian praxis vs the first table: religious worship of the Triune God.

In the Mass what every sense calls bread and wine (accidents showing and composing the thing) is believed and preached as the highest God, and commanded to communicants and bystanders under latria — the cult Pontificians themselves wall off from every lesser cult.

title: Annotatio III §.X (3)(a) cont.: Highest idolatry species — even without their Transsubstantiation hypothesis; God’s definition, not ours
english: That is the highest species of idolatry — which even Pontificians never deny if Transsubstantiation is not supposed, and must not deny without that hypothesis.

They cannot make their hypothesis certain by Revelation or Reason; and idolatry turns on God’s definition, not on whether a human opinion is true or false — whenever what is not the highest God is estimated, saluted, or given highest cult as if it were.

title: Annotatio III §.X (3)(b): Instituted praxis — cup as well as bread; Mass/Transsubstantiation snatches the cup from the laity
english: (3)(b) Instituted praxis from Christ binds every communicant to the cup and wine no less than to the bread.
Mass and Transsubstantiation’s rationale snatch that cup from all the laity — so it also hits the second table, withdrawing from the neighbor what Christ ordered by ‘Do this.’

title: Annotatio III §.X (4): Faith of the first centuries — if they taught Transsubstantiation, Jews and Gentiles would have hissed at once
english: (4) Faith and praxis of the first centuries: if the earliest Christians had professed Transsubstantiation, none then mistook ‘This is my body / blood.’
That dogma’s rumor would have flown at once to neighboring Jews and Gentiles and met not only contradiction but every hiss — from such fervent mystery-defenders it could not have stayed quiet.

title: Annotatio III §.X (4) cont.: No such sneer in Trypho/Celsus/Julian/Porphyry — nor in Justin, Tertullian, Origen, Arnobius, Minucius
english: Yet we nowhere read that even once from the fiercest enemies — Trypho, Celsus, Julian, Porphyry — who hunted every handle to calumniate Christian dogmas.
Nor from the careful apologists Justin, Tertullian, Origen, Arnobius, Minucius Felix.

title: Annotatio III §.X (4) close: Thyestean charges hit Gnostics only; ancients lack Adoration/Elevations/Circumgestations; stop before (5)
english: Thyestean banquet charges stuck to Gnostics alone (maliciously counted as Christians); true Christians never even mentioned the Eucharist there, much less explained or defended this mystery — mere calumny, exploded.
And the ancients’ constant lack of later Transsubstantiation-rites (Adoration, Elevation, Circumgestation) amply shows they utterly ignored Transsubstantiation.
Stop before (5) Natura Sacramentorum.

title: Annotatio III §.X (5): Natura Sacramentorum — at least a triple assault on sacrament-nature
english: (5) Transsubstantiation assaults the Nature of the Sacraments under at least three heads.
Strimesius marks the assault as at minimum triple — three named wounds to what a sacrament is.

title: Annotatio III §.X (5)(1)–(2): Removes the material Sign; turns Signatum into the Sacrament of Signatum itself
english: (1) It removes the material Sign — bread and wine — leaving only accidents, void of substantiality and (on their view) of materiality too.
(2) It turns the Signatum (Christ’s body and blood) into the sacrament of that Signatum itself — sign and thing collapse.

title: Annotatio III §.X (5)(3): Eliminates the sacramental proposition — bread gone when the priest says Hoc est Corpus meum
english: (3) By the priest’s pronunciation it kills the sacramental proposition.
Bread no longer survives while he finishes of bread: ‘This, or this bread, is My Body.’

title: Annotatio III §.X (6): Ratio / Philosophy theoretical — overturns substance, accident, spirit, body, place, penetration
english: (6) Cleaner Reason / Philosophy — theoretical first.

It overturns essential ideas of substance and accident, spirit and body, penetrability, extension, locality: strips finite substance of essential accidents, frees accidents from inherence, spirits Christ’s body by denying extension, impenetrability, and place — which even omnipotence will not admit as contradictories via miracle.

title: Annotatio III §.X (6) cont.: Admits sign-accidents that must enter the substances; practical enmity — oral God-eating (Cicero / Averroes)
english: It also admits bread/wine species that must enter those substances (bread’s quantity not really other than the bread; wine’s motion in the cup unfit for bare accidents, yet seen in exhalable particles that shrink the wine-mass).

Practical philosophy too: it butts natural piety — oral God-eating. Cicero: who is mad enough to think what he eats is God? Averroes: no worse race than Christians, who devour with teeth the God they adore (Hottinger pp. 214ff).

title: Annotatio III §.X (6) close: Natural humanity — corporal chewing of Christ’s flesh vs Lev. blood ban; stop before §.XI (7) Sense
english: It also butts natural common humanity: commanding Christ’s human flesh chewed and His blood drunk with the corporal mouth — acts unfallen human nature spontaneously abhors.
God once expressly barred the Jewish people from all animal blood (Lev. 7:27; 17:14) so that abhorrence would be the surer.
Stop before §.XI (7) Sense.

title: Annotatio III §.XI open (7): Sense — bread and wine not annihilated; body and blood not corporally substituted
english: §.XI (7): cleaner Sense — not one only but several.

Sight, touch, taste, and smell distinctly prove bread and wine are not annihilated in the Eucharist, nor Christ’s body and blood corporally put in their place; their joint distinct testimony is not to be doubted.

title: Annotatio III §.XI (7): Scripture backs multi-sense testimony — reading/hearing; Reason’s empire over senses
english: Revealed Scripture itself backs that: (1) it trusts itself to our senses in reading and hearing — rash if senses deserve no faith.
(2) it gives Reason empire over the senses within limits — pointless if sense-acts are fallible.

title: Annotatio III §.XI (7) cont.: Christ and John appeal to sense (Luke 24:39; 1 John 1:1) — many senses surer than one
english: (3) Christ and John appeal to sense to confirm truth: Luke 24:39 (handle me; a spirit has not flesh and bones); 1 John 1:1 (that which was from the beginning).
If one well-constituted sense deserves faith, how much more several conspiring species — all men trust many senses more than one.

title: Annotatio III §.XI (8): Nomenclature — ‘Transsubstantiation’ misfits; nearer annihilation of one substance and creation of another
english: (8) By its own name: it wants ‘Transsubstantiation’ = conversion of substance into substance.
But if nothing of bread and wine remains, the truer name is annihilation of one substance and creation of another — not Transsubstantiation.

title: Annotatio III §.XI (8) cont.: Wren — bread-substance flees at Hoc est corpus meum, leaving accidents behind
english: Wren (Increpatio Bar Jesu / Racovian Catechism refutation p. 342), on those who alone know these ‘depths’: bread-substance did not pass into body-substance.

Terrified at ‘This is my body,’ it vanished so fast it dared not even pack its accidents and drag the poor species along — still less did divine-body substance pass into that vanished bread-substance.

title: Annotatio III §.XI close: Translocation / Transfiguration, not Transsubstantiation — ask for Vicesubstantiation; stop before Annotatio IV
english: So where is the Trans? This is translocation (body from heaven into bread’s place) and transfiguration (holy body under the fugitive bread’s leftover figure) — not Transsubstantiation.
Ask the Roman correctors to fix Autun’s misnomer: if error must breed error, start from another letter and call it Vicesubstantiation.
Stop before Annotatio IV (true Eucharistic sentence through the ages).

title: Annotatio IV open: De Vera circa Eucharistiam S. Sententia through all Christian ages to this day
english: ANNOTATIO IV opens: On the True Sentence concerning the Sacred Eucharist.
It is the sentence taught through every age of the Christian era down to this day (Autor p. 37).

title: Annotatio IV §.I open: History of the true Eucharistic sentence — foundation in Institution words
english: §.I: we now briefly write the history of that true Eucharistic sentence.
Its beginning and foundation sit in the Institution words themselves — This is my body, This is my blood — placed there by Christ.

title: Annotatio IV §.I: Institution propositions include a trope — not one that eliminates body and blood
english: Those words (bread taken, blessed, broken, given; cup blessed and offered) do include a trope as full propositions — Annotatio I’s reasons; even Lutherans must admit it, a few explicitly, all implicitly.
But no Orthodox — Lutheran or Reformed — will say the trope is the kind that eliminates Christ’s body and blood from the Sacred Supper.

title: Annotatio IV §.I: Soul of the orthodox sentence — true real presence and participation of body and blood
english: The soul of the true, genuine, orthodox Supper sentence is this:
Christ’s Body and Blood are truly and really present in the Eucharist — properly, not by bare figure — and are participated in by all who use the Supper per Christ’s Institution.

title: Annotatio IV §.I cont.: Cosinus opens papal Transsubstantiation history with infallible Institution words
english: Cosinus (Most Reverend) rightly opens his History of papal Transsubstantiation with the Institution words: This is my body given for you; This is my blood poured out for you — the whole Church confesses them infallible and most true.
Anyone who twists them into a fiction and bare figure, denying Christ’s truthfulness, we neither can nor ought to tolerate or excuse in our churches.

title: Annotatio IV §.I close: Scripture true — Caro mea / Paul communion; stop before §.II (John 6 & Paul on mode)
english: Whatever Holy Scripture teaches must be true and undoubted for us — so also Christ’s My flesh is truly food and my blood drink, communicated through bread and cup per Paul.
Paul called the bread the communion of Christ’s body and the cup the cup of His blood.
Stop before §.II (John 6 and Paul as the mode-commentaries on Institution).

title: Annotatio IV §.II open: Cosinus mentions John 6 and Paul as mode-commentaries
english: §.II: Cosinus (Most Learned Bishop) aptly brings in two discourses here.
John 6 — eating Christ’s flesh and drinking His blood; and Paul — communion of Eucharistic bread and cup with Christ’s body and blood.
